title: How to follow Singapore Grand Prix on the BBC
description: All the key BBC coverage details for the Singapore Grand Prix, the sixth and final sprint event of the season, which takes place from 9-11 October.
fullText:
Round 17 of the 2026 Formula 1 season heads to the Marina Bay Street Circuit for the Singapore Grand Prix, from 9-11 October.

The weekend is also the sixth and final sprint event of the campaign.

Red Bull's Max Verstappen won the sprint after George Russell crashed out at the end of the first lap in the wet.

There were nine retirees in total - a record number of DNFs in a sprint race.

Heavy rain caused a delay to the start of the sprint, meaning that qualifying will start 30 minutes later than scheduled at 14:30 BST.

Sunday's 62-lap grand prix, which takes place at night in Singapore, begins at 13:00.

Verstappen wins sprint after Russell crashes out

Commentary of the race will be available across 5 Sports Extra, BBC Sounds and the BBC Sport website and app.

You can also ask your smart speaker to "play 5 Sports Extra".

Make sure to listen to every episode of the Chequered Flag podcast. For the first time this year, the post-race show for every grand prix is available to watch on BBC iPlayer and YouTube.

Qualifying: 14:30-15:30 - 5 Sports Extra

Race: 13:00 with build-up from 12:45 - 5 Sports Extra

The weekend has been declared a heat-hazard event for the second race in a row. A heat hazard is an official status for an event where it is forecast that temperatures will exceed 31C at some point during the race.

Qualifying and Sunday's grand prix, which starts at 8pm local time, are forecast for thundery showers during the day, but conditions should dry out before the night-time action takes place.

Temperatures at Marina Bay should reach highs of 32C.

title: What could Rangers' 2012 case tell us about Man City's uncertain future?
description: From sanctions and stripped titles to starting from scratch, BBC Scotland explains how potential consequences for Manchester City compare with the financial collapse of Rangers in 2012.
fullText:
In the wake of Manchester City's unprecedented guilty verdict, the scramble to source similar situations to help shed light on what could come next continues.

But finding a direct comparison has been a struggle because of that very word: unprecedented.

Some have attempted to draw parallels with the demise of Rangers in 2012 as an ominous, dark cloud of uncertainty hangs over the Premier League leaders.

From sanctions and stripped titles to starting from scratch, BBC Scotland explains how potential consequences for City compare with the financial collapse of the Ibrox club and which led to a giant of the British game being dumped at the bottom of the Scottish football ladder.

Clubs fear political interference in Man City appeal

Rangers boss McInnes 'not a fan' of extended break

What Guardiola said about Man City charges

It's a long story that, at this stage, doesn't really compare a whole lot to City's.

Rangers' case ultimately became an insolvency event after the club racked up huge tax liabilities. The Employee Benefit Trust (EBT) scheme was a major part of that.

Under former owner Sir David Murray, Rangers paid money into EBTs for employees - including players, managers and directors - for about a decade at the turn of the millennium.

In total, more than £47m came out of the trusts to more than 80 individuals. HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) argued the payments should have been taxed as earnings and therefore that Rangers owed substantial sums.

After lengthy court and tribunal proceedings, the Supreme Court definitively ruled in favour of HMRC in its fight with Rangers over the use of EBTs. That came five years after the old company's liquidation.

City, meanwhile, have been found to have arranged "sham contracts" with a number of commercial partners as part of a scheme to disguise more than £830m of funding, according to the Premier League.

The Manchester club have been found guilty of all charges related to serious breaches of the league's financial rules between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons. City have appealed against the verdict and deny any wrongdoing.

With the threat of serious sanctions hanging over City, we wait to find out what comes next.

In Rangers' case, entering administration in February of the 2011-12 season meant a 10-point deduction was triggered. They finished the campaign in second, 20 points behind champions Celtic.

No further penalties were applied, with liquidation ensuing in June 2012.

Rangers were also never stripped of any honours they won during the years they used EBTs, which were ruled to have not gained them "any unfair competitive advantage".

Where things get a bit fiddly, confusing and the source of debate among fans, is the distinction between Rangers the club and Rangers the company.

Following the liquidation, the football assets - including Ibrox, the training ground, name and brand - were acquired by a new company led by Charles Green.

Despite the team continuing to play at Ibrox with the same colours and badge, jibes about Rangers not being the same club are heard from opposing fans at every match.

After Green bought the assets, a vote took place to decide whether Rangers could remain in the top tier. Ten of the 12 top-flight clubs voted against the application, with Kilmarnock abstaining and Rangers voting in favour.

Rangers then had to apply to play in the lower leagues, which at the time were governed by the Scottish Football League, a body separate from the top flight, then called the Scottish Premier League.

This shares similarities with the current set-up in England, with the Premier League separate from the English Football League, which governs the Championship, League One and League Two.

Premier League expulsion has been hypothetically discussed as a potential sanction for City. That could mean they then have to apply to be accepted into the EFL, just as Rangers did with the old SFL.

The Scottish FA recommended Rangers enter the second tier, but that was rejected by the majority of SFL clubs, with 25 of the 30 voting for Rangers to enter the fourth tier instead.

There were fears that without Rangers in the top flight, TV deals would be under threat without Old Firm derbies, putting clubs at financial risk.

Neil Doncaster, the league's chief executive, initially described the reduction in broadcast income as "slight" but acknowledged "there will be money coming out the game as a result of Rangers not being in the top flight".

So what would the loss of Manchester derbies do to the Premier League's?

Then manager Ally McCoist continued in his post following Rangers' demotion and led the team through the fourth and third tiers with relative ease.

The Ibrox icon recently described the 2012 ordeal as an "absolutely horrendous" situation because of the job losses that occurred.

"You're not talking about your centre-forward or centre-back," he said on Talksport. "I had one of the older lads in tears, not a player, just someone who had a wee job, because he was losing his job. It was heartbreaking."

On the pitch, however, McCoist recalled a bizarre but "unbelievable" journey through the lower leagues, hailing the commitment of the fanbase.

"I'll never forget one of the opening games," he added. "We played Brechin and the game got delayed because the ball got stuck on the top of a hedge."

The former striker also said he was dragged off the team bus by the Peterhead chairman to speak to fans in a marquee and did the half-time draw in a social club before his side faced Annan Athletic.

McCoist left midway through Rangers' first Championship season, which ended with them being denied a third straight promotion when they were beaten 6-1 on aggregate by Motherwell in the play-off final.

Mark Warburton arrived in the summer of 2015 and was the man to guide Rangers back to the Premiership.

Just one league title, delivered under Steven Gerrard in 2020-21, has come in the following decade.

Attempting to translate how that would look for City is a challenge given the difference in financial disparity between England and Scotland.

Even in the fourth tier, the budget Rangers were operating with still allowed them to attract some of the Premiership's top talent. That continued throughout their rise through the divisions.

It would be difficult to picture City enticing Premier League players to join them in the event of a severe demotion. And that is before you consider their squad being ripped apart.

Due to the nature of Rangers' plight, they lost a host of integral players without being able to recoup a penny.

The likes of Steven Davis, Steven Naismith and Allan McGregor were among those to lodge objections to a transfer to the 'newco'.

For City, they would at least be able to bring in cash for departing stars, permitting any potential contract clauses.

City fan Matt Mellor joked he "can't wait to see Erling Haaland bag a hat-trick against Grimsby" in League Two next season. McCoist isn't convinced.

"When you go down there, you're effectively starting from scratch, because the players won't stay," the Rangers great said.

"If you're talking about Manchester City, you're starting again. You're officially starting again."

title: What to do with Joao Pedro? FPL gameweek six dilemmas
description: BBC Sport's Fantasy Premier League expert FPL Pras gives his answers to some of the biggest dilemmas facing managers in gameweek six.
fullText:
BBC Sport's Fantasy Premier League expert Pras gives his answers to some of the biggest dilemmas facing managers heading into gameweek six.

Despite being the most sold player of the international break, Chelsea forward Pedro is still owned by about 65% of FPL managers. From a points-per-million point of view he remains one of the best picks in the game, and Chelsea's fixture run is excellent for a long stretch. Unless manager Xabi Alonso rules him out completely, I would hold and use the bench.

This is a tough week for captaincy. Erling Haaland is away at Liverpool. Cole Palmer is home to Bournemouth. Bukayo Saka has the Saturday lunchtime kick-off at home to Leeds. Bruno Fernandes is at home to Spurs.

Fernandes has the best fixture and the best chance of a big score, but not many own him. Of the rest, you can talk me into any of them. I am leaning safe and sticking with Haaland. Even in a tougher game, if Man City score he should be the one involved.

If I wanted to be different, I would look at Saka or Palmer, both at home. What puts me off Saka is the possible Havertz injury that will impact their attack, plus an early kick-off straight after a long break. What puts me off Palmer is Joao Pedro. If he is not fit, the Chelsea attack suffers, as we saw in gameweek five against Brentford.

For a new buy, yes. The Arsenal defender has a slight niggle from the England camp. Cristhian Mosquera is fit, and William Saliba is on the mend as well, albeit with an unclear timescale for his return. I would not sell him if I already owned him though - he still represents excellent value.

On a wildcard, or with a free transfer though, there are better defenders in the £5m price bracket, in my opinion.

Fulham play all three promoted sides in the next three games. Gonzalo Garcia at £6m is the one I like. He may be on penalties, and the underlying numbers have been better than the FPL returns suggest. Josh King is the other option. His data (0.44 xGI) is strong and the minutes have been good with 90 minutes in three of the first five games.

Not an urgent sell, although there are concerns there from an FPL point of view with his role.

Under Andoni Iraola he is playing as an eight, not as a 10, and not at right-back. That is the worst of the three for route to points. No real attacking threat from the 10 spot, no defensive contribution from full-back. What is left is set pieces and the odd shot from outside the box. I would not rush him out though.

Close to it, at the price. The Brighton midfielder is still under £6m, he plays 90 minutes, and 47 points already explains why he is the most-transferred player this week.

Ownership is about 30%. Sunderland away, then Crystal Palace at home, is a decent run of fixtures. He is just an easy set-and-forget midfielder who keeps playing 90 minutes and keeps trickling points in.

title: 'You can be a mum and a footballer - they can co-exist'
description: Northern Ireland striker Simone Magill tells BBC Sport NI about balancing motherhood with her return to football and how her life has changed since giving birth to daughter Skye earlier this year.
fullText:
"Football will always be a large part of my life but it's very much what I do, not who I am.

"Ultimately, I'm Skye's mum and, to me, that's the most important thing."

Through her 16-year footballing career, Simone Magill has been something of a trailblazer in Northern Ireland.

From a senior debut at the age of 15, helping the country to a major tournament debut and becoming captain, she has been there and seen it all.

But after giving birth to her first child, Skye, in May, her focus is paving the way off the pitch, as well as on it.

"I think we get labelled as athletes, and that is our complete entire identity," Birmingham City striker Magill told BBC Sport.

"Obviously there's been a massive shift now. I'm a mum first and foremost and that is the highest title that I will ever have.

"Family is so important. It's my priority, and it's so nice for me to have that greater purpose now.

"It's hard and it can be overwhelming, but it's the greatest joy that I've ever experienced in my life."

Family, football and Dalglish - what drives NI boss McArdle?

'Nothing impossible' as NI begin long road to Brazil

Magill is speaking at the Northern Ireland camp in the lead up to Friday's World Cup play-off with Portugal.

While she is stepping up her training four months on from giving birth, the first round of play-offs have come too soon.

However, after conversations with manager Michael McArdle, who has spoken about the importance of family, the 31-year-old is in camp to train with the squad.

More importantly, Skye and her husband, Mark, are with her for the duration.

It is a glimpse into what the future will look like when Magill is back playing for Northern Ireland.

"It's so different, but it's so special. I'm really enjoying being back in, and I think I find it weirder having my husband here than having Skye," she said.

"It's just amazing that I'm able to do this and the support that I've been given to allow me to do this has made things so much easier."

After nearly a year away from the squad, from when she announced her pregnancy last November, she says the support that the Irish FA and her Northern Ireland team-mates have provided has meant "I don't need to worry about anything".

Skye and Mark have become fully integrated in the camp and join the team for meals and in downtime.

Then, when it comes to on-pitch matters and meetings, Mark is able to look after Skye and Magill can focus on the football side of things.

"Mark has his daddy-daughter days with her while I'm on the training pitch.

"Then when I'm here with the girls in and around the hotel and free times, we're all here mingling with Skye.

"She's now got 23 aunties who are all very hands-on."

Before camp, Magill admits there was a bit of apprehension about how integrating back into the group with Skye may look, but "I feel a sense of obligation to pave the way".

While she is not the first Northern Ireland player to have a child and return to playing - experienced defender Sarah McFadden gave birth to her second child in 2024 - Magill is the first to have the family integrated into the camp.

"So it's the unknown of what things are going to look like," she said.

"It's relatively new in the game and I suppose I'm one of the first people certainly here and at club as well to do this.

"There are going to be certain things that we might need a little bit more support with, but we don't know that until we go through each phase and we're navigating that all collaboratively."

Magill feels that having Skye with the group is "lovely for the mood" and "gets everyone involved" as the new arrival is the most popular member of the camp.

She added that having Skye and Mark in camp has been "game-changing", and pointed to how a new mother in a more traditional job would have a year off, while her career means she is looking to get back on the pitch as quick as possible.

"If I didn't have that support then it almost questions, 'can I still play football if I can't bring her?'

"But it means that I can fully focus on being a footballer, but equally put everything into still being a mum at the same time."

While Skye has yet to be given a club team to support - Magill has played for Everton and Aston Villa before joining Birmingham and Mark supports Manchester United - there is no debate surrounding her international allegiance.

Despite Mark being from England, Skye has already been decked out in a mini-Northern Ireland kit.

"It's so important for me that she can come back to Northern Ireland often and just be surrounded by Northern Irish accents, to show her where I've come from and my roots. It's really special."

Magill said that she and Mark, who got married in 2021 after meeting at university, had always wanted to start a family and "we almost had to remove football from that decision".

While she stopped playing matches when she found out she was expecting, she was still active in training and the gym right up to a few weeks before Skye was born.

Just four weeks after her arrival, Magill was back doing gym work and she was back on the pitch after 13 weeks.

Now fully training again, she hopes to be back playing matches later in the autumn.

"It's funny because when I announced my pregnancy, I think the natural assumption from a lot of people in the scope of wider things thought that that was probably going to be the end of my football career.

"But I was like, 'well, no, absolutely not'.

"I very much wanted to be a voice and showcase that you can be a mum and a footballer, and those things can both co-exist."

Magill has spent longer away from playing matches than when she sustained an ACL injury at Euro 2022, but the stresses of rehab are absent.

For Magill, Skye has given her a new drive and purpose. Only five games away from a century of international caps, she dreams of walking out onto the pitch with her in her arms.

"Skye will not necessarily remember any of this, but I will.

"When she's older she can look back and see the hard work that I put in to come back and play, and it was all for her.

"All throughout my pregnancy I was almost manifesting that moment that when I make my return and being able to carry her out onto the pitch, I think, you know, that's what's driving me."

Magill said that McFadden was a role model for her when it came to balancing family and football, and now she wants to inspire other players to take the same step.

"We have a lot of younger members in the squad now and hopefully it is a very normal thing for them to see that this can be done.

"You know that there's a player playing for the team that has a child and she's able to bring the child in.

"That's very important to be normalised now in our sport and I'm just so thankful that the support systems are in place to allow me to do this.

"I've always wanted to inspire people on the pitch, but hopefully this is something I've done off the pitch that could also inspire future generations to show that it's possible."

title: Maresca will be demanding a siege mentality from Man City - Pulis
description: BBC Sport columnist Tony Pulis explains why Manchester City players have a great chance to show unity and togetherness when they travel to Anfield on Sunday.
fullText:
If I was manager of Manchester City now, after they were found guilty of breaking Premier League financial rules, my whole psychology with my group of players this week would encompass one major point:

"No-one is going to like us, but we won't care."

I loved being the underdog and I loved to prove people wrong, and that is what I would demand now - a siege mentality from my squad and supporters alike to prove to people that, irrespective of what is happening off the pitch, on the field and the terraces we respect our club and we are going to fight on.

City will be vilified by everyone else but their players have a great opportunity to show unity and togetherness, starting on Sunday away to Liverpool.

When the Premier League returns this weekend, the spotlight will be on one game in particular - at Anfield.

As well as preparing for such a huge match, City's players will be arriving back from international duty and going straight into an off-field fight that has turned into a media frenzy.

The allegations seem relentless with finger-pointing from every Tom, Dick and Harry jumping on the bandwagon in hammering a club that has dominated the Premier League for over a decade.

It feels like every positive gained by City over the period in question and beyond has been smashed into oblivion. Yet, despite all of the above, the club have remained firm in denying all charges.

So, where does this leave Enzo Maresca and his City players as they prepare to take on Liverpool?

Firstly, although they themselves have not been involved in any of the allegations about the club breaking the Premier League's financial rules, they must understand that supporters at all away grounds will be baying for their blood.

City have become a team that, whenever they play, will provide an opportunity for all critics to attack them, and from all angles - including the frenzied media outlets.

So, as the manager, Maresca must first act to reassure his players that the club is not in any way going to take a step back from defending their own position, and also the position of the players, staff and supporters.

Once that is established, I would then expect every player to concentrate on what they are being paid for, which is to win games.

There should be no distractions or any questions that do not relate to the games they are involved in. No excuses about what is happening off the field would be tolerated, and that would be my final word on the matter.

If the verdict about City breaking the Premier League's financial rules is upheld, it will come at a heavy cost to the club and its reputation.

I feel there needs to be more attention paid to all of these rules, and their fairness, because professional football at the top level is now dominated by massive financial investment.

Even if you just consider player transfers, it's not unusual for around a billion pounds to be exchanged between clubs in England and around the world during each transfer window.

While individual players at the top level are being bought and sold for more than £100m, smaller academies are being plundered by the bigger clubs.

They can hoover up the best young players for much smaller 'compensation' fees, enabling them to polish them up and sell them on later for much more - without any Financial Fair Play rules to regulate how much they profit.

That's one way of dealing with FFP, I suppose, but is it for the good of the game, or the players involved?

Over many years of Premier League governance, clubs have broken the FFP rules that are in place. Some have not been caught yet, I'm sure, but others have and have been punished. It keeps happening, so are the current rules right?

Do we need to try to change them or are we taking a bigger risk by leading clubs to find different ways - or loopholes - to try to break the financial shackles that are currently in place?

The money in our game today is extraordinary and today massive corporations, billionaires and even countries are buying our clubs and want to invest more and more into the product but are not able to.

Gone are the days of local business owners buying their local clubs.

In the Premier League, Tony Bloom at Brighton and Matthew Benham at Brentford are the last men standing and, in the Championship, the Coates family at Stoke City and Steve Gibson at Middlesbrough are among the few to have had a taste of the top flight.

I always see the top clubs having the power financially to remain at the top but it's important there is a way for the smart guys - people like those I named above - at clubs without the big bucks or big histories, to play a leading role in the top league in world football.

At the moment all the negative media attention is on what Manchester City have done wrong but the likes of Brighton, Bournemouth and Brentford have achieved success by being smart, without the 'big club' tag.

It's great to see, but surely the rules need to reward all clubs for being smart. Doing the right thing should give everyone the chance to compete at the highest level.

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

title: Sutton's predictions v Starsailor frontman James Walsh
description: BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton takes on Starsailor frontman James Walsh, plus the BBC readers and AI with his predictions for this weekend's Premier League fixtures.
fullText:
All eyes will be on Anfield on Sunday to see how Premier League leaders Manchester City react after being found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they have been accused of breaching.

"It's a mammoth game," said BBC Sport football expert Chris Sutton.

"Everyone is looking at this game to see if City's players appear deflated and how much it will affect them.

"We don't know what the implications are for this season, either. They are top of the league at the moment but will they get a massive points deduction that changes that?"

Sutton is making predictions for all 380 Premier League games this season, against AI, BBC Sport readers and a variety of guests.

For week six, he takes on Starsailor frontman James Walsh, who supports Liverpool.

Starsailor have released a 25th anniversary edition of their debut album, Love is Here, this week and are playing it in full, with a string ensemble, on their UK and European tour this month.

Do you agree with their predictions? You can pick your own below.

The most popular scoreline selected for each game is used in the scoreboards and tables at the bottom of this page.

A correct result (picking a win, draw or defeat) is worth 10 points. The exact score earns 40 points.

Want to make more predictions? You can play BBC Sport's new Match of the Day predictor game every week, featuring six fixtures from domestic and European competitions.

When Love is Here was released, Liverpool had just completed an unprecedented treble of FA Cup, League Cup and Uefa Cup.

They are not holders of any trophies at the moment, but James is optimistic about winning some silverware under new manager Andoni Iraola.

"You have to be realistic whenever a new manager comes in, especially with the big signings we made last year, Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz, not hitting the ground running," he told BBC Sport.

"I think just give him a chance to implement his way of playing football and give Isak and Wirtz a chance to prove themselves this season.

"I don't see us winning the title but I'd be more than happy with the FA Cup or even the Carabao Cup, and having a good run in Europe.

"It's a bit greedy but of course you do like to see your team win something every season. Three more trophies like in 2001 would be pretty good!"

Chris Sutton and James Walsh were speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The AI predictions were generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to 'predict this weekend's Premier League scores'.

Brighton were brilliant when they beat Arsenal before the international break - the Seagulls really harried and hassled the champions and went toe-to-toe with them.

I don't think Leeds will go about things the same way, but they will still provide a stern test.

Daniel Farke's side are really solid but also carry a big threat too, and they are a very different proposition to the side Arsenal thumped 5-0 at Emirates Stadium at the start of last season.

So, this game will tell us a lot about where Arsenal are and how they have recovered from that Brighton defeat.

I'd still back the Gunners to find a way to win, especially because they are at home, but it will be a lot closer than last time. Leeds don't concede goals as freely any more.

James' prediction: Arsenal have just had a bit of a wobble and you wonder if it was just an anomaly, because Brighton have had quite a few scalps, or if it is going to be a slightly more difficult season for them this year.

I guess we will start to find out here but I've been impressed by how resilient Leeds have been, to stay unbeaten, so I have made this my outlier prediction to give them some credit for their start. They will probably get thumped now but someone has to give them a chance. 1-1

Brentford were one of the teams who definitely didn't want the international break, while I feel like it might have done Aston Villa the world of good.

They have made very different starts to the new season - Brentford are still unbeaten and, while I kept on predicting Villa would win, the only time I was right was when they beat Tottenham last time out.

Despite the difference in their form, I am going to stick with Villa here, even though the Bees have been seriously impressive so far.

Johan Manzambi is fit again and seems to have found his best form while playing for Switzerland. He could make the difference here too.

James' prediction: Villa have lost some key players but I still expect them to get it together at some stage and maybe this is the game, against a Brentford team in really good form. 2-1

Bournemouth have not won yet under Marco Rose, and they are also without key midfielder Alex Scott for a while as a result of his injury on international duty.

I feel like the Cherries have been a bit unlucky with their results under Rose so far, because they have conceded some costly late goals, but Scott's absence is a huge blow for them.

Chelsea are already turning into a team that are a nightmare to predict - defensively they have got huge issues, but they have got such a talented attack.

Some people thought they would be up there challenging for the title but they look far too inconsistent to do that.

Anything could happen in this game and I was tempted to say Bournemouth will get something out of it.

But Cole Palmer will be rested and refreshed after his injury so I am going to base my prediction on how I expect Chelsea's frontline to click.

James' prediction: I don't see Bournemouth getting anything here. 2-0

Ipswich lost last time out, against Everton, but they gave it a real go even when they went down to 10 men midway through the second half.

I know I keep predicting the Tractor Boys to lose but it's not a case of me just doing them over every week - I actually hope they stay up.

This is a tough game for them, however, because while Fulham are winless so far, they have deserved more than they have got.

The Cottagers were unlucky not to beat Manchester United before the break, and I was impressed with them when I watched them draw with Liverpool last month too.

Three points would be huge for either team, but I can see this ending up as a draw.

James' prediction: Fulham have been a bit unlucky with their results so far but I can see them getting chances against Ipswich. 1-2

I'd usually back Sunderland at home but Brighton are playing some brilliant football and they must be full of confidence.

The Seagulls sneaked a win at the Stadium of Light last season and this will be just as close - but this time the points will be shared.

James' prediction: Both teams play some great attacking football and I can't pick a winner. Brighton have made an amazing start to the season but if Sunderland show that never-say-die spirit they had against Manchester City, they will get something. 2-2

A win would be big for Manchester United boss Michael Carrick after their shaky start to the season but the implications for his future would be bigger if his side lose.

Everything tells me that Carrick's side should probably take the three points because Tottenham are so flaky at the moment, but I am just not sure about United either.

Spurs are bottom of the table for a reason - they have been terrible so far - but United got away with one in their draw against Fulham before the break.

I am not sure much will have changed for either team since then, so it is hard to make a case for anyone to win this, but I am going with Bruno Fernandes to settle it with a bit of magic.

James' prediction: This is a high-pressure fixture for both teams but, being at home, United should edge it, and give their fans a bit of respite. That will put the heat on Roberto de Zerbi rather than Carrick.

Unlike some of the other teams I've already mentioned - where you can see what they are trying to do and that it will click eventually - it feels like Spurs are not as close to getting it together. I've got a lot of friends who are Spurs fans and I hope for their sake that they get better soon, but this feels like a game too early for them. 1-0

Crystal Palace have started slowly under Pierre Sage but he is not the only new manager who has not really settled in yet.

Nottingham Forest lost at home to Coventry last time out, and they have been a bit up and down under Oliver Glasner so far.

But I'm expecting Glasner to get a decent reception on his return to his old club, and I have a feeling he will take home the three points too.

James' prediction: Palace will win this one, and there will be a few goals too. 3-2

Hull's unbeaten start ended at Newcastle last time out but even then they almost snatched a point after going 2-0 down early on.

The Tigers deserved something from the game for the way they finished it - I had gone for them to get a draw with my prediction and I should have been right.

This game smells of a really obvious 1-1 draw to me too.

A win would be massive for Hull's confidence, as well as their hopes of staying up, but Everton already look like they are just going to grind through the season and I don't see them losing this.

James' prediction: A lot of Everton fans I know seem to be feeling cautiously optimistic after the way they have started the season. As good as Hull have been, I can see Everton's good form continuing. 1-2

I've heard people suggest that City's players will be frazzled because of what is going on with the club off the pitch, but I don't see it that way.

I suspect that, along with the City fans, there will be this siege mentality now where they think 'everyone hates us, everyone wants us to lose, everyone wants us to be relegated' - even if I don't think that is actually the case, because there are actually a lot of balanced football fans out there.

City are likely to get a hostile reception at Anfield but I think they will be able to handle it.

Liverpool are still a work in progress under Andoni Iraola too. They have not convinced me so far when I've watched them this season.

Based on all of that, I am going for City here. I can just picture Erling Haaland scoring their winner, and celebrating with a big grin on his face.

James on what should happen after City were found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges brought against them by the Premier League: I am not sure we should start handing out titles and cups to everyone who lost out to City during the period in question, including Liverpool. You can't really take away those memories and emotional moments from the City players and fans, and just hand them to another team, but maybe on the official record those wins should be chalked off, or at least have an asterisk next to them.

It does also mean there is a very strange feeling around this fixture and the whole season too. City and Liverpool have had lots of huge games against each other in recent years when the title has been on the line but this time we don't know what will happen to City and if this result will even matter in the end.

James' prediction: This is a strange game for Liverpool because if we win then the narrative is going to be that we have beaten the cheats. If we lose, then people are just going to say well City have had this massive and unfair advantage that has played out over all these years, not just that specific period of their charges.

So, it is going to be a hard one for all 22 players to get their heads around the backdrop and compete against each other - but I still think Liverpool will win. 3-1

Coventry Building Society Arena, 20:00

Newcastle are an exciting watch with the way they set about games and have so much pace in their team, but I don't think they have much control of matches.

This feels like a great opportunity for Coventry to follow up their first win of the season with another positive result.

Beating Nottingham Forest last time out was such a massive result for the Sky Blues - but can they back it up with another victory?

I am not sure they will. A draw feels like the obvious result to me.

James' prediction: I have got a lot of friends who are very passionate Coventry fans and it is great to see them back in the Premier League as they were when I was growing up - I always associate Steve Ogrizovic with them because he played for them for so long back then.

I know a lot of Newcastle fans too, and they are just as passionate about their club. I would definitely hear from someone if I write either team off, so I think I'll go for a draw to keep everyone happy. 2-2

It seems like a very long time ago, but before the international break Chris got four correct results with one exact score from the 10 games in week five, giving him a total of 70 points.

That was enough to beat AI - which managed five correct results with no exact scores for a tally of 50 points - and also the collective efforts of the BBC readers, who got three correct results with one exact score, and ended up on 60 points.

But the weekly win went to his guest, legendary guitarist Johnny Marr, thanks to his exact score in the final game of that weekend, Fulham's 1-1 draw with Manchester United.

That meant Marr ended up with five correct results and one exact score, which gave him 80 points and sent the guests to the top of the BBC predictions table.

It was another tough week for predictions, with only two games where everyone picked the right outcome - Everton's victory over Ipswich and Manchester City's win against Sunderland.

title: Christa Pike walking for the 1st time after failed execution, lawyer says
description:
Christa Pike is "up and walking" in the hospital after surviving last week's failed attempt to execute her in Tennessee, a member of her legal team said Thursday.
Lawyer Stephen Ferrell told the BBC that he had learned she was moving around her hospital room, although he had not spoken to her.
"What's been described to me is that physically there's quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she's not able to use them very much,” he said. “She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far."
Ferrell described her mental state as "kind of good and bad," adding, "Good that she is fairly with it, but she's also somewhat foggy.
fullText:
Christa Pike is "up and walking" in the hospital after surviving last week's failed attempt to execute her in Tennessee, a member of her legal team said Thursday.

Lawyer Stephen Ferrell told the BBC that he had learned she was moving around her hospital room, although he had not spoken to her.

"What's been described to me is that physically there's quite a bit going on, that her arms are very injured and she's not able to use them very much," he said. "She is up and walking for the first time today, but just around the room, not very far."

Ferrell described her mental state as "kind of good and bad," adding, "Good that she is fairly with it, but she's also somewhat foggy. She can lose her train of thought really easily and forgets where she's going."

He said he assumed Pike's situation would "keep improving," but added that "there could be some permanent damage. We don't know that yet."

Pike's attorneys said Wednesday that she was feeling "angry and confused" after waking up in the hospital, and that the failed execution attempt left her with severe physical health challenges that put her on a "long road to recovery."

Pike had been unconscious and in critical condition in the days after two doses of pentobarbital failed to end her life on Sept. 30, they said.

"On Monday night, it was our understanding that Christa was brain-dead and that life support would be removed the next day," Randy Spivey, a member of her legal team, said during a press conference Wednesday afternoon. "But on Tuesday, to the shock of everyone … Christa woke up and began talking."

Spivey said the effects of the pentobarbital have caused her to develop a blood clot, pneumonia and left her arms and hands "tremendously swollen," to the point where she's not currently able to use them. He added that Pike is still dealing with significant "cognitive confusion," but is "very aware" that the state had tried and failed to end her life.

The press conference came shortly after a hearing in which a judge granted Pike's attorneys' request to order the state to preserve all evidence connected to the execution, including medical equipment, communications related to the decision to call off the procedure or related to her emergency care and "anything that was in the actual room." The judge also ordered that any "barriers" that may prevent Pike from communicating with her attorneys while she's in the hospital be removed.

Pike's lawyers have repeatedly asked for Pike's death sentence to be commuted. During Wednesday's hearing, a lawyer representing the state declined to answer when asked whether Tennessee might attempt to execute Pike for a second time in the future.

Dr. Joel Zivot, a medical expert who has consulted with Pike's legal team, told the Associated Press on Tuesday that Pike's regaining consciousness "bodes well for a good recovery," but said that the full picture of her long-term health won't be clear for some time.

"She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk," he said. "There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here."

Fallout from the failed execution has brought intense scrutiny to Tennessee's execution procedures. Gov. Bill Lee suspended the one remaining execution scheduled for this year and announced that the state's top prison official, Correction Commissioner Frank Strada, would be stepping down at the end of October.

Pike's lawyers said the resignation was "justified, but it does nothing to help Christa now. What happened to her Wednesday reflects a systemic failure that goes far beyond any one person," they said in a statement, according to ABC News.

Pike, 50, was sentenced to death in 1996 for the murder of her classmate, Colleen Slemmer. Her execution was scheduled to be carried out after 30 years on death row, but was called off after the drugs she was administered did not kill her. She was taken to the hospital, where she received life-saving care.

Both of Pike's arms were "swollen, burned, and blistered" when she arrived at the hospital, her lawyers wrote in a legal filing. Her lawyers believe the IV lines were placed incorrectly or her veins burst, so that some or all of the drug went into the tissue of her arms instead of her bloodstream.

"It was cruel, and it was torturous," attorney Randy Spivey said the day after the execution attempt. "It was also predictable."

Spivey said Pike's legal team warned the state of Tennessee and the courts that her medical condition of thrombocytosis "would cause her to suffer an agonizing death." They said it could increase clotting and pain during the execution process and that her veins are difficult to access. Pike's attorneys said the state and the court dismissed their client's concerns.

In audio recordings obtained by the New York Times, Pike had said two weeks before she was due to be executed that she was concerned about the lethal injection, citing a recent botched execution attempt in Tennessee of Tony Carruthers in May, when staff were unable to locate a vein. "Tony Carruthers lived out my worst nightmare," Pike can be heard saying in the audio, which was shared by her lawyers.

"I do not have good veins,' she said. "And I don't want to go through that."

"She was not seeking to delay her execution," attorney Stephen Ferrell told reporters on Oct. 1. "She was seeking to have that execution performed humanely and as quickly and as painlessly as possible."

Following the failed execution, Lee ordered "a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred" and said that another execution scheduled for Dec. 3 later this year had been paused.

"This is a tragedy," he said. "There is no one who wanted what happened last night to happen. It's deeply disturbing to me that this has happened in this state."

Pike's attorneys said in response that the governor's independent review doesn't go far enough after being in solitary confinement for more than 20 years and the botched execution attempt. "Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty," Spivey said. "The governor must commute Christa's sentence now."

May Martinez, the mother of Pike's victim, Colleen Slemmer, told NBC News the execution attempt had been a "mess," adding, "They didn't say anything, and then, all of a sudden, they asked all the victims to leave. We didn't know anything until we got up to the office and saw the commissioner. And he said that it didn't work ... and she's on her way to the hospital."

U.S. Sen. Marsha Blackburn, the state's Republican candidate for governor, said Tennessee should look at other forms of execution. "If it's lethal injection, if it is electric chair, what we do know is we have to find a way to do this — and do it successfully," she told The Associated Press.

Tennessee officials have not said whether they will try to execute Pike again, or explained what went wrong.

Her condition could complicate any future attempt. Under Supreme Court precedent, a person can't be executed unless they have a "rational understanding" of why they are being put to death, the New York Times reported. Dr. Joel Zivot, an Emory University anesthesiologist retained by Pike's defense team, told the BBC it is "very possible" she suffered a brain injury because resuscitation was delayed.

Pike's lawyers have asked Lee to commute her sentence to life in prison. Lee had denied her clemency before the execution attempt.

President Trump questioned how the execution could have failed, telling reporters it "shouldn't be very difficult," according to AFP. United Nations human rights chief Volker Türk urged Tennessee not to try again.

Pike had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. on Sept. 30 for killing Slemmer in 1995, at the age of 18. She would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.

An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start, a stay that was subsequently overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court.

Media witnesses said officials raised the curtains to the execution chamber at 7:27 p.m., showing Pike strapped to a gurney. "I'm going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life, and that is in love," she said in her "last" words.

However, Pike remained conscious after the first dose. Nashville Banner reporter Steven Hale said she lifted her head off the gurney at 7:54 p.m. She also reportedly asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way.

Tori Gessner, a journalist with WKRN News 2 in Nashville, said Pike was seen pointing at her arm and asking, "Does this happen like that?"

Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m. At that time, an announcement was made to escort media witnesses out of the area.

Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced was "singular and unparalleled."

Seven other people have survived medical problems caused by an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has remained alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.

"I've witnessed, I believe, five executions in Tennessee," Gessner said. "Nothing about today was normal, typical at all, and the court delay was just the tip of the iceberg."

A source told NBC News that there was no medical oxygen or mask in the execution chamber, meaning they had to be brought in from a prison clinic. Some of the medication had worn off by the third time staff checked on Pike, the source added.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said that it "followed every step of the state's lawful, established execution protocol approved by the attorney general's office."

The state's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered "if the inmate is not deceased" after the first set. It does not specify what happens if the subject is still alive after the second set.

Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday with the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in "unnecessary agony" and that the execution was violating her right to be free from cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit and a district court.

Pike was sentenced to death in 1996 after being convicted of first-degree murder of Colleen Slemmer the previous year on the University of Tennessee Agricultural campus.

According to legal documents filed with the Supreme Court, Pike "tortured, and killed Colleen Slemmer" on Jan. 12, 1995 because Pike "just felt mean that day." Pike is reported to have cut Colleen's throat multiple times and crushed her skull with a piece of asphalt.

Pike was also convicted of attempted first-degree murder after trying to strangle fellow inmate Patricia Jones in 2001.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center (DPIC), there were 75 botched lethal injections between 1982 and 2010. Compared to other methods, lethal injections face complications at a significantly higher rate. There have been a number of botched executions since 2010 that don't appear in the DPIC's tally.

Most of these were executions that went wrong in some way, but still ended in death. But there are seven known instances in which an execution failed entirely. One of them was earlier this year in Tennessee, when staff were unable to find a vein to administer the lethal drugs to inmate Tony Carruthers.

More than 20 pharmaceutical companies have also refused to have their products used in executions, which has left states struggling to find the drugs they need to perform lethal injections. In some cases, they have experimented with unproven alternatives, with disastrous results.

An Oklahoma prisoner named Michael Lee Wilson said he could feel his "whole body burning" as he was being executed using a controversial drug cocktail in 2014. There have also been instances of prisoners gasping for air, heaving and coughing, convulsing and being subjected to "three hours of pain" before finally dying.

In April 2022, Tennessee called off the execution of Oscar Smith about an hour before it was scheduled to begin after the state discovered that its lethal injection drugs had not been properly tested. An independent investigation found that the state had repeatedly failed to follow its own drug-testing protocols between 2018 and 2022.

Tennessee then revised its protocol, resuming executions in May 2025 and using a single, lethal drug: pentobarbital.

There's also growing evidence that lethal injection may not provide a peaceful death even when everything appears to go right.

Difficulties with lethal injections have led some states to revive previously discarded execution methods. South Carolina carried out three executions by firing squad last year. There had been three total firing squad executions in the U.S. in the previous half-century combined.

There were 47 executions in 2025, according to the DPIC, higher than the recent average of fewer than 30 per year. These included the lethal injection of South Carolina inmate Marion Bowman, who received twice the intended drug dose, and Tennessee inmate Byron Black, who reportedly showed sustained cardiac activity for nearly two minutes after prison staff pronounced him dead.

title: Evans to defend title in extended WRC calendar including Scotland
description: The inaugural Rally Scotland will take place in October as the 2027 World Rally Championship comes to the BBC.
fullText:
The inaugural Rally Scotland will take place from 3-7 October in an extended 2027 World Rally Championship (WRC) calendar released by the FIA and the sport's promoters.

The gravel event in Aberdeenshire will form the 12th round of a 15-event calendar, as it joins the USA as new events on the schedule.

It is the first time the United Kingdom has hosted a round of the WRC since 2019, and BBC Sport will provide extensive live coverage of the rally.

It will also be a home round for new World Rally champion Elfyn Evans, who won the title in dramatic circumstances in Sardinia on Sunday after rival Oliver Solberg crashed at the end of the final stage.

In doing so, Evans became the first WRC champion from the UK in 25 years and joined the late Colin McRae and Richard Burns as the sport's top-level title winners.

Northern Ireland drivers Josh McErlean and Jon Armstrong also competed at the top level of the sport in 2026 and will be aiming to return next year.

In addition to Rally Scotland, the BBC's coverage will include five live stages plus the Power Stage on all WRC rounds, highlights programmes, plus digital clips and content across BBC platforms.

How Evans defied history to join rallying greats

Evans ends Britain's 25-year wait for WRC champion

The season will start on the icy tarmac roads in Monte Carlo from 21-24 January before rounds in the snow in Sweden and vast landscapes of Safari Rally Kenya.

Three tarmac events in a row then take place in Croatia, the Canary Islands and Japan, before the Acropolis Rally in Greece.

The WRC's Italian round moves from September to July, and will move from the gravel roads of Sardinia to tarmac in Rome.

The high-speed events in Estonia and Finland retain their back-to-back summer slots before the USA hosts its first WRC round in 39 years from 26-29 August.

The WRC last held a points-paying round in the USA at the Olympus Rally in 1988, and the championship will return as a gravel round after a successful candidate event in June.

Rally Scotland takes place in early October before a South American double-header, in Paraguay and Chile, and Rally Saudi Arabia round out the calendar.

The event in Saudi Arabia was set to end the 2026 season but it was cancelled due to the ongoing conflict in the Middle East.

Rally de Portugal will not feature in the 2027 calendar but is in talks to return in 2028.

The upcoming season will mark a new era of the sport with the introduction of a new promoter along with WRC27 regulations which will limit costs and reduce the horsepower of the top cars.

It will also mark the return of Ford as a manufacturer to the sport in a collaboration with the M-Sport banner.

2027 World Rally Championship calendar

Rallye Monte-Carlo 21-24 January

Acropolis Rally Greece 24-27 June

Rally Scotland 30 September-3 October

Rally del Paraguay 21-24 October

Rally Saudi Arabia 25-28 November

title: 'Nothing impossible' as NI begin long road to Brazil
description: Northern Ireland defenders Nat Johnson and Rebecca Holloway tell BBC Sport NI of their dream of reaching a first ever Women's World Cup as NI go through the play-offs.
fullText:
A World Cup staged in Brazil is the stuff of dreams for any footballer and the chance to experience that is on offer for Northern Ireland as they begin their play-off journey against Portugal with hope of securing a spot at next year's tournament.

It will be a difficult ask for Michael McArdle's side, which has been hit by a spate of injuries and features five new faces, but there is a quiet confidence in the group before what will be, for some of them, the biggest games in their careers to date.

First up, in what is set to be an arduous journey in search of a World Cup debut, is Friday's home leg at Inver Park (19:30 BST) against the Portuguese.

"When you're growing up, Brazil is the place to be, it's the home of football. It really doesn't get much better than that," said Norwich City defender Natalie Johnson.

"The fact that we are at this point and that it could be a reality, you don't need much more motivation than that.

"There's a lot on the line, but we are taking it one game at a time and I think if you look at it that way, nothing is impossible. Obviously there is that dream at the end of it, but we're focused on the game in front of us."

Family, football and Dalglish - what drives NI boss McArdle?

What will new call-ups bring to Northern Ireland?

Elmore and Grant named in Northern Ireland squad

As one of the lowest-ranked European sides in the play-offs, it is a difficult route to next summer's tournament for Northern Ireland.

If they overcome Portugal they will then face Croatia or Iceland in the next round. If they make it through those games, they will likely have an inter-continental play-off to make it the whole way to Brazil.

Portugal inflicted two defeats on in NI in Euro 2025 qualifying and sit 28 places higher in the Fifa world rankings, but Johnson and her side are not daunted by the task in front of them and instead want to embrace it.

"We absolutely believe these games are winnable," she added.

"We have a lot of experience in this team and the young players coming in bring their own individual experience and they really add to the squad. It's a good balance and we are going in to get something out of this.

"Any Portugal side is going to be very technical and we're expecting a very fast-paced game. We're going to have to be at our best to face that, quick football, and that's what we're working towards.

"On paper it might look like there is a big gap between the teams, but at the end of the day, it is a game of football and I think particularly on our home pitch it will be a much more level playing field."

Birmingham City defender Rebecca Holloway is one of the few survivors from the squad that qualified for Euro 2022, NI's first major tournament.

There have been a lot of changes to the squad since, but Holloway is excited for the future rather than dwelling on past achievements.

"It feels like a long time ago in a way, especially when you look at how much the squad has changed, but I think that's also what is very exciting," she said.

"It's like a new generation coming through and I think it's also important that we have some experienced players here to help those new faces. We're excited to see what they can do and encourage them to play with confidence and freedom and do what they are good at.

"We're slowly closing the gap on Portugal and the so-called bigger nations. They had a narrow 2-1 win over us at home in 2024 after a 4-0 away defeat, I think that shows that we are getting closer."

McArdle's youthful side do not have far to look for inspiration as to how to punch above their weight.

After assembling in camp on Monday, the team watched Northern Ireland's men's side 0-0 draw with Georgia.

That stalemate ensured Michael O'Neill's side stayed top of their Nations League group after picking up eight points from four games without conceding a goal.

"It was brilliant watching them play with such youth and energy and the exciting football that they are playing.

"This younger generation play with no fear and I think that is what the men's senior team are doing.

"I am hoping the young players see that and we can adopt the same attitude. I think we were all watching thinking we can't wait to do this on Friday."

title: 'Are you accusing me of receiving money?' - what Guardiola has said about charges
description: BBC Sport examines Pep Guardiola's comments about the Manchester City financial rule-breaking case during his time managing the club.
fullText:
"Let me be clear: we will get through this together. I love you all."

Comforting words of solidarity from a long-standing leader can be a great source of strength and unity at a time of crisis.

And many Manchester City fans will have felt just that after former manager Pep Guardiola posted on social media last week in response to the club being found guilty of deliberate financial rule-breaking over nine years.

To some, Guardiola's intervention came as a surprise. After all, he is no longer in a managerial position having left City in the summer, and so was under no obligation to comment.

In the past, Guardiola - who joined City in 2016, most of the way through the 2009-18 period the charges relate to - had insisted guilty verdicts would change his relationship with the club.

He was outspoken on some matters during his time in Manchester, including Catalan independence and Israel's military offensive in Gaza.

But in some instances he sidestepped questions on human rights in the United Arab Emirates, whose government includes key members of City's hierarchy, and didn't broach the UAE's alleged role in the ongoing conflict in Sudan, which has accused it of being complicit in genocide. The UAE has strongly rejected the allegations.

City are, of course, appealing against the guilty verdicts, and Guardiola remains employed by owners City Football Group as a global ambassador.

Next week he is expected to attend City's Champions League tie against Paris St-Germain - the club's first home match since the guilty verdicts were announced.

But what did he say about the Premier League's case against the club over the years?

BBC Sport has taken a look at every significant comment Guardiola made on the subject during his time in charge at Etihad Stadium.

Senior figures worried about Man City being in next season's Champions League

Rival clubs want range of punishments for Man City

"Do you know the question you're asking me?

"Did I receive money for another situation, right now, today? Honestly, do you think I deserve to have this type of question, the day we won the treble... did I receive money? Are you accusing me of receiving money?

"I listen to my chairman and my CEO, and I trust them. They tell me we are fair and we absolutely follow the rules. I believe them."

Guardiola's first comments on allegations of financial rule-breaking by Manchester City were delivered furiously, at a media conference in the immediate aftermath of a 6-0 victory over Watford in the FA Cup final.

He had been asked by Sky News' Rob Harris whether he had ever received separate, undeclared payments from the club in addition to his contracted salary, after the Football Leaks website published hacked information suggesting former manager Roberto Mancini had been paid in such a way.

Guardiola appeared to take the questions as an attack on his personal integrity.

Mancini said last month: "It's not an issue that concerns me. It's nothing new because this matter has been discussed for the last four or five years.

"Manchester City has not been found guilty, and the alleged double contract is not my concern. It's their issue, not mine."

19 February 2020 - bullish over Uefa appeal

"We appeal. When someone believes they are right, they have to fight. The club has to fight and I trust the club 100% what they have done and they have explained to me.

"This situation is not finished and we will wait. But until it is resolved you have to play and play, and that is what is going to happen."

Guardiola was responding after Uefa found City guilty of breaking its Financial Fair Play (FFP) rules, and banned the club from European competition for two years.

He was bullish regarding the club's right to appeal.

14 July 2020 - Champions League suspension overturned

"We were damaged. The people say we cheated and were lying - and many times. The presumption of innocence wasn't there."

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) had lifted the Uefa suspension and cleared the club of the more serious charges, finding some were unproven or that in some cases too much time had passed since the alleged rule-breaking.

Guardiola suggested in response that the wider football world had simply assumed the club was guilty and fair treatment had been lacking.

7 May 2022 - trust in City hierarchy

"Why did I defend the club and the people? It's because I work with them.

"When they are accused of something, I ask them: 'Tell me about that.' They explain and I believe them.

"I said to them: 'If you lie to me, the day after I am not here. I will be out and I will not be your friend any more. I put my faith in you because I believe you 100% from day one and I defend the club because of that.'"

Guardiola made clear he had built a level of trust with those in the City hierarchy that meant he inherently believed them.

But he also insisted he would resign if the club were found guilty, and distance himself from anyone who had 'lied' to him.

Guardiola had, of course, left the club in the months before the guilty verdict was confirmed last week. But in response he reaffirmed his kinship with City and chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak.

Manchester City and the 115 Charges Explained

10 February 2023 - first response to 115 charges

"My first thought is that we are already being condemned. I am fully convinced we will be innocent.

"Personally, I am happy we are here. We have the chance to defend [ourselves]. I think we have good lawyers. I think the Premier League, supported by 19 teams, will have good lawyers too.

"Just in case we are not innocent we will accept what the judge in the Premier League decides, but what happens if in the same situation that Uefa happened we are innocent - what happens to restore or pay back our damage?"

In an extraordinarily tense media conference after the Premier League announced it was pursuing 115 charges against City, Guardiola again insisted the club were innocent and suggested confidence their legal team would secure a result in their favour.

The Spaniard again suggested the media and public were predetermining City's guilt without a fair hearing.

23 May 2023 - frustration with process

"We would love [the verdict] tomorrow - this afternoon better than tomorrow.

"What we won on the pitch, we don't have any doubts."

A few months into a process that would take just over three and a half years, Guardiola expressed exasperation with the amount of time the Premier League investigation was taking and the doubt being placed on his team's achievements by pundits, the media and fans.

24 November 2023 - staying to manage in League One

"You are questioning like we have been punished. And in the moment, we are innocent until guilt is proved.

"I know the people want it. I know, I feel it. I will wait. Wait and see it and after the sentence has been done we will come here and explain it.

"There is more chance [for me] to stay if we are in League One than if we were in the Champions League."

Guardiola made two key pledges here - a media conference in response to the verdict when it was eventually revealed, and to continue managing the club in the lower leagues if such a punishment was handed down.

His summer exit thwarted the latter, but he would repeat the media conference promise later.

23 August 2024 - final weeks before hearing

"I am happy that it starts soon and hopefully it will finish soon. We will accept [the verdict], like we have always done."

In the months before the legal hearing into the charges began, Guardiola again expressed a desire for haste.

13 September & 21 September 2024 - hearing begins

"I know what people are looking for. I know what they are expecting - I know it because I have read it for many years.

"Everyone is innocent until guilt is proven. It's like everyone doesn't expect us to be not just relegated, they want us to disappear off the face of the earth."

Guardiola again insisted the football world was against City from the outset, as the legal hearing into the case began.

7 February 2025 - anticipating a final verdict

"In one month, I think there will be a verdict and sentence."

Briefings at the time indicated a verdict was expected in early 2025. Guardiola was under the same impression, but in reality it was a long way off.

The independent commission panel expressed its frustration with the time taken when it eventually published its findings last week.

23 May 2026 - leaving Manchester City

"I trust them. I spoke with them and trust how they behave and how they did. What happened, happened.

"If you find me, yeah, but that will be difficult."

On leaving City, Guardiola underlined his belief in the club's innocence for a final time and his belief that individuals in the club's hierarchy were telling the truth.

In the final line, Guardiola again insisted he would give a media conference once the verdict was given - if journalists could find him.

No such media conference has been announced. The only subsequent comment Guardiola has made was last week's social media post.

The post featured photos of him holding trophies and posing with key City ownership figures including Al Mubarak and CEO Ferran Soriano - the men under pressure - but no players.

What the verdict means for his legacy is something football fans around the world will determine for themselves.

title: Engine size limits and working with Iraola - the Liverpool academy approach
description: Liverpool academy director Alex Inglethorpe talks to BBC Sport about the value and future of Liverpool's academy.
fullText:
One of the first things you notice in Alex Inglethorpe's office at Liverpool's AXA Training Centre is a framed image gifted by Trent Alexander-Arnold.

It is a picture from 2019 of the academy director and player watching a game together. Alexander-Arnold left for a new challenge at Real Madrid last year, after 20 years on Merseyside, but his story is one of inspiration for everyone that enters Liverpool's academy.

He joined as a six-year-old in 2004 and went on to win the Premier League, Champions League, FA Cup, League Cup, Community Shield, Uefa Super Cup and the Fifa Club World Cup with Liverpool.

"The ideal for any academy, and certainly for us, is wanting young players - and hopefully they're local players - to improve the first team and in doing so, they come and win trophies," says Inglethorpe.

"At Liverpool the bar is high, so to have a player capable of winning everything that you could possibly win is a dream."

Inglethorpe and his team oversee the development of younger players and ensure there is alignment between the academy and the first team.

One of the phrases used is 'the first team pitch is only 300 metres away from the academy building in Kirkby, but the journey might take 10 years to get there'.

Under new boss Andoni Iraola, players like Rio Ngumoha, Trey Nyoni, Lewis Koumas and James McConnell, who have spent time at the academy, have all featured this season.

"We were fortunate because of how the calendar worked, with players still at the World Cup and a delayed return. Andoni and his staff spent a lot of his first week here watching the academy," says Inglethorpe.

"So we felt ahead, in terms of building a relationship from the outset."

At the Kirkby academy, phones are handed in on a morning and there is a clause in contracts with a maximum engine size limit for cars that are driven into academy premises.

"It comes back to passing your audition. First impressions matter," says Inglethorpe.

"Often before you've kicked a ball, the car you drive or the watch you wear can have an impact on how you're thought of - and that could be first team staff or players looking at you.

"We've believed in the idea of 'earning the right' for some time."

Last week, Manchester United signed 16-year-old winger Isaac Konde from Liverpool on a one-year scholarship followed by a five-year professional deal. Both clubs are now in talks over a compensation package.

In February, a tribunal ruled Liverpool must pay at least £2.8m to Chelsea for Ngumoha. The 18-year-old left Chelsea in September 2024 to join the Reds and signed his first professional contract a year later.

Both are recent examples of the current climate around talent.

At Liverpool, the belief is they have been sensible and responsible with a view to deferred gratification in most cases, but the wage structure is currently under review.

"It's always a compliment when other clubs want your players as it means you're doing something right," says Inglethorpe.

"But I think the market of players at 16 is distorted because of Brexit and because you can't recruit like you would do before. There's always been movement of players but it feels a little more extreme now.

"When there's a clamour for talent - fees, wages and everything else will shift accordingly, so it's dealing with what we have and adapting to a new situation."

When Curtis Jones moved to Inter Milan in the summer, it left Liverpool without a first team player born in the city.

"I acknowledge the fact that ideally Liverpool would love to have a team full of Scousers," says Inglethorpe.

"But it is testament to the supporters that if you adopt the characteristics of a Scouser - and you only have to see the likes of Bill Shankly, Kenny Dalglish and others over the years - you can be treated as one of their own.

"So if you are fearless, passionate, play tough and demonstrate those qualities, then it doesn't matter if you've come from an L1 postcode and got a purple bin or not. That's the beauty of the club and the crowd."

One name to keep an eye on is 15-year-old Luca Eden. The midfielder was born in the Wirral and has already represented England at youth level.

Last month, he became the youngest player to feature in the Uefa Youth League for Liverpool, beating a record previously held by Joshua Abe, Ngumoha and Alexander-Arnold.

"We've got plenty of Scousers in the academy and plenty who I think will play for the club. But if not and a lad comes from Warrington or wherever, that's not a problem," Inglethorpe insists.

One of the most challenging aspects of Inglethorpe's role is letting players go. Liverpool released eight players from their academy set-up at the end of last season.

Inglethorpe explains how the likes of Harry Kane, who was coming through the academy at Spurs when he was a youth coach there, and Alexander-Arnold weren't necessarily the best in their respective youth cohorts.

"At that stage, there's too many unknowns. You can't predict how players will react to adversity and natural bumps in the road," says Inglethorpe.

"I've been proven wrong so many times in the past. A good example would be Jarell [Quansah] - someone who was always liked and never in danger of leaving but probably never seen in the top three in the group."

Quansah left Liverpool for Bayer Leverkusen in 2025 and has since won eight caps for England.

"There are no certainties - the point of the academy is to allow them to fulfil their potential," says Inglethorpe.

"Sometimes players need to leave to gain an opportunity. There are lots of lovely examples of boys leaving and having good careers, and I'm not convinced they would have had the same career if they stayed at Liverpool.

"The linear and most productive way is to break in, but there's different pathways that can lead back to playing for Liverpool - and that is the dream."

Just before the academy players go on the pitch, there is a sign that says: "Don't look sideways" - referring to where the first team train.

Next month will mark 14 years at Liverpool for Inglethorpe. So what's his definition of success?

"Anyone would want to take something on and leave it in a better place, and I think we've done that," he says. "Ultimately we have had players in the first team winning major trophies and we're fortunate to be part of that era."

The 'Kids Cup', when Liverpool beat Chelsea in the 2024 Carabao Cup final. Faced with an injury crisis, Jurgen Klopp relied heavily on academy players and his side finished the match with a team whose average age was under 22. Klopp called it his "most special trophy".

"It's definitely a moment in time. The longer the game went on, Jurgen was taking off the seniors and putting another one of the boys on. It was an incredible show of belief," says Inglethorpe.

On another wall in Inglethorpe's office is a magnetic board with headshots of every player in the academy on the left and the first team squad on the right. Ultimately, the motive is for everyone to make the journey across the board.

With a £20m revamp to the academy facility planned to be completed by 2028, the determination to carry on producing first team players is stronger than ever.

"There are exciting times ahead with the potential for the other end, and I'm really excited for the future," says Inglethorpe.

"In Julian Ward [the new sporting director], we have someone who is hugely invested in the academy and has been on this journey for a long time."
