title: Sheff Utd expect to avoid points deduction - CEO
description: Sheffield United CEO Stephen Bettis tells BBC Radio Sheffield the Blades expect to avoid an EFL points deduction but will not reinvest a summer transfer haul in January.
fullText:
Sheffield United's CEO says the club do not expect to receive an English Football League points deduction and the owners would "fight hard" if any such sanction is imposed.

The EFL launched an investigation after the company used to buy the club was placed into liquidation by the High Court in August.

COH Sports Bidco Limited (CSBL) agreed to purchase the Championship club for just over £100m in December 2024 but about £35m is still owed on the deal.

A winding-up petition was filed in July against CSBL by United World - the club's former owners - with insolvency events able to trigger a 12-point penalty under EFL rules.

Blades chief executive officer Stephen Bettis spent an hour in the BBC Radio Sheffield studio on Tuesday night, with the potential points deduction top of the agenda.

Bettis said: "The EFL are investigating the process and what has happened.

"The 12-point deduction only relates to if the club or a company within the group goes into insolvency. The advice our owners have got from their lawyers is that the club certainly didn't go into insolvency - we're funded, we're paying all our bills on time.

"The company that no longer is in the group has now had a winding up order against it.

"The position of our owners is that the winding up petition happened after that entity was no longer within the Sheffield United group. While it was within the group it never had a winding up order, it didn't become insolvent - their belief is that that stops the 12-point deduction happening."

BBC Sport has contacted the EFL for comment.

Bettis conceded there remains a risk of potential fines or points deductions, adding: "The EFL are still investigating that and there is still the risk of that from their perspective."

"I think if any decision is made to go down that path obviously the owners will fight that quite hard."

BBC Sport reached out to the EFL for comment and were told "matters still remain ongoing".

Though not a direct comparison, in 2009 Southampton were docked 10 points by the EFL after their parent company went into administration and the football club claimed there was not a financial link between the two.

Bettis added: "It wasn't a parent company for Sheffield United when it happened, that's quite an important difference.

"The EFL have been aware of this for four months, if it was clear cut we'd have been charged already, in my opinion. It's clearly not clear cut and it continues to go on.

"The owners have cooperated fully with the EFL investigation. They are now deliberating internally and we're waiting for their response."

Asked by BBC Radio Sheffield's Rob Staton if that means the club are not expecting a points deduction, Bettis said: "From the advice the lawyers for our owners were given - that is what we've been told.

"I'm not going to sit here and categorically say we're not at risk, until the verdict is given I'm not going to make myself look an idiot.

"There's still that risk, whether it's a fine, a points deduction, all of those are on the table still and until they are not we have to be open and understand that's the situation."

Bettis told Football Heaven that "discussions continue" between the Blades owners and former owner Prince Abdullah bin Mosaad Al Saud over a payment of nearly £35m which they feel should be reduced.

"The existing owners have issues with the previous owner, they are continuing to discuss and potentially feel the sum of money outstanding should be a lesser sum. Those discussions continue," he said.

"I don't believe for one minute the new owners are trying to not pay Prince Abdullah the monies outstanding, but think the sum needs to be adjusted."

Bettis also said director Timothy Ryan has passed the fit and proper owner test with both the EFL and Independent Football Regular and said he had been told the prospect of co-chair Steven Rosen facing disqualification by the EFL was "not an issue".

title: How fans are falling in love with football again
description: BBC Sport speaks to Dorking Wanderers owner and manager Marc White about the growing use of social media helping non-League teams grow.
fullText:
"I know that if they don't edit out the right bits, I'll get banned every week."

Marc White is one of the most recognisable faces in non-league football.

From the baseball caps to the foul-mouthed rants on the touchline, the founder, owner and manager of Dorking Wanderers has become a star of the lower levels of the English football pyramid.

It has been helped by a documentary series called 'Dorking Uncovered' on the YouTube channel 'Bunch of Amateurs', run by Rich Phippen, as they rose from a team of mates paying a fiver each to rent a pitch to the National League South.

They have been promoted 12 times since they were founded 26 years ago. Their only relegation came in the National League in 2024.

White, 52, is the longest-serving manager in the top six tiers of English football - which he jokes is always at risk with behind-the-scenes cameras following their every move.

"I love the fact that so many people watch, we had half a billion views in 2025," he tells BBC Sport.

"I'm involved in the edit because if I wasn't, I would probably be banned constantly. I'll probably be the first football manager to get a lifetime ban."

Social media now plays a huge role in promoting non-league football.

With local newspapers' ability to cover non-league now strangled by dwindling resources, clubs have taken it upon themselves to expand their reach on their own platforms.

Those around the game believe it helps build stronger relationships with the community and helps expand marketing opportunities as well as advertising matches.

From goal highlights, interviews or in-depth features like Dorking Uncovered, it is helping grow interest in non-league, with attendances growing. In Dorking's division, average attendances reached 1,221 during the 2024-25 season - that was a 134% rise on the average a decade before.

White started Dorking Wanderers just outside the M25 radius with his friends because they were bored of paying for Premier League matches and just wanted to play.

He believes the rising costs of watching top-tier football, either by buying tickets or TV subscriptions, is pushing more and more people to non-league.

But they have to know where to find it and social media helps that.

"I think a lot of people underestimate how little people know about their local football club," said White.

"And when you're now talking about decades of people that have never picked up a newspaper, and that target audience probably watches the Premier League and they have no idea what's going on near their local high street, where probably the beer is cheaper, the travel certainly cheaper, and they know a lot more people there.

"And it's quite a social connection for them. So, you know, I think for me that the power of social media largely is taking the clubs to their own target market and also taking the target market to the clubs. It's kind of connecting the two."

There are other ways online is growing attendances. Aaron Hunt gained thousands of followers streaming on Twitch about his success with his local club Daisy Hill FC, based in Westhoughton, Bolton, on the management simulation game Football Manager online.

Hunt was invited to be chairman of North West Counties Football Counties side, whose stadium is now sponsored by YouTuber AngryGinge and called GingePower Stadium after he streamed one of his visits to a game to over one million people.

Then there is also the Wrexham factor and others being inspired by Ryan Reynolds and Rob Mac leading the Welsh club from non-league to the Championship.

One of the latest celebrity names to invest in a team outside the Football League is YouTuber KSI, who bought a stake in Dagenham and Redbridge this year while claiming he can take them to the top tier.

"Just more eyeballs, more exposure," said White. "We've seen a flurry of well-known names. But obviously, there's only one thing better than a well-known name, and that is a well-known name that's social media connected. And KSI, he's the perfect candidate for that.

"And it benefits every single club in the league because he's bringing attention to the product. And that's great.

"We spoke briefly when we played them, but I think it's all a bit of an eye-opener for him, really. There's no glamour.

"It will be just great to see the impact that has over the period of time. But I think it's brilliant."

For White and Dorking, the dream is to reach the Football League. They are two more promotions away and have started this season in mixed form.

"We think that getting to the Football League would make us one of the world's - it sounds mental - but we do think it'll make us one of the world's most recognised sports successes," said White, whose team average a crowd of around 1,600 at their Meadowbank home in Surrey.

"I mean, if we go anywhere in America, who are obsessed with the English football pyramid, they know us.

"I've always wanted to win at Wembley, too. So maybe if we could go up via the play-offs, that would tick two boxes."

He has courted controversy. Last year, he was given a six-match touchline ban for a comment he made on a podcast about women.

Despite being widely shared on TikTok and Instagram and YouTube, White isn't on social media himself.

"I get plenty of clips sent to me," he said. "But if you saw some of them that get edited out, I'd be out of the game.

"I've never been bothered about the cameras. If they went tomorrow, it would be all about the football like it always has been.

"I love the fact that it resonates with loads of people that might have played non-league football, Sunday football, might have given up, might have followed a team, no longer in love with the game. That's our market.

"It's like people that fell out of love with the game, people that have become disillusioned with the Premier League, the TV sport, they're the people that love us the most."

title: Is it too early to look at Premier League table?
description: Just five games in, it might seem a bit early to pay much attention to the Premier League table - but it's probably more settled than you think. BBC Sport takes a look at the statistics behind the early season standings.
fullText:
Just five games in, it might seem a bit early to pay much attention to the Premier League table - but it's probably more settled than you think.

While it would be no surprise if Manchester City and Arsenal finish as the top two - outside of any points deductions or sanctions directed City's way - will Brentford really qualify for Europe, Hull stay up and Tottenham be involved in yet another relegation battle? Recent history certainly suggests it is likely.

It has to be mentioned there is a huge asterisk hanging over the Premier League table at the moment after Manchester City were found guilty of the majority of the Premier League charges levelled at them.

The Premier League leaders have appealed but, if the guilty verdict remains, potential sanctions could have a significant impact on the table. Until then, we can only deal with the table as it is now.

If we look at the Premier League after five games last season and where teams ultimately ended up, the final table was already starting to take shape as 13 of the 20 sides finished within four places of where they sat even at this early stage (65%).

Eventual champions Arsenal were second, Sunderland were already seventh ahead of finishing there eight months later, and two of the three sides that were relegated were already in the bottom three.

There were some notable exceptions. Aston Villa and Tottenham effectively swapped places at either end of the table, with Villa rising from the bottom three to finish in the top four and Spurs dropping to 17th.

It is a similar story across the last 10 seasons of the Premier League. More than two-thirds of teams finished within four places of where they were after five games (138 out of 200), with 27 of those sitting in exactly the same position 33 games later.

Another 50 teams finished between five and nine places from where they were at this stage, meaning that just 12 teams in the past decade moved up or down the table by double digits after this point, with three of those coming last season.

However, one part of the table that does not settle quickly is the top spot. The side leading the Premier League after five games has gone on to win the title in just one of the past six seasons - Manchester City doing so in 2023-24 - and just three times in the past 11 seasons.

Even the fact that Manchester City have five wins out of five so far does not mean much. They also won their first five games under Manuel Pellegrini in 2015-16 and in Pep Guardiola's first season in 2016-17 but did not go on to win the title on either occasion (although they did in 2023-24).

Chelsea in 2018-19, Arsenal in 2022-23 and Liverpool last season were also top with a 100% record at this stage but had little to show for it at the end of the season.

However, the eventual champions have been in the top two at this point in each of the last four campaigns, suggesting - potential punishments aside - it will be Manchester City or Arsenal that lifts the trophy. The last team to be outside the top two after five games and win the title were Manchester City in 2021-22, who were fifth with just 10 points.

The top end of the table overall has sometimes settled surprisingly quickly in recent years. The top eight after five games in 2024-25 finished as the top eight at the end of that season (although not in the same order), while the top six in 2019-20 and top seven in 2016-17 were also in place at this early stage.

While being top after five games has not meant much in recent seasons, being bottom certainly has.

After finishing just one place above the drop in the last two campaigns, Tottenham could well be in trouble once again as the side bottom of the Premier League after five games has been relegated in six of the past seven seasons.

Being bottom this early did not used to be such a bad omen. Between 2013-14 and 2018-19, only one of the six sides that were propping up the table after five games ended up going down - Newcastle in 2015-16 - while Crystal Palace finished as high as 11th in 2017-18.

In fact, the good news for Tottenham fans is that the last time they were in this situation, they finished eighth. The club were bottom with just two points after five games in 2008-09 but, after replacing manager Juande Ramos with Harry Redknapp three games later, still finished in the top half.

Looking at the relegation battle more broadly, at least one of the teams in the bottom three at this stage has been relegated in the last eight seasons - so one of Tottenham, Fulham and Coventry will very likely be heading to the Championship in May.

The pool of contestants for this season's relegation battle may already be decided too as the three sides that ultimately went down in the past three seasons were all in the bottom six after five games, which would add Bournemouth, Aston Villa and Crystal Palace to the mix.

The last sides to be outside the bottom six at this point but relegated were Leeds and Southampton in 2022-23, who were both in the top half (7th and 9th). With their teams currently sat in 8th and 11th place, Hull and Ipswich fans will hope that is still the case at the end of this campaign.

While the season may well have barely begun, the Premier League table is already starting to take shape.

title: Two icons, a glorious farewell and a potentially bitter ending
description: As Lionel Messi's international career ends in fond farewell, Cristiano Ronaldo's is at risk of petering out. BBC Sport takes a look at what could be the end of the international career's of two football greats.
fullText:
On a night where one football legend received a grand farewell from his country, about 6,000 miles away, another released a lengthy statement discussing all the ways in which he had been wronged by his national team coach.

Argentina great Lionel Messi took the adulation of the crowd in Buenos Aires as his glittering international career ended with a goal against Benin on an emotional night.

Meanwhile, Portugal star Cristiano Ronaldo released a statement on social media, accusing manager Jorge Jesus of an "absolute breach of trust" while admitting he should be held accountable for his own actions.

The former Manchester United and Real Madrid forward left his country's Nations League camp last week after being an unused substitute against Norway and then finding out he would not start against Denmark.

Portuguese journalist Jose Delgado says "things will never be the same again" for Ronaldo and Portugal - so is this the beginning of the end?

Jesus has said the door is open for Ronaldo to return to the national team, but is it? Or will this saga continue, potentially closing the book on the international career of one of the greatest players of all time?

BBC Sport takes a look at what could be the end of the international careers of two football greats.

A rivalry that changed football

Watch: Rivals - Messi v Ronaldo

Listen: Sporting Giants - Messi v Ronaldo

The Ronaldo saga has been rumbling on for some time, with many fans critical of former Portugal boss Roberto Martinez's insistence on starting Ronaldo at this summer's World Cup.

At 41 years old, Ronaldo is not the dynamic player he once was and many suggested his presence hindered the team rather than helped.

However, things came to a head on Sunday when Ronaldo was an unused substitute in the Nations League win over Norway. The player subsequently left camp after finding out he would not start against Denmark in November.

On Tuesday, Ronaldo released an almost-2,000 word statement on Instagram in which he said Jesus had twice "broke his word" and accused him of an "absolute breach of trust" for firstly not playing him against Norway after saying he would, before going back on a decision to present an agreed version of events to the media.

Ronaldo apologised to fans and team-mates for leaving the camp and said the consequences of that must be "assessed and punished" while also dismissing any suggestion that he had played his last match for Portugal.

"We will have one or more farewell matches, there will be time for that," the statement said.

Manager Jesus said on Sunday the door remains open for Ronaldo to return if he chooses to, but many are suggesting the damage is already done.

Ronaldo wants Portugal 'punishment' but not retiring

Portuguese football journalist Delgado told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I don't think there is a way back. In the statement, Ronaldo says he will return to the national team but at the same time he calls Jesus a liar three times.

"In the polls in Portugal made about this issue, only 15% of the Portuguese were on Ronaldo's side and people think we owe him a lot but his time is already done and he must understand it.

"The problem is that Ronaldo does not understand it, he wants to keep playing as if he was 24, not 41.

"Things will never be the same again. No matter what happens, no matter if he plays again or if you have a game to say goodbye to Ronaldo things will never be the same.

"What Ronaldo did for Portuguese football is unique and incredible and we must thank him for all the service he gave to Portugal. But at 41, he has no place in the best XI of Portugal."

Manager Jesus has reportedly said that he had not seen Ronaldo's statement as he was watching the Portugal Under-21s game.

Al-Nassr forward Ronaldo has scored 146 goals in 234 Portugal appearances - both world records - helping them win Euro 2016 and the Nations League twice.

It seems unlikely that Ronaldo will voluntarily retire from the national team before he hits the elusive 1,000-goal mark he is chasing for club and country - he currently has 979.

But have his actions made the situation untenable?

When it comes to fans, opinions appear to be split.

On several billboards in Lisbon posters have been put up praising Ronaldo and criticising Jesus.

They read, in Portuguese: "Thank you Cristiano Ronaldo for everything you did for Portugal. You will always be our captain.

"Jorge Jesus was not up to the task. Lack of sensitivity. Treating a captain wrongly. Inflated ego."

At the Denmark game, some fans wore T-shirts spelling out 'Love you Jesus' while others were head-to-toe in Ronaldo merch.

In stark contrast, Messi brought the curtain down on his illustrious Argentina career, where he has won one World Cup and two Copa Americas, in front of an 85,000-strong sellout crowd inside the Monumental in Buenos Aires.

The 39-year-old announced his retirement from international football in August after Argentina finished runners-up at the World Cup and following the death of his father Jorge.

Messi marked his final appearance for La Albiceleste with a goal before addressing the adoring fans in a speech lasting nearly 10 minutes.

Some of his team-mates were in tears as Messi admitted he did not want to leave the field.

"There are so many emotions going through me right now," he said. "I'm surely forgetting many things I would like to say because this is a very difficult moment for me. The first person who comes to my mind is my dad.

"I leave grateful, proud and at peace. Thank you for everything."

Writing on social media on Wednesday, , externalMessi added: "Yesterday was my last match and I'm already missing the light blue and white jersey.

"I know I'm taking the right decision. It was an incredible journey, full of joy and some sadness, but I know for sure that every step I took was worth it."

Messi also thanked his family, team-mates and clubs and paid tribute to another Argentina legend, the late Diego Maradona.

His Instagram post also drew a response from Ronaldo, who wrote: "Leo, after so many years of defending your country, you've made history that will last forever.

"I have the utmost respect for what you've accomplished with Argentina. A hug."

Owner, businessman & player: Messi has big plans as a golden era ends

Messi departs as the record appearance-maker and goalscorer for Argentina but will continue his club career with Major League Soccer (MLS) team Inter Miami.

It seems the eight-time Ballon d'Or winner wants to enter the world of football club ownership and is making moves to do so.

He already owns two clubs - Spanish fifth-tier side UE Cornella and second-tier CD Eldense - as well as being a partner in the restaurant chain El Club de la Milanesa, which plans to open five branches in Catalonia.

Messi also has a lifetime deal with Adidas and a collection with drinkware brand Stanley as well as investing in the property and hotel industries.

Football expert Guillem Balague said: "Coach Lionel Scaloni insists that if Messi ever wants to carry on, he can, and there is no embarrassment in changing one's mind. But that chapter seems closed.

"Ask the people around him what comes after that and they smile, because Messi has never really planned beyond his next game.

"Even so, the shape of what lies ahead is already in front of us. He will stay inside football, because he would struggle to live without it, but his other business interests stretch far outside the game."

title: Rice close to agreeing new Arsenal deal
description: Declan Rice is close to agreeing a new long-term Arsenal contract, sources have told BBC Sport.
fullText:
Declan Rice is close to agreeing a new long-term Arsenal contract, sources have told BBC Sport.

The England midfielder has become a crucial player for the Gunners since his arrival from West Ham for £105m in July 2023.

His current deal expires at the end of next season but BBC Sport revealed in March that talks over a new contract were underway with the process now at an advanced stage.

The 27-year-old has made more than 150 starts for Arsenal, and is also a key player for England, with manager Thomas Tuchel saying this week he is one of the best midfielders in Europe.

Rice would receive a significant pay increase to his reported £240,000-per-week salary, putting him on a par with the club's best earner Bukayo Saka, who is believed to earn about £350,000 a week.

The news comes after Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta's new four-year deal with the Premier League champions was announced on Wednesday.

title: Family, football and Dalglish - what drives NI boss McArdle?
description: BBC Sport NI's Andy Gray sits down with Northern Ireland manager Michael McArdle to discuss his long career before his biggest managerial test in the World Cup play-offs.
fullText:
As Michael McArdle sits down for an interview with BBC Sport at Windsor Park, he cuts a relaxed figure.

The Scot had just announced his squad for the World Cup play-off with Portugal, for what will be the biggest game of his managerial career to date.

McArdle has only been in the Northern Ireland hot seat since March, when he was announced as Tanya Oxtoby's permanent successor, but has more than 25 years of experience working in football.

There's a clear passion for what he is doing, as he balances the reality of playing one of Europe's top-ranked sides with the dreams of reaching a first World Cup just months into his new role.

But there is one word that keeps cropping up across various topics - family.

McArdle, 48, was born and bred in Moodiesburn to the east of Glasgow, and still lives there to this day.

He met his wife, Tammy, in the village when they were both on the same paper round at the age of 12, and they have now been married for 28 years.

He has three children, Connor, Mya and Cole, and is about to become a grandad for the first time. It's clear how much his family means to him.

But when he talks about family, it's not just in terms of his own life. It is an embodiment of what he is trying to achieve with Northern Ireland.

"Family's crucial to me. We're all a family when we represent the country," he said.

"That's a family of players and a family of staff, but also as an ecosystem and domestic game.

"We're all the one family when we're together and that's a message that will always be strong while I'm at the helm."

What will new call-ups bring to Northern Ireland?

Elmore and Grant named in Northern Ireland squad

If Northern Ireland are to make it to their first World Cup in Brazil then there are a number of hurdles they will need to clear.

It would perhaps surpass even the fairytale of qualifying for Euro 2022, when Kenny Shiels led a squad largely made up of amateur players to the promised land.

A change in format has made replicating that feat more difficult, and if Northern Ireland can beat Portugal over two legs then they will face Croatia or, more likely, Iceland.

The Portuguese and Iceland have beaten Northern Ireland over the past two years or so - both quite convincingly.

Even if McArdle's young squad can defy the odds, they will likely face an additional inter-continental play-off in February due to their rankings. It's a tall order.

But that does not stop McArdle and Northern Ireland from dreaming. If anything, it is to be encouraged.

"I think the dream piece is crucial, so we've dreamed about how we get there and what it'll feel like when we do it.

"The other piece of it is the reality. We know it's a highly challenging task first of all to get through Portugal."

McArdle talks about moments within matches, and working with his staff to plan for in-game scenarios.

There's also the excitement that comes with such a big match, and McArdle admits he is "loving" his time in charge.

"You look forward to every game but it's one of those ties that gives you the opportunity to test yourself at the highest level.

"Also the excitement of possibly achieving something and punching above our weight, which we're special at doing."

In his career in football, McArdle has held a number of coaching, academy and development positions.

Before he joined Northern Ireland, he was head of elite women's football at the Scottish FA, and also had a brief interim spell in charge of their senior team.

While the belief is there, McArdle knows he is working on something longer-term, and that can be seen in the make-up of a young squad, which has been hit by a number of injuries to senior players.

While his first two international windows came in quick succession, with two victories over Malta followed by losses to Turkey and Switzerland, the summer has allowed him to spend time around the Women's Premiership in Northern Ireland, building relationships with players and those working in the league.

"I was still getting to know them as people, not as footballers, so that was really important for me to build those relationships.

"Not just the players, either. Getting to know the head coaches a bit more and some of the clubs at boardroom level, to understand how can I serve them and help the club evolution, the domestic league and pathways as well."

While captain Simone Magill is a big loss for the play-offs, she will be with the group for the camp as she builds towards a return to action and provide experience to what is a young group of players.

Not only that, but she will have her newborn daughter, Skye, with her for the duration. McArdle says having those moments are "special".

"Having Simone, Mark and Skye on camp is great. First of all for Simone and Mark to experience what the future is like when Simone's representing Northern Ireland.

"It gives us that window of opportunity and it's something we've planned together over the summer months.

"I think that's crucial because it's one thing knowing the players and the girls that represent us, but also the families that support them as well.

"I'm very passionate about that and I don't underestimate the power of it."

Given the themes throughout, it's no surprise what drives McArdle.

He grew up idolising the likes of Kenny Dalglish, who once was a loan player from Celtic at Cumbernauld United juniors near where he grew up.

His coaching influences are close to home too, and he cites Michael O'Halloran, a youth coach in Glasgow, and Sir Alex Ferguson, who was a "god" coming from the east end of the city.

Further afield, the likes of Arrigo Sacchi - whose AC Milan side he used to watch on VHS in the 90s - Jose Mourinho and Rafa Benitez have all factored into his thinking.

"What drew me towards Sacchi, Mourinho and Benitez was not just the tactical side of the game, but how they managed it and their leadership.

"They didn't play professionally and it kind of aligned with myself, although I didn't realise at the time."

But it's in Moodiesburn where his DNA is, and it is the values he learned there that have shaped him into the coach he is today.

"Growing up in the village and growing up as a family I was always going to care for people and be in a service role.

"It was always going to be my calling. I'm just blessed that football has given me the opportunity to develop a knowledge and skill set to work at the highest level of an industry."

McArdle's passion for football is clear, but family also plays a role in helping him escape the demands of the job.

He goes to the theatre with his daughter, Mya, or to the cinema or concerts with Tammy.

A sports fan, he also goes and watches his sons play football, without the stresses of management and coaching.

"Representing my family is everything to me.

"We've stayed in the same village all our lives. You represent the village as well and that becomes a big piece of what we do.

"So those aspects of family fuel you."

title: Test cricket's biggest scandals - your results revealed
description: See what BBC Sport readers voted as Test cricket's biggest scandals, together with contributions from the TMS team.
fullText:
On Friday, Australia will play their first Test in South Africa since the sandpapergate scandal rocked the cricketing world eight years ago.

To mark one of the biggest controversies the game has ever seen, Test Match Special asked you which is Test cricket's biggest scandal.

Ten of the most notorious scandals in Test cricket were picked out by a TMS panel and readers of the BBC Sport website then ranked them.

The results have been revealed on the TMS podcast by BBC chief cricket commentator Jonathan Agnew, former England fast bowler Steven Finn and TMS scorer Andy Zaltzman.

The full results are below and you can listen to the podcast here.

Pakistan had already lost the series in England in 2006, yet were cruising to victory in the final Test at The Oval. However, Australian umpire Darrel Hair asked for the ball to be changed midway through the afternoon session on the fourth day. Ball-tampering was suggested and Pakistan refused to play after tea. The match was abandoned and years later awarded to England, after some back and forth.

Agnew: "Pakistan weren't accused of ball-tampering, they were found guilty of ball-tampering, on the field, without any opportunity to defend themselves. The rule at the time was if the umpire on the field suspected ball-tampering, the ball was changed and penalty runs were awarded. It didn't feel fair."

Zaltzman: "It ended up with England awarded the Test so therefore they won the series 3-0. It means that whenever we look at the biggest first-innings deficit overturned to win a Test, this game comes out on top - 331 runs. It irritates me slightly."

England's Test match against Pakistan in 1987 was stopped mid-game for more than 24 hours when the tourists' skipper Mike Gatting became embroiled in a row with home umpire Shakoor Rana.

Agnew: "I'm a bit surprised this is so low. The knock-on was England didn't tour Pakistan for many years. England felt they were being stitched up by Pakistani umpires. There was a total lack of trust, going both ways, between England and Pakistan for a very long time."

Zaltzman: "This was before neutral umpires and there was a sense umpiring wasn't quite as fair as it could have been, which all exploded in that moment."

Finn: "It blows my mind that there weren't neutral umpires. My first summer of Test cricket had DRS and neutral umpires."

The third Test in the 1975 Ashes was abandoned when the pitch was vandalised overnight by supporters of George Davis, who had been jailed for armed robbery the previous year. "George Davis is innocent" was written on the wall around Headingley.

Finn: "I can't fathom turning up to a Test match and the pitch - the most sacred, untouchable of places - it's staggering that people managed to do that."

Zaltzman: "It highlights how vulnerable cricket is to this sort of thing. A small bit of the field is damaged and the whole game has to be abandoned."

Agnew: "There was no security. These days, the grounds are locked down. It was set up for an England win, but could have been a really good game of cricket. It's a bizarre story."

When Australia's richest man, Kerry Packer, failed to boost the ratings of his Channel Nine TV network with live cricket, he created his own product: World Series Cricket. The plan was simple - Packer recruited the best players in the world to stage his own matches.

Agnew: "Virtually everything you see about modern cricket can be traced back to World Series. It was incredible, innovative and exciting. I was 18 years old, playing club cricket in Melbourne and captivated by the coverage."

Finn: "There's a similar revolution going on at the moment with T20 leagues allowing players to drift away from Test cricket. The temptation to be involved in something new and exciting would have been very interesting."

Zaltzman: "It was extremely high-calibre cricket, but not even counted in first-class statistics, let alone Test stats. I don't really see it as a scandal at all, it was more cricket growing up. This really modernised the sport."

In the 1994 Lord's Test against South Africa, Michael Atherton was caught by TV cameras rubbing dirt on the ball. Atherton's explanation was that he was trying to maintain the condition of the ball, rather than alter it. Trouble was, he told the match referee he was using the dirt to keep his hands dry.

Agnew: "This was a really tough time. I've thought about this a lot over the years and I'm not sure Michael knew the rules at the time - cricketers often don't. It's OK to rub your hand in the dirt, but you can't put soil on to the ball. It was a huge story. It was everywhere."

Our top five kicks off with the Pakistan spot-fixing scandal of 2010, when no-balls deliberately bowled in the Lord's Test ultimately resulted in three of the tourists' players - team captain Salman Butt and fast bowlers Mohammad Asif and Mohammad Amir - spending time in jail.

Finn: "This was my first summer of Test cricket. It was such a weird atmosphere. We were warming up, looked up to the Pakistan dressing room and there were two officials in suits and blazers reading the News of the World. That was the day we went on to win the game. We didn't celebrate any of the wickets because of what transpired."

Zaltzman: "Amir had burst on to the scene as a teenager - he'd only bowled three no-balls in his previous five Tests. As a cricket fan, one of the deep sadnesses was Amir was one of the best talents to have emerged in years. It was an individual tragedy. A young player had been led astray."

The Australians feature again here, but this time the guilty party was England, who developed a plan of intimidatory fast bowling aimed at the bodies of the hosts' batters in the 1932-33 Ashes series.

Agnew: "For me, this would be bottom. It was an entirely legitimate ploy. They call us whingeing Poms, but the Australians were pretty good at whingeing about the way [Harold] Larwood was bowling."

Finn: "Cricket is a game of small margins. You use the laws and the bandwidth within those laws. Play on, I say."

The most recent of the scandals in our list is Sandpapergate, when Australia's cricketers were found to have used sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball during their Test match against South Africa in Cape Town.

Finn: "I was completely and utterly baffled and shocked that someone thought this was a good idea and they would get away with it. There are so many cameras and you are so acutely aware when you are playing that those cameras have the ability to zoom in. To think you'd be able to pull sandpaper out of your pocket, rub it on the ball and then hide it down your pants is completely unfathomable. I was shocked they had taken altering the state of the ball to that kind of level."

Agnew: "If you're a bowler you want to control what's happening with the ball and you'll see if something has gone on with it. For me, there are some unanswered questions. It was one of the most stupid things ever seen on a cricket field."

A close second in our vote was the Basil D'Oliveira affair of 1968, when England's tour of South Africa was called off over the inclusion in their squad of mixed-race all-rounder D'Oliveira. At the time, South Africa was operating under a system of racial segregation known as apartheid.

Agnew: "You can actually trace this affair all the way up to the birth of a new nation. When you unpick it, look at the consequences, it was eventually the birth of a new South Africa. For me, this would be number one."

Zaltzman: "There's still a lot that is not known about the decision to not pick D'Oliveira in the original England squad. There had been pressure put on him by the English cricketing establishment - the establishment came out very badly from that. It had a huge impact on the world and the gradual dismantling of apartheid."

Top of the list is former South Africa captain Hansie Cronje, who admitted to match-fixing having become involved with Indian bookmakers. Cronje's most infamous plot came in a dead-rubber fifth Test against England at Centurion Park in 2000. The match had been badly affected by rain, but Cronje was adamant the teams should do all they could to ensure it did not end in a draw.

He negotiated with England skipper Nasser Hussain for both teams to forfeit an innings, leaving the tourists with a final-day run-chase, which they completed. England were unaware, but Cronje had engineered a result.

Agnew: "This was unbelievable. It came to light by accident. The Delhi police were trying to tap a phone of a bookmaker and accidentally tapped the phone of Hansie Cronje. Thank goodness they did because hopefully it is now much more difficult for a player to manipulate games of cricket."

Zaltzman: "At the time, we all thought it was good. Cronje's generous deal made a contest on the final day of a dead rubber. Until the true story came out, we didn't realise what had gone was criminal. The shock of the story merits its place in this countdown."

Finn: "A lot of these things have been the catalyst for necessary change in cricket and this was the biggest one."

title: How promotion, relegation and knockouts work in Nations League
description: With more than half of the 2026-27 Nations League group stage completed, BBC Sport looks at what will happen next in the competition.
fullText:
England will close in on qualification for the 2026-27 Nations League quarter-finals if they beat Czech Republic at Wembley on Tuesday night.

Thomas Tuchel's side sit second after three matches in Group A3, with a win all but confirming their place in next March's quarter-finals.

Tuesday night will mark the final fixtures of the fourth round of group stage matches. The final two full rounds will be played in November's international break.

The eight teams to finish in the top two of the four League A groups will play in the knockout rounds that start in March 2027.

Teams finishing at the top of groups in leagues B and C will earn promotion for the next Nations League cycle, while teams that finish second in a League B or League C group will face a third-place team from the league above them in a promotion/relegation play-off.

The losers of the relegation play-offs, as well as the bottom-placed finishers from groups in League A and League B will be relegated.

As the Nations League format is changing for the next cycle, taking place across 2028 and 2029, all League D teams are guaranteed promotion to League C.

Additionally, no teams from League C will be relegated at the end of this cycle.

The new format will consist of three larger leagues, meaning there will not be a League D in the next campaign.

Portugal are the only side guaranteed to play in the quarter-finals at present, having won their opening four matches in Group A4.

Spain will join them from Group A3 on Tuesday, should they beat Croatia and Czech Republic fail to beat England.

If England and Spain both win on Tuesday, England would need just one point from their final two matches against Croatia and Spain next month to book their place in the last eight.

In Group A1, France and Italy sit in the top two spots. Belgium are a point behind Italy in third. Two of those three sides will advance to the quarter-finals.

It is a similar tale in Group A2. Netherlands and Greece are the top two, three points clear of Germany in third. With Serbia bottom on zero points, two of the current top three will advance.

In A4, Denmark are second and three points clear of Wales and Norway. One of the trio will join table-toppers Portugal.

The quarter-finals are played across two legs in March's international break.

The winners of each tie will advance to the semi-finals in June 2027, which are played in a one-off match across Wednesday 9 and Thursday 10 June. The final takes place on Sunday, 13 June.

While England's League A campaign has gone well so far, Wales' has been trickier.

In a tough group with Portugal, Denmark and Norway, Wales have picked up three points from four games after beating Norway 2-1 in Cardiff.

With Portugal already qualified for the last eight, Wales will need close to maximum points in their final matches against Norway and Portugal to stand any chance of making the last eight.

A third-place finish would put them in a play-off to avoid relegation in March, while coming last in the group would guarantee a drop down to League B.

Like England, Scotland have three rounds of fixtures remaining. They face Slovenia at Hampden Park on Tuesday.

Going into that tie, they are third in League B1 but only behind Slovenia on goal difference. A win for Sebastien Pocognoli's side would put them second behind Switzerland heading into the November break.

With Scotland's penultimate match coming against bottom of the table North Macedonia, wins in their next two games would all but seal a place in the top two heading into their final match against Switzerland, who are expected to clinch the automatic promotion spot.

Northern Ireland have had a successful international break with two wins, two draws and no goals conceded in their four matches in Group B2.

They sit top of the group by a point, with their remaining matches against bottom side Georgia and second-place Hungary.

Should they beat Georgia and Hungary fail to beat Ukraine in November's first round of fixtures, they will guarantee top spot and promotion. A win for them and Hungary doing the same would mean the two sides face off in a promotion-decider in the final round of games.

The Republic of Ireland are third in Group B3 following five points from their first four matches.

Their remaining two fixtures are against the top two teams Austria and Kosovo. Wins in both would guarantee a top-two finish and would also put them in a strong position to win the group, depending on goal difference and the result of Austria's meeting with Israel.

Once the Nations League campaign is concluded, all 54 competing nations will be ranked based on their performance in this edition of the competition.

That ranking will have a direct impact on qualification for the 2028 European Championships, being held in England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland.

Regular qualifying will take place between March and November 2027, with play-offs for the remaining spots in the tournament to take place in March 2028.

As there are four co-hosts and none of them have been granted immediate qualification, the number of how many qualify will effectively determine how many play-off spots will be up for grabs.

Uefa have said that up to two places will be given to the best-ranked co-hosts that fail to qualify for the tournament via its primary qualification route.

Scenarios have already been designed for occurrences where either two, one or zero co-hosts are given entry spots.

Depending on which play-off format is required, either eight or 12 teams will enter.

A total of 24 teams will enter the European Championships, 20 of them will consist of the winners of the 12 qualifying groups and the eight best runners-up from those group.

The remaining runners-up will enter the play-offs, alongside the Nations League group winners from League A, League B and League C that failed to finish in the top two of their Euro 2028 qualifying group.

If extra teams are required, the best-ranked League D group winner will enter the play-offs.

Any additional play-off spots that become available after that will filter down to the next-highest ranked Nations League finishers until the play-off spots are filled.

title: Wet races and why future of F1 engines appears to be V8 turbos - Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.
fullText:
Red Bull's Max Verstappen won his first race of the season in a dramatic rain-affected Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Kimi Antonelli finished second in the Mercedes and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who fought his way back to the front after an incorrect tyre choice at the start, completed the podium.

Antonelli extended his lead in the championship to 84 points, after team-mate George Russell retired with an engine failure.

This weekend, it's the Singapore Grand Prix - Formula 1's original night race.

Before the race at Marina Bay, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

Do we miss out on exciting wet-weather racing because an overly cautious approach is applied when rain occurs prior to the start of the race? We are watching the best drivers in the world, who have wet tyres, but it seems when it rains prior to the start of a race, the action gets under way too late. - Sam

This question comes up a lot whenever there is a wet race, but in this specific situation the delay in starting the race was not caused by any conservatism when it comes to wet running.

The cars were sent out on formation laps when the track was still pretty wet on Sunday in Malaysia, but then a bug in the wet-weather engine settings provided to the teams by the FIA affected a number of cars, including those of Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton on the front row.

That meant the formation laps had to be aborted, and a new code written and given to the teams to upload to ensure that did not happen again.

It just so happened that in the intervening 25 minutes, there had been no more rain, so the track was pretty dry by the time the race started. Although it has to be said that it took a safety car on lap nine before the drivers who had started on treaded intermediate tyres came in for slicks.

On a generic level, there is no fundamental objection in F1 to racing in the wet - most of the drivers enjoy it. But there is now a collective agreement that they will not race when they can't see where they are going.

So races are not started when that is the case - as it was at the original start time in Malaysia.

But if you cast your mind back to Brazil in 2024, and Verstappen's brilliant drive from 17th on the grid to victory, that was run in wet conditions.

F1 needs to have hard look at itself - Sainz

After the Bahrain Grand Prix, Lewis Hamilton said that, had he started on the intermediate tyres, he could have won the race. Given the race data and his pace, do you think that's a realistic claim had Ferrari put him on the inters at the start? - Michael

The truth is that Hamilton - and anyone else - will never know, because there was no direct comparison between his pace and Max Verstappen's in similar conditions.

In the first few laps, Hamilton was on slicks and Verstappen on intermediates. When Verstappen switched to slicks, Hamilton's tyres were much older.

On the very few laps when Hamilton was in clear air before he caught Isack Hadjar, his pace when generally nowhere near Verstappen's but then his tyres were nine laps older, so you would not expect it to be.

And then once he finally passed Hadjar, there were only three laps to go.

On one of them, Hamilton was within 0.1secs of Verstappen, on the other two he was 0.5secs and 1.2secs off. But how much were either of them pushing?

What we can say is that Verstappen looked imperious all weekend, and it was probably going to be difficult for anyone to beat him - even Hamilton, who, it's worth saying, on Saturday was not sounding that confident of challenging him.

But it's just a whole load of ifs, buts and maybes, isn't it?

Malaysia, true to form, brought a great race, chaos and weather. It was sold out. Fans have loved it, missed it, drivers liked the track. We know why it dropped off the calendar but what would it take to come back permanently? - Nick

Malaysia dropped off the calendar because the government there was no longer willing to pay the rights fee, feeling that the expense did not justify the return.

It returned only because the Crown Prince of Bahrain was keen to stage his race, F1 was happy to accommodate him, and he managed to strike a deal with the Malaysian government.

There's no doubt the race was a success. It had a record crowd of 261,000 this year, more than double the previous largest weekend attendance of 126,690, reflecting F1's growth around the world.

If Malaysia was keen on returning to the calendar on a more permanent basis, there is no reason why F1 would not listen to them.

But whether that led to a deal would depend on whether one could be struck that satisfied both parties.

With Red Bull running their own powertrains, what part does Ford play? - John

Max Verstappen's victory in Malaysia on Sunday was not only a landmark because it was Red Bull's first of the season - it was also their first as a power-unit manufacturer.

Red Bull Powertrains was set up specifically to make an engine for the new 2026 regulations, so the team could be in control of their own destiny following Honda's official withdrawal from F1 at the end of 2021.

Ford came on board as a partner early on, and this is much more than simply a badging deal in return for finance/sponsorship money.

Team principal Laurent Mekies said on Monday: "Ford has been with us on this project since pretty much the very beginning.

"They are a key strategic partner for us on these operations. They are helping us on a number of topics.

"Specifically, to give you a few examples, they are manufacturing some of the key elements of the engines.

"So, some of these key elements are manufactured in Milton Keynes (at the Red Bull campus), some of these key elements are manufactured at Ford. And they are a 200,000-people company. And therefore, also in terms of engineering, if and when we need specific support on some topics, we are able to get access to some very good specialists they have.

"Some of these specialists are actually with us in Milton Keynes, and they are able to help us on some specific topics. So it's a mix of manufacturing of key components and some very specific engineering support on some other topics."

Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app

Max Verstappen spoke recently about how much he enjoyed the endurance racing at the Nurburgring. And how he liked "pure" motorsport with the V8 engines and would welcome that or even the V10s back in F1. Is that even possible now? Or has F1 fully embraced the electric/hybrid system, and there is no going back? - Peter

This is a really complex topic, with many conflicting elements to it.

Verstappen - and Fernando Alonso and Lando Norris - has expressed his view this year that to return to "pure" racing, F1 should go back to naturally aspirated engines with no hybrid element.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem has also been pushing a return to naturally aspirated engines, first V10s early last year, and more recently V8s.

Ben Sulayem has cited the evocative sound of V8s as one his main reasons, as well as lighter cars.

But naturally aspirated engines would use more fuel, so the cars would for half the race or so actually be heavier than they are now. The FIA has even investigated the idea of refuelling returning - which is not popular with the teams.

In F1 these days, only Alonso and Lewis Hamilton survive from the days when the drivers could push flat out throughout a grand prix with no concerns about tyre management.

But occasionally circumstances align to allow that to happen again. And in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, on the low-abrasion Baku circuit in the final stint, it did.

Race winner George Russell said afterwards: "The final stint, I think, is the most amount of fun I've had in a race for as long as I can remember because the tyre felt great. We were pushing flat out every single lap. It was like qualifying one after another.

"You needed to be so alert around this circuit because the walls are so close, especially through the castle. You're threading the needle.

"Those final 10 laps felt really, really fun. And it almost felt like the stories I hear of the drivers in the early-mid 2000s, of when every lap was like a qualifying lap.

"The heart rate is higher, you're pushing the limit every single lap, there's no management. We've had a lot of conversations this year about power-unit energy management, but the tyre management is still there and it has been there for years and years (since Pirelli came in in 2011).

"But just with how the temperatures and the circuit fell out today, with the tyres there was no management, and that was exceptionally fun."

On a romantic level, there is an argument that this is what F1 should be about - drivers pushing themselves and their cars to the absolute limit all the time.

And, it's worth pointing out, tyres are as much of a problem on this front as engines - much more so, in fact, before this year.

But it's not as simple as that.

Statistics show that the years of refuelling from 1994-2009 had the least amount of on-track overtakes in history.

Then there are the optics of using more fuel at a time when F1 is trying to go net-zero carbon by 2030, even if the racing is a tiny percentage of the sport's overall footprint.

Naturally aspirated engines would also be extremely loud - which would put at risk races such as Miami and Las Vegas close to or in population centres.

And then there's road relevance. The manufacturers are not in F1 for fun. They're in it for marketing reasons. Most road-car engines these days are turbos, and have some degree of hybridisation.

The upshot of all that is that it looks like F1 is heading to a new engine formula - for either 2030 or 2031 - that features V8 turbos with in the region of 15-25% electrical power, mainly to be used as a push-to-pass system.

Bosses are aware of the mistakes with energy starvation that have been caused with the latest rules, and the idea will be to allow the drivers to operate with maximum power all the time, with the electrical elements used to facilitate overtaking.

title: Owner, businessman & player: Messi has big plans as a golden era ends
description: Lionel Messi's Argentina career will end in a friendly against Benin. BBC Sport looks at what next for the 39-year-old?
fullText:
Lionel Messi is about to play his last match for Argentina.

On what will be his 208th appearance, the country's most-capped player and record goalscorer will bid an emotional farewell in a friendly against Benin at the Monumental in Buenos Aires on Tuesday (Wednesday 00:00 BST).

Arguably Argentina's greatest ever player - only Diego Maradona comes close - announced his retirement from the national team on 31 August, six weeks after the World Cup final defeat by Spain, saying he had nothing more to give.

Coach Lionel Scaloni insists that if Messi ever wants to carry on, he can, and there is no embarrassment in changing one's mind. But that chapter seems closed.

His club career though goes on. The contract with Inter Miami runs to the end of the 2028 season, but it is reviewed year by year, and nobody close to him expects him to walk away a day before he has to.

In fact, it is quite likely he will renew it if he feels, mentally and physically, up for it.

Ask the people around him what comes after that and they smile, because Messi has never really planned beyond his next game.

Even so, the shape of what lies ahead is already in front of us. He will stay inside football, because he would struggle to live without it, but his other business interests stretch far outside the game.

Messi retires from Argentina duty with 'nothing left to give'

How Messi's decade of dominance almost never happened

Messi used to like the idea of being a sporting director or an adviser to the president, close to the decisions without all the travelling and the phone calls.

And asked recently whether he would rather be a coach or an owner, Messi chose owner.

A coach lives and dies by every Saturday and has to worry about far too many things for Messi's liking.

An owner shapes the direction of a club from a little further back. Having said that, he would be an owner who does not stop at approving the appointment of a manager and stepping away. He would want to be involved in everything.

The groundwork is being laid in Spain. UE Cornella, on the edge of Barcelona and in the fifth tier, is the nursery where young players grow. He bought it in April.

CD Eldense, in the second division, announced Messi as its new owner on 1 October, subject to authorisation from the Spanish sports council, the CSD.

Eldense will be the club that leads his football operation, but the target this season is not to get relegated, so former Villarreal boss Javi Calleja got the job with the arrival of the new owner.

The plan is to run both through people he trusts, who will act as a link between Messi and the clubs until the day he can give them his full attention.

For now he follows every Eldense match closely on his computer. After Eldense beat Real Oviedo by four goals to one, his first message as owner was an Instagram post that read "Aupa Deportivo".

The pull of his name has been felt as well. Around a dozen sponsors came forward within a couple of days, some of them brands that had been talking to the previous owners without ever closing a deal, and some that already have a relationship with him.

In Uruguay he and Luis Suarez founded Deportivo LSM in May 2025, and they won promotion to the country's third tier in its first season.

A network of more clubs was discussed at the start. But the sums needed to lift them up the divisions have cooled that idea quickly, and it is not on the table today. Messi's focus is to see whether Eldense can establish itself in La Liga.

There is a link to Miami as well. As part of his contract with Inter Miami, he will have some shares in the club when he retires. A franchise of his own is not part of the plan.

Could he go home to Newell's Old Boys, the club where he played as a child in Rosario? The idea has never been formally discussed.

It may have crossed his mind while drinking mate with Suarez, in the way a return to Barcelona or a spell at Napoli, the club of Maradona, might have.

Nobody close to the player expects it though. Everything is built around Europe and Miami, and the perfect home is waiting for the family in Castelldefels, close to the sea and Barcelona.

A rivalry that changed football

Goals, records, tears ... Messi's most iconic moments

Newell's will still be close, because the club is one of the sixteen academies at this year's Messi Cup.

If owning clubs is one love, youth football is the other, and his regular presence at his son's games and the Messi Cup are the proof.

He puts his money and his time into a tournament for Under-16 academies, which began in 2025 with eight teams.

Last year, the organisers expected him to come to one or two games, perhaps only the final, but to everyone's surprise, he sat through every match on every day.

This year the teams doubled to 16, from 25 October at Inter Miami's facilities in Florida, including Atletico Madrid, Chelsea, Barcelona, Inter Milan, Arsenal, UE Cornella, and others.

Away from the pitch, Messi has built a portfolio that helps explain why Forbes put his net worth at about $1.1bn, external in June, with earnings of around $140m over the previous year split between football and business.

His best known endorsement is the lifetime Adidas deal he signed in 2017.

The most visible piece is MiM Hotels, six boutique properties from Ibiza to Andorra, which Melia has run under a rental agreement since 1 November 2025.

MiM takes its name from Messi and the Majestic hotel group, and runs the hotels inside its Melia Collection.

In Rosario, his family firm invests in Carrasco M, a development of 24 homes by the Parana river, with Ángel Di María's property agency handling the sales.

He is also a partner in the restaurant chain El Club de la Milanesa which plans to open five branches in Catalonia, the first in Castelldefels.

He has a mate collection with the drinkware giants Stanley, the brand's first multi-year deal with an athlete, and he gave his opinion on materials and colours.

The business side began with his father. Jorge Messi, who died in August aged 68, looked after his son's affairs from the start, and some of his early advice led the family into trouble with the tax authorities in Spain.

The company then grew into branches for TV production, marketing, media and commercial partnerships, among others, all well established by the time Jorge fell seriously ill.

Messi trusts the people who run them, some of them with him since his early days at Barcelona, and a thorough filter means he only gets offered and chooses what he is comfortable with.

He sets his own relationship with the business world, and nobody imposes anything on him.

In Miami last November, Messi told the America Business Forum: "Business is something that interests me. I would like to keep learning because I know nothing and I am just starting out."

The portfolio his circle has prepared is already impressive while he finds more football targets to keep the flame alive.

title: What we learned from Wales' Nations League window
description: On the back of a demanding four-game international window, BBC Sport Wales assesses the key talking points from Wales' Nations League A campaign so far.
fullText:
Craig Bellamy didn't waste his words when asked for his thoughts on Wales' opening four games of their return to the top tier of the Nations League.

It is hard to argue after a window that saw Wales lose three of their four fixtures, beaten in Portugal and Denmark and – following the lift of an eye-catching win over Norway – beaten again by the Danes.

That said, Wales' hopes of staying in League A – and the possibility of securing a Euro 2028 seedings boost – remains in their own hands going into next month's final pair of fixtures.

But what lessons can Wales take from the two-week test of their credentials?

In the immediate aftermath of the Denmark defeat, Bellamy had the new four-game window on his mind.

The former striker insisted the idea made "no sense" and suited the bigger nations, some of whom – such as Jurgen Klopp's Germany – named two squads for the four games.

Any hopes of extended time with the squad to make a coaching impact on the training pitch evaporated amid the reality of the travel and recovery between games.

And the fear that an untimely injury to a key player would see them miss four games rather than the two they would have previously was proven to have foundation when Harry Wilson and Joe Rodon were deemed unfit before a ball was kicked.

It would have been a problem in the past during the peaks of Gareth Bale and Aaron Ramsey and the like, but is even more so now.

Throw in the intensity with which Bellamy wants to play, and the drop off in energy was evident after a relatively promising start against Denmark.

"I felt we were a little bit flat, not as intense as we wanted it to be," reflected midfielder Jordan James. "That was expected after a really tough game the other day."

The issue goes beyond the pitch with a few too many empty seats on Sunday night's game for anyone's liking.

There was some hope among Football Association of Wales officials that the additional fixtures would create further momentum in the window, but the draining impact of cost and travel for fans seemingly took its toll – and will hit the revenue.

Wales' issue in all aspects is that they have no option but to get used to it.

Euro 2028 qualifying – and the chance of playing in a major tournament on home soil – will adopt the same format for games next September and October.

Bellamy bemoans new schedule after Denmark loss

Hojlund penalty condemns Wales to Denmark defeat

It has highlighted a problem for Bellamy that seems difficult to solve.

"I look at the players who came off the bench; Wes Burns plays in League One, Mark Harris plays in League One and Josh Sheehan has played for years in League One," summed up former Wales striker Iwan Roberts.

"That is the problem: when the starting 11 is not working, Craig Bellamy looks over his shoulder, and it's not nice to say, but he's looking at League One players to try to make the difference."

He added: "We just haven't got the strength in depth to make the impact that you need in games when we haven't got the players that were out injured in this international break."

Already without several key figures, David Brooks - who has not started a league game for Bournemouth this season - was also forced to withdraw midway through the camp due to injury to further limit Bellamy's options.

Fresh from his terrific display in which he netted Wales' opener and won the free kick for Neco Williams' stunning second, Dan James did not feature against the Danes on Sunday.

Kieffer Moore was also not introduced until late on with the score at 1-0 to Brian Riemer's side. It brings us nicely to the next point...

In the immediate aftermath of the defeat by Denmark, Roberts questioned: "I think questions have to be asked when we are chasing the game, when we did concede that goal with 15 minutes to go, why on earth he didn't bring Kieffer Moore on until 83 minutes? And he didn't bring Dan James on at all."

Prior to the match, Bellamy had confirmed James was not fit enough to start, although he had hoped the Leeds United winger would have been able to feature off the bench.

Ahead of the four-game window, Bellamy cited his desire for Wales to find "the next Harry Wilson" in the absence of the 29-year-old.

But many supporters were subsequently critical of the head coach's remark given that no new debuts were given during the international window while some others who have struggled to hit the desired heights for their country were given more opportunities.

No player has scored more Wales goals since Bellamy took charge than Harry Wilson.

His absence was sorely felt as Wales failed to score in three of their opening four League A matches.

It led to former Wales frontman John Hartson calling for more calm from other attackers such as Brennan Johnson, Kieffer Moore and Lewis Koumas.

"We are snatching at things. We need to slow it down a little, you've always got a bit more time," he told BBC Match of the Day Wales.

"We're playing at the highest level with lots of players at Championship level, but they have to find a way."

A fully-fit Wilson could be transformational for Bellamy and Wales as they bid to achieve their goal of avoiding relegation back into League B next month.

These four games were evidence of the new levels Ethan Ampadu has reached.

The Leeds skipper offered performances that simply highlighted his growing maturity. He made his mark on games in a way he might not have in the past and showed he is very much a player Wales can rely on.

"He does it every week, eight out of 10 every game," said former striker Sam Vokes.

"The crowd were singing his name at the end, he gives everything."

A "dream" player was how former striker Nathan Blake put it, while Robert Earnshaw suggested Wales can expect more going forward.

"There's more levels to him," he said. "Look at Harry Wilson last year – Ethan can do the same. There's more to come."

Denmark away was a pretty dismal night, but there were positives in Portugal.

And if Denmark at home felt a game too far, there was plenty to like about the Norway win that gives hope to cling to.

Especially given that, before this window, Wales had yet to win a game at this level of the Nations League.

Ultimately, when the disappointment lifts a little, Wales were beaten by single goals in two games – with the most recent via a penalty following an avoidable mistake.

"The quality's high which we expect," said Jordan James. "You get punished for little things, but I've also realised that you can play at this level. We've competed well and the last two games we've been well in them."

How much money do clubs get for Nations League players?

Haaland 'gave me his shirt... but didn't take mine'

The win over Norway – coupled with their defeat by Portugal on Sunday – means Wales are still third heading into the final games, courtesy of the head-to-head nature of this competition's tie-breakers.

Over the previous three Nations League campaigns combined, teams that finish bottom of a League A group have an average of 2.92 points after their six games.

Wales already have three points, and they still have to play Norway in Oslo and Portugal in Cardiff in November.

Before the current international camp even started, Bellamy spoke about targeting third place.

That would give Wales a chance of avoiding being relegated to League B and it would also improve their seeding for the Euro 2028 qualifying draw.

So what about teams who finish third in League A?

In the 2020-21, 2022-23 and 2024-25 campaigns combined, teams finishing third in League A groups have ended with an average of 6.42 points from six games.

It means Wales would realistically need one more win, or maybe two draws, to stand a chance of finishing third.

Even if they finish fourth, the tweak to the format means that only the two worst-ranked bottom sides go down automatically, with the other two heading into a play-off against a League B runner up.

With Serbia, Turkey and Czech Republic yet to register a point, they may already have done enough to line up a two-legged battle for survival in March, with Bosnia-Herzegovina, Ukraine, Scotland and Kosovo among the potential opponents.

title: How perfect storm has rained on Derby's parade
description: BBC Sport looks at how Turki Alalshikh's aborted takeover of Derby County has contributed to a poor start to their Championship season.
fullText:
It was supposed to be a new dawn at Derby.

Instead, the Rams have been left to pick up the pieces after the last-minute collapse of Turki Alalshikh's takeover on the eve of the season.

This month, Mo Fuseini's last-gasp goal rescued a point at Burnley which stopped Derby going into the international break bottom of the Championship.

Yet they have just five points from their opening eight games and remain in the relegation zone.

So what impact has the aborted takeover had at Pride Park and what can head coach John Eustace do to salvage the season?

This season was supposed to be the one when the Rams pushed for promotion.

When Eustace took over in February 2025, Derby were fourth-from-bottom in the Championship and questions were asked why he swapped a promotion challenge with Blackburn, who were fifth, for a relegation scrap.

Internal difficulties and restrictions at Ewood Park played a part but Eustace was sold a long-term plan which was survival, consolidation and then challenging for a top-flight return.

Yet this term's promotion assault was significantly hindered when Alalshikh pulled out of his planned takeover an hour before the deal was due to be completed in August, leaving Derby scrambling after a summer of work.

The collapse blindsided the club and transfer plans were affected despite owner David Clowes remaining committed to bankrolling the Rams.

Derby chief executive Stephen Pearce has denied the summer disruption impacted recruitment but it is undeniable plans suffered.

"From a transfer perspective we hadn't lost anything we wanted to do," he told BBC Radio Derby.

Eustace admitted, though, they had to understandably review targets following the takeover collapse.

"Obviously, we had our targets that we were looking at and who we wanted to bring in," he told the Derby Telegraph this month.

"When the takeover eventually didn't happen, we've lost a lot of momentum on players that we were looking at."

Eustace wanted Liam Millar only for Birmingham City to sign the Hull City forward on loan for the season and Derby moved for Fuseini - who was due to join Blues before they signed Millar - from Union Saint-Gilloise on deadline day.

Ben Brereton-Diaz scored eight goals in 41 games for Derby on loan last season but the Rams' situation meant they could not move quick enough to bring him back and, by the time they did, the Southampton forward had committed to going to Sheffield United.

Birmingham winger Patrick Roberts was another on the list but the 29-year-old's wages were a stumbling block.

None of the players on loan last season had options to buy meaning the Rams needed to renegotiate for those who returned, with Bobby Clark costing £6m from Red Bull Salzburg as the club were left open to market forces this summer.

That did at least help them re-sign midfielder David Ozoh for £4m on deadline day, when Crystal Palace valued him at £10m at the start of August.

Clark, Ozoh and Sammie Szmodics - who has already hit the requirements to make his £2.7m move from Ipswich permanent - were influential last term but their returns only ensure the squad has returned to the same level as last season, rather than significantly improving it.

Pisa striker Henrik Meister, who has scored just twice in a year, joined on loan and was seen as a good back-up to Carlton Morris and Patrick Agyemang but the 22-year-old Dane has needed to lead the line with that duo injured.

He then suffered a head injury against Birmingham this month while Agyemang has been out since April with a serious Achilles problem.

Injuries have formed part of the problems at Pride Park with reigning player of the season Matt Clarke unlikely to be back before December.

Goalkeeper Jacob Widell Zetterstrom is also out for six weeks while Brighton loanee Eiran Cashin is sidelined and Derry Murkin, expected to be the Rams' first-choice left-back, is out until after Christmas.

It all means Eustace has been unable to field the same back four in successive games since August.

The head coach and Derby have been unlucky, with Eustace especially left powerless and having to continue to firefight 20 months after joining.

There was a clear intention not to be in the same position as this time last year, with a promotion challenge expected - and Derby resisted interest for players including Agyemang and Zetterstrom - but it is a frustrating mirror image.

With eighth place now enough for a play-off spot, it was viewed as an achievable target this year. Instead, their season is, so far, following a similar path after eight points from the opening 10 games of last term.

Yet last season, their form from the final 36 games - if averaged across the whole campaign - would have been enough to finish fifth rather than ending eighth, four points adrift of the top six.

It is proof Derby - who host Wrexham on Saturday - and Eustace can succeed despite their current position, but only adds to the frustration of another slow start.

His job is not under threat and it is recognised the former Rams midfielder is the best man to steer them away from trouble, with a track record to prove it.

He was sacked by Birmingham when they were sixth in 2023, with Blues going on to be relegated after appointing Wayne Rooney as his successor, while he saved Blackburn from the drop in 2023-24 before leaving them in the play-off places.

But, after the perfect storm which has enveloped Pride Park, Eustace needs the pieces to fall into place again.
