title: Inside Northern Ireland's football conveyor belt
description: BBC Sport NI spends the day at the IFA JD Academy Residential at Campbell College where Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill catches up with the young players hoping to graduate to a full-time career.
fullText:
Northern Ireland manager Michael O'Neill has made no bones about his desire to give youth a chance.

Included in the squad this international window are teenagers Ceadach O'Neill, Tom Atcheson, Braiden Graham and Kieran Morrison, while 21-year-old Patrick Kelly and 22-year-old Terry Devlin have begun to stake their claim for regular inclusion.

A golden generation, or is this simply Northern Ireland's football factory - the IFA JD National Academy - beginning to bear fruit?

As Northern Ireland fans began to digest Monday's 0-0 draw at home to Hungary, following a 1-0 win in Georgia on Friday which has ensured a positive start to their Nations League campaign, O'Neill visited Campbell College which is home to the academy where teenage hopefuls seek to develop into potential stars at club and international level.

"I know about all these players in here, know the clubs they are attracting attention from, their positions," O'Neill told BBC Sport NI.

"We have regular meetings as staff every month with regular updates on the academy and where those players are going.

"Our job is to prepare them as best as possible and guide them if that opportunity comes to take the next step into the professional game in England or Scotland."

The academy at Campbell College is a residential, designed for 24 elite young players at under-15 and under-16 level, providing preparation for life away from home should that come to pass.

While athletes, they remain students with equal emphasis on football and life skills. Education in the classroom is a key component because, in the world of professional football, there are no guarantees.

Academy student Bailey Magee plays at club level with Glenavon.

His day is typical for a 16-year-old with school dominating until mid-afternoon. Once the bell rings, however, it is time to hit the gym and the pitch before returning to any school work in the evening.

If his dream of becoming a professional footballer comes true, then spending so much time away from home will be worth it.

"Going away with Northern Ireland has helped me because I'm able to stay away from home and you get used to that a wee bit," said Magee.

"The hardest times are [after] Christmas because that's when you're coming back after spending a long time with family.

"The IFA and Campbell have done really well when you're trying to mix the two and balance football with studies.

"I'll work hard until the end of the year and whatever happens, happens. I'll maybe do A-Levels, maybe a B.Tech or full-time football academy with the likes of Linfield or Larne, so there are loads of different pathways for us."

Those sentiments are shared by 15-year-old Kayson Braniff who is currently on the books at Linfield.

"My dad had drilled it into my head that we need our studies," he said.

"It's not as if football is everything, studies come first because you definitely need them in case football doesn't work out."

Clubs in England have the ability to integrate young players into their systems from a young age, which can mean those from NI playing catch-up if and when they make the switch in their mid-teens.

Therefore, preparing potential stars for the rigours of life in a new environment with new coaches can only be enhanced by time in the NI academy which O'Neill believes makes teenagers "better equipped" to make their mark at an English or Scottish club.

Helping young players realise their professional dream is intrinsic, but for Northern Ireland, unearthing new stars to graduate into the senior team is equally important.

"Two or three years ago we brought players in a bit younger than their club career suggested they were at that level, but it pays dividends now," said the current boss.

"You need the right people in the right positions to make that work and I think we have that.

"Players have decisions to make on their club situations and international situations, but your pathway is very important as it builds a loyalty within players.

"We want young players from whatever part of the community they come from to be part of this pathway to become senior international players."

Pathways are all well and good, but watching previous graduates from the academy go on to wear the green jersey or star in Champions League games like Conor Bradley ensures it is a tangible goal for those currently involved.

The current Northern Ireland manager taking such an active interest helps too.

"He's a really nice guy and to think I could be in that team in the next few years, which is the goal, it's really reassuring," Magee said of his sitdown with O'Neill on Tuesday.

Braniff agreed O'Neill's interest confirms "he cares about the youth".

Both are hopeful they can follow in the footsteps of previous graduates. If that results in a move to a full-time club, it will represent another success story for the academy.

"It doesn't matter who it's for or where it is, so long as it's a professional team and a professional contract," said Braniff.

Watch our full behind the scenes access, external on the BBC NI YouTube channel right now.

title: The five titles that got away as Evans seeks WRC glory
description: As Elfyn Evans looks to finally clinch the World Rally Championship title in Sardinia, BBC Sport looks back at the five times he finished runner-up.
fullText:
Few leading sports stars have been so tantalisingly close to crowning glory for so long without achieving ultimate success as rally driver Elfyn Evans.

The 37-year-old from Dolgellau in north-west Wales has been runner-up in the World Rally Championship (WRC) five times in the past six years.

But that could all be about to change.

With this year's WRC calendar truncated by the removal of the planned Saudi Arabia finale, Evans takes a 17-point lead into the now season-ending Rally Italia Sardegna from 1-4 October.

If Evans can maintain his advantage over team-mates Sami Pajari and Oliver Solberg it will be a crowning moment for the Welshman, who would become only the third Briton to win the WRC title - joining Colin McRae and Richard Burns.

As he prepares to grasp history in Sardinia, BBC Sport looks back at the five times Evans fell just short of his dream.

No change for leader Evans after WRC drops finale

White, Netherlands, Evans and sport's other great runners-up

BBC to broadcast World Rally Championship from 2027

Evans does have a world title - winning the WRC Junior Championship in 2012 which earned him a full-time seat in M-Sport's Ford Fiesta.

However, it was a move to Toyota Gazoo Racing in 2020 that put his senior career into overdrive.

Only huge last-event misfortune cost him instant success in a season cut from 13 races to seven by the Covid-19 pandemic.

After placing third at Monte Carlo in his first Yaris outing, Evans and co-driver Scott Martin excelled at a weather-shortened second round to win Rally Sweden.

It put the Welshman top of the WRC driver's championship for the first time, and although record-breaking Sebastien Ogier would temporarily reclaim the lead, a second victory in Turkey saw Evans take at 14-point advantage over the Frenchman into the final event.

With 10 of the 16 stages complete, the less experienced of the two drivers remained on course for a maiden championship success.

But Evans' dream ended in devastating fashion when he crashed down a bank after being caught out by treacherous snow-covered mountain roads.

Ogier claimed a seventh world title by just eight points to leave his team-mate "gutted".

"When I braked on that, it was just like glass and there was no chance of us slowing down at all. It completely caught me by surprise," said Evans after the race, later admitting "it was a massive disappointment", which made him "more determined" for the year ahead.

Evans took that determination and experience into the new year and soon grabbed the lead in the season-opening Rallye Monte Carlo.

However, local favourite Ogier went on to win in Monaco, and then three more of the first six rounds to take a commanding grip of the 2021 championship.

The Welsh driver was not about to give up though. A second rally win of the season in Finland. and second place in the penultimate round at Rally Catalunya, once again forced the title race into a final-event decider at Monza.

With a potentially bridgeable gap of 17 points, the two Toyota rally crews swapped the lead throughout - but Ogier and co-driver Julien Ingrassia eventually came out on top to claim both the rally and the title.

"It's been a pretty OK year," a typically level-headed Evans reflected at the end of the race.

"Of course, I can't help but feel a little disappointed right now, you always look to the places you could've done better."

The following year could certainly have been much better - as Evans struggled with the newly introduced hybrid cars.

Going off the road in the opening round and forced to retire from three further rallies, Evans finished 2022 in fourth place, more than 120 points behind first-time champion Kalle Rovanpera.

"2022 fell below our expectations," a defiant Evans told the BBC before the 2023 campaign.

"We're coming into the new season looking for improvements - and we're hoping we can challenge for the title."

And challenge he did - winning round four in Croatia to take a share of the championship lead, tied with Ogier and one point ahead of Rovanperra.

However, a crash at Rally Portugal set his title bid back as he was forced to retire in round five and - despite a victory in Finland - Evans had to concede the title with one round to go.

A crash and a disappointing finish at the Central European Rally may have handed back-to-back titles to Finnish team-mate Rovanpera, but the Welshman was to end the season on a high.

Victory at Rally Japan was his third of the campaign - the best return in any season to date for Evans who declared "it feels nice after last year".

With Rovanpera following Ogier's lead for 2024 in deciding not to contest a full calendar, surely this would be the year their Toyota team-mate would finally get to stand atop the WRC podium?

Sadly for Evans, the opening paragraph of the BBC report for the season's first race set the tone.

'Elfyn Evans faded to finish a disappointing third behind winner Thierry Neuville at Rallye Monte Carlo.'

As it turned out it was second place in the driver's championship come December, but it was another disappointing season for the Welsh driver, with Neuville instead becoming a first-time world champion after Evans' years of waiting.

And Evans, of course, was runner-up - though only just.

As Neuville lined up in Nagoya needing just six points - he collected 17 - to end his own streak of five championship runners-up spots, the Welshman began Rally Japan in third place.

For the second year in a row, Evans saved his best for last and a back-to-back Japanese victory brought a double silver lining.

Not only did it see him overhaul Ott Tanak to claim runners-up spot for a fourth time, it also saw Toyota snatch the manufacturer's championship.

However, the big personal prize remained as elusive as ever.

"We're sorry we couldn't deliver [the drivers'] championship," Evans said, "but we'll try again next year."

A revamp of the points system for 2025 was welcomed by Evans; it also brought his tightest title race yet.

After second place to Ogier in the Monte Carlo curtain-raiser, the re-energised Welshman won in Sweden and Kenya - rallies the Frenchman sat out.

With a 36-point advantage, Evans had opened up the largest championship lead ever recorded after three rounds of a WRC campaign.

But he would not win again that season and though he never finished lower than sixth, Ogier gradually whittled away at his lead until it came down to just three points with one round to go.

That race was a brand new entry to the calendar, and there was uncertainty over what lay ahead at Rally Saudi Arabia.

The terrain proved brutal for all the drivers. Tyre problems galore saw the leaderboard shifting like the sand. It ended with Ogier in third and Evans in sixth.

The points-swing was seven. The Frenchman had won a record-equalling ninth WRC title by four points, and Evans had fallen just short for the fifth time in six years.

"We've done what we can, that's it," was his reaction.

"We're competitors at the end of the day, we always want better, we always want more."

But there is only one more thing to do. Finally shake-off the tag of nearly-man.

He grabbed the 2026 championship lead with victory in February's Rally Sweden and has refused to let it go.

Once again his rivals are Toyota team-mates. This time it is Pajari, who won three rallies in a row, before Solberg triumphed in Rally Chile at the start of September to put himself back in the title reckoning.

Evans will require at most 19 points to guarantee him the title, but has not finished higher than third in the past five rallies since winning in Japan.

He will also have to cope with being first on the road in Sardinia - sweeping the gravel which has frequently caused him trouble in the past.

"I think especially with opening the road, normally in Sardinia it's a significant disadvantage to run first," concedes Evans who says he will "ignore the championship situation".

"You can't really afford to [think about the lead]. I have plenty of experience of what not to do," he muses.

"But you know how it turns out. I think it's far less certain than what it appears on paper."

True, but maybe by Sunday, the paper in the history books will show Evans finally proved he is not just another runner-up.

title: Punish Man City this season, say other club chiefs
description: Manchester City's punishment for breaching Premier League rules should be handed down before the end of this season, senior football figures tell BBC Sport.
fullText:
Manchester City's punishment for breaching Premier League rules should be handed down before the end of this season, senior football figures have told BBC Sport.

The Premier League said on Tuesday that City had been found guilty of all charges relating to breaches of its financial regulations between the 2009-10 and 2017-18 seasons.

They included artificially inflating revenue by more than £900m through "sham" sponsorship deals.

City have repeatedly denied guilt and signalled an intent to lodge an appeal by the end of this week.

There have been fears that the process, which has taken three years since City were charged, could be drawn out for much longer.

However, senior figures within football have told BBC Sport they see no reason why the case cannot be concluded by the end of this season.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, one club official said: "It benefits everyone for this to be resolved as quickly as possible."

When asked if they believed it would be, they said: "Instinctively yes, but it has to be done right.

"We can all see what the risks are if it's not. But those risks have been there throughout the process, as they've won the league multiple times during it."

Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions

Guardiola backing Man City after guilty verdicts

Burnham 'really concerned' if Man City owners sell up after rule breaches

Another source said the process "should" be resolved by the end of the season, and they hoped any appeal would be "compressed".

The final decision rests in the hands of the independent commission, with the Premier League board - and City - able to suggest a suitable punishment before the panel makes its decision.

There is increasingly a desire to have the case resolved by the end of the season amid fears that allowing City to get to the end of the campaign without punishment could lead to uncertainty and farce, particularly if they were to win the title.

One section of the Premier League regulations says an appeal should conclude no more than 12 weeks after it is filed, and a decision should be made within 30 days of its end.

Procedures can be hurried to meet certain deadlines, like the end of a league season.

However, Ferran Soriano, the club's chief executive, has suggested the case will run for a long time.

Manchester City cannot make a further appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas), but could potentially claim the process was not impartial at the High Court.

The Premier League's statement, formally announcing the guilty verdicts read on Monday, said it wants the process to be "concluded as soon as possible".

Meanwhile, City club sponsor Etihad Airways said it is considering legal action against the Premier League.

In a statement issued on Wednesday, the United Arab Emirates-based airline said it "categorically rejects any finding, conclusion or implication that suggests the airline has ever been involved in improper commercial arrangements".

It added: "The Premier League's public communication of the commission's findings, following a period of selective leaks and reporting, has further created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the redacted published findings."

Etihad, City's main sponsor since 2009, also said it was given no opportunity to engage in a process that now reflects "adversely on the airline".

The statement added: "Etihad is deeply concerned by the way this matter has been communicated publicly.

"The lack of clarity and transparency, together with the selective disclosure of information, has created damaging implications for Etihad despite the airline not being named in the published decision.

"The Premier League must take responsibility for the consequences of the way in which these findings have been presented.

"Etihad will seek the relevant legal counsel on the options and recourse available to protect its interests."

The Premier League declined to comment when contacted by BBC Sport.

title: Criminal investigation? Relegation or expulsion? The key Man City questions
description: BBC Sport takes a look at the key questions following the guilty verdicts handed down to Manchester City.
fullText:
The verdict that football fans around the world had been awaiting for years is in - Manchester City are guilty.

The club still insists it is innocent of the financial rule-breaking charges first brought against it by the Premier League in 2023, and can appeal, so the legal wrangling is far from over.

And the verdict has unleashed some huge questions for both the near and long-term future.

The Independent Football Regulator (IFR) has said the independent commission's decision raises "serious issues".

BBC Sport has taken a look at the key questions in the case and what we know about each of them so far.

The deadline for Man City to make their appeal is Friday.

In previous instances - including the guilty verdicts and punishments handed out when Everton and Nottingham Forest breached spending rules - the appeal was heard and a decision made before the sanctions against the clubs was announced.

The clubs then appealed against the sanctions, too, and had their punishments reduced.

So precedent indicates that City's appeal will be considered and decided upon before punishments are declared. Though that is not guaranteed. And a subsequent appeal against any sanctions could follow.

Exactly how long the process - which will be heard by a new three-person commission - will take is as yet unclear.

One section of the Premier League regulations says that an appeal should conclude no more than 12 weeks after it is filed, and a decision should be made within 30 days of its end.

Procedures can be hurried to meet certain deadlines, like the end of a league season.

Man City cannot make a further appeal to the Court of Arbitration for Sport, but could potentially claim the process was not impartial at the High Court.

The Premier League's statement, formally announcing the guilty verdicts read on Monday, said it wants the process to be "concluded as soon as possible".

The phrasing may not offer any exact insight but the tone - of both the statement, and the strong language used in the independent commission's findings about the length of time the case has taken - is notable.

"It has taken us much longer than we would have wished, and much longer than we had anticipated would be the case when the hearing concluded, to produce our decision," the commission wrote. "That is regrettable."

It is clear that those in charge want the matter wrapped as quickly as can be done.

And it is arguably to the benefit of both Manchester City and all of the other clubs in the Premier League and English Football League to know where they stand sooner rather than later.

City are top of the Premier League, having taken a maximum 15 points from their opening five matches, but whether they are genuinely in a title race will be unclear as long as players, fans, and club owners are in the dark about what their punishment will be.

Were the appeal and sanctions process to drag on beyond the end of the season, it would be possible that legal challenges could be brought by teams who finished below City in the table, or are relegated, or were knocked out by them in the domestic cups, which would be far less viable if the club's 'real' position is known before that point.

There are two key scenarios here.

The first is that one of the sanctions Manchester City are given is so significant a points deduction that they finish this season (or another future campaign, if the process takes longer) in the Premier League's bottom three and are automatically relegated to the Championship.

The second scenario is that they are expelled by the Premier League, which would require 15 of their rival clubs to vote in favour of a motion decreeing so.

Were that to happen, the club's future would be much less clear and would require them to apply to the Football Association for re-entry.

Because the EFL and National League are separate entities from the Premier League, neither would necessarily be obliged to accept an entry request from Manchester City.

And, even if a request were accepted by the EFL, its 72 clubs would have to vote whether or not to accept them.

That is where the possibility of City beginning a reascent in League Two - or potentially even lower - arises from.

There is a huge sporting and financial difference between dropping down to the Championship, with the high possibility of being promoted back to the Premier League after a single season, and starting again far lower down the pyramid.

When Juventus were relegated from Serie A to Serie B in Italy, after being found guilty of match-fixing charges in 2006, they were able to retain some of the world's best players, including Gianluigi Buffon, Pavel Nedved and David Trezeguet.

They were willing to put up with a single season in a lower tier and, when the club returned to Serie A after winning the Serie B title, they immediately finished third and qualified for the Champions League.

If City faced only a single season outside the Premier League, players on long, lucrative contracts would likely be far more inclined to stay, and the economic damage of losing access to the top flight's TV rights income would be hugely reduced.

Guardiola backing Man City after guilty verdicts

Man City Q&A with Kieran Maguire & Dale Johnson

The Fraud Act 2006 states that dishonestly making a false representation with the intention of making a gain or avoiding a loss can lead to individuals being imprisoned for 10 years and facing an unlimited fine, if charges are brought and proven.

"Surely the Man City findings are now a police matter," said Lord Cruddas, a banker and businessman.

"If accounts have been falsified and auditors have been misled then it is potentially a criminal matter. The auditors will call in the police, directors are personally liable for any fraud of a UK company even if it is foreign-owned."

For the case to move from football wrongdoing to something more, there would first need to be an investigation by the relevant authorities.

The bodies who can investigate potential financial crimes in the UK include regional police forces, the National Crime Agency, HMRC and the Serious Fraud Office.

BBC Sport has contacted each of those bodies and been given no indication that any kind of investigation has begun, but some do not routinely confirm investigations owing to confidentiality.

Greater Manchester Police said: "No referral has been made by the relevant authorities in relation to any alleged criminal offences."

But former Manchester City chairman David Bernstein - who left the club five years before its current owners took control - raised the possibility during an interview on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"This is very serious and I wonder whether some of these issues might need to be referred to authorities outside of the league," Bernstein said.

"My immediate thoughts are - can the board of directors continue and should the people involved be suspended immediately?"

Football finance expert Kieran Maguire feels wider investigation may be unlikely.

"HMRC might consider it but there is not a lot for them to go on," he said. "There is certainly no corporation tax to recover. Football clubs lose money and City would have lost more money had it not been for the activities it undertook."

Fans and pundits have been making the point since news of Manchester City's guilt first broke - if they deliberately flounced the rules over the course of nine years, how can their owners possibly be trusted to run the club moving forward?

There is potentially a role to be played by the IFR, which was established in 2025 with the goals of protecting the heritage of English football, ensuring the financial soundness of clubs and promoting resilience in the ownership and spending of clubs.

The IFR awards licences to all 116 clubs in English football's top five tiers, which permits them to operate.

Club owners, directors and senior executives are subject to an enhanced suitability framework - a beefed-up version of the old-school 'fit-and-proper person's test'.

The Football Governance Act 2025 allows the IFR to suspend or revoke licences awarded to clubs as a last resort in cases of wrongdoing.

"The IFR has powers to assess the suitability of owners, directors and executives and we will use these powers where appropriate, in the interests of protecting the sustainability, honesty and integrity of English football where there is clear evidence of wrongdoing by individuals", IFR chairman David Kogan said in a statement.

"This includes taking account of findings made by the Leagues. However, as the proceedings remain ongoing between Manchester City and the Premier League we will await further developments.

"We hope it can be resolved quickly for the sake of fans."

And there is another possible scenario too - government intervention.

In 2022 Roman Abramovich was forced to sell Chelsea by the UK government, following the launch of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Abramovich's background as an oligarch meant the government froze his assets and threatened to conduct a full seizure.

Within three months the club had new owners.

The Manchester City owners are not subject to any action by the UK government, and all that has been formally declared is that the club broke football financial rules.

But the precedent exists that the government can be part of a process in which a football club owner is ousted.

Relations between the UK and UAE - whose royal family controls City's ownership group - were previously strong but have weakened to a degree in recent years.

Any form of ousting would prove a severe test of diplomacy.

title: £1.2bn on transfers with £830m inflated in sponsorships - Man City's 'asterisk era'
description: BBC Sport analyses Manchester City's dominance of English football during the period in which they were breaching financial rules.
fullText:
Outside Manchester City's Etihad Stadium is a lustrous silver statue of Sergio Aguero - mouth agape in ecstasy, kit swirling over his head - depicting his goal celebration after securing the club's first Premier League title.

It is the immortalisation of the most famous goal in English league football history, when City snatched the trophy away from Manchester United in the dying seconds of the 2011-12 season.

But what if the goal never happened? What if Aguero had never played for the club? What if City had opted to abide by football's financial rules instead of purposefully breaking them through a "disguised funding scheme"?

The revelation that the club has been found guilty of the charges brought against it by the Premier League three and a half years ago has left football fans around the world questioning the legitimacy of City's achievements between 2009 and 2018, when they were the most successful club in English football and cemented themselves among the global game's elite.

Some fans are referring to it as the asterisk era, and there is a possibility City could be retroactively stripped of the honours they earned during the period, with some clubs seeking legal advice over potential financial compensation.

So how exactly did City's "hugely overstated" income impact their actions in the transfer market, how key were the players who were brought in, and what does it all mean for both the past and the future?

Manchester City spent about £1.2bn on new players in the transfer windows between summer 2009 and January 2018.

In that time, the club won seven major trophies - three Premier Leagues, one FA Cup, and three EFL Cups - having previously gone without a significant honour since 1970.

The players they purchased during that time included some of the world's best, in all areas of the pitch. Multiple were signed for figures in the tens of millions every summer and made a huge contribution to the club's consistent success.

The graphic below demonstrates how much City spent in each summer and across the whole time period, and contrasts it with the amount of money that the commission which has found the club guilty determined had been falsely pumped into the club by its owners, under the guise of sponsorship income.

City did not only generate revenue from sponsorship funds in that time. And income is also spent on many things other than transfers, including player wages, utilities, insurance, infrastructure, marketing, foundations and more.

But the figures underline the fact that City would simply not have been able to purchase the quantity and quality of players they signed during their era of domination had they not been conducting what the commission described as a "concerted campaign to falsify" their financial accounts.

If City's financial power had been slashed by the extra £830m the commission says they falsely added to their books from sponsorships which were in large part funded by their owners, their transfer spend would surely have been massively reduced.

Add in money from falsely reported image rights and contracts and the total reaches £920m.

Chop the amount in half, say, and maybe they would only have brought in half the amount of players. Or the same amount, but heavily reduced in quality.

Which potentially means no Aguero, no David Silva, no Yaya Toure, no Kevin de Bruyne, or at least a significant reduction in the number or ability of the less glamorous players who were key cogs in the trophy-winning machine.

Would those successes have been achieved had the rule breaking not been going on in tandem? And what would the impact have been on all the other clubs who have played in the Premier League during that time?

Nobody will ever know. The seasons cannot be replayed. And so the outcomes exist in a kind of mixed reality where the world watched them happen, but isn't sure if they're really 'real'.

The era provided the foundation for City's ongoing success, too, meaning more trophies and TV income, and the chaos of the situation has also unleashed doubt about the present and future.

A quick quiz question - what do The Wizard of Oz, Super Mario Bros 2 and the ninth season of Dallas all have in common?

Feel free to grab yourself a hot drink and mull it over for a moment.

If you figured out that the plots of all three never really happened - because in their endings it was revealed that they existed only in the dreams of one of the lead characters - then very well done indeed.

So do the guilty verdicts mean the Premier League seasons between 2009-10 and 2017-18 should now be considered a figment of our collective imaginations too?

City have until Friday to mount an appeal. If that appeal is unsuccessful, then, at some point, the club will be given some sort of punishment.

Whether sanctions will retcon the past in any way is unknown.

And about moving forwards? Right now football fans, both of City and other clubs across the country, do not know whether the football they are watching is 'real' or not.

Are City actually top of the league and in a title challenge, or will they be docked points later in the season?

If they are linked with another team's star player, could that transfer happen or will they be unable to make deals at some point?

Will they be in the Premier League next season or will they be expelled and will there need to be a quite significant rejigging of the pyramid to accommodate them somewhere else?

And then there are questions about what comes later down the line.

Is anybody else breaking rules right now, which fans will only find out about in the future?

Does the potential for years of results to be retroactively kiboshed undermine the Premier League's popularity with fans, players and sponsors?

And can the action fans are watching week in, week out ever fully be trusted again?

The answers to those questions will determine the future of the biggest league in the world's most popular game.

title: Does Horner have a chance of Ferrari job? F1 Q&A
description: BBC Sport F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
fullText:
Mercedes' George Russell took his first victory since June by holding off Max Verstappen to win the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

Verstappen's Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar completed the podium on his return after missing three races with a broken wrist.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli finished fifth in Baku, meaning his advantage over team-mate Russell has narrowed to 66 points.

This weekend, Formula 1 heads to Malaysia, the host of the Bahrain Grand Prix - an event originally due to take place in April but which was postponed because of the war in the Middle East.

Before the race in Sepang, BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

Does Christian Horner really want the team principal job at Ferrari, or even have a shot at it? - Ben

This topic has become a subject for conversation in recent days following an interview Horner did with the Times, external as he promotes his new book.

Horner said: "At this stage in my life, there's only one team for which I would accept non-participation in ownership."

Asked whether he would take a job there, he replied: "Would I consider Ferrari? I mean, Ferrari is the biggest brand in Formula 1. It's the dream. And arguably it's the sleeping giant of Formula 1."

Ferrari team principal Frederic Vasseur made his views about Horner's intervention pretty plain after the Azerbaijan Grand Prix when he said: "Mr Horner is looking for a job - that, everybody knows - everywhere."

Vasseur said the speculation surrounding the team meant Ferrari were "not working in the perfect serenity".

Horner's comments seem to make it clear that he would consider a job offer from Ferrari. But the key questions are under what conditions he might accept it, and whether he would be offered it in the first place.

Horner has made it very clear over the years that he believes an F1 team needs one person in charge and in overall control.

It's highly unlikely he would get that at Ferrari, where chairman John Elkann and chief executive officer Benedetto Vigna will always have more authority than any team principal.

Even at Red Bull, where Horner had theoretical leadership at the F1 team, he was ultimately answerable to headquarters in Austria and that is what led to his removal in the end.

It's hard to imagine how Elkann and Vigna could or would countenance any situation where they were removed from any input into the F1 team.

And it's even harder to imagine a situation where that was not the de facto position even if a team boss had been given assurances they would be left alone.

Then there is the question of whether Ferrari would want Horner.

Horner comes with baggage. All of the above for a start, and on top of that there is the cloud under which he left Red Bull.

There is no doubt that he was a remarkably successful team principal there, the team winning eight drivers' titles, six constructors' championships and 124 grands prix in his two-decade tenure.

However, the team unravelled in his final 18 months in charge, in the wake of the accusations of sexual harassment and coercive, controlling behaviour that were made against him by a female employee.

Red Bull dismissed those allegations after two internal investigations led by external lawyers.

But they were a key factor in Adrian Newey leaving his position as chief technical officer - along with internal politics in which Newey felt his role had been diminished by Horner.

Newey was followed out of the door by long-time sporting director Jonathan Wheatley and head of strategy Will Courtenay.

Horner was finally dismissed following a slump in form which Red Bull bosses concluded the team did not appear to be capable of arresting under his leadership.

In the Times interview, Horner says that the only justification he was given by Red Bull for his sacking was "it was more Christian Horner Racing than Red Bull Racing".

He adds at other points in the interview: "I am a bit of a Marmite character. I know I'm not everybody's cup of tea. It's impossible to be." And: "I'm the cure and the problem."

Clearly, any decision as to whether Horner is the person you want to lead your F1 team would need careful consideration.

It's also worth mentioning that Ferrari driver Lewis Hamilton has made it pretty clear over the past few years that he has little time for Horner.

'I still feel as fast as anybody' - Alonso on why he's staying in F1

Why hasn't the FIA made a decision on the final two races of the season? They've cancelled the final rounds of the World Rally Championship and World Endurance Championship because of the Middle East conflict. Surely they should be confirming the changes in the calendar now? - Nigel

To start with a point of order, it is Formula 1 that decides the calendar - as in, the commercial rights holder - not the FIA, the governing body. The FIA's role is effectively only to rubber-stamp F1's decision.

As things stand, F1 is planning to end the season as the calendar was originally scheduled - with Las Vegas followed by Qatar and then Abu Dhabi, external over the last two weekends in November and the first in December.

Although the war continues between the US/Israel and Iran, the advice F1 has been getting is that the situation in those two countries is stable, and there is not a high risk of attacks on civilian infrastructure.

The UK Foreign Office, for example, does not advise against travel to Qatar and Abu Dhabi., external It simply says the situation there "remains unpredictable" and that "there is a risk of more attacks and unforeseen escalation in the region".

And the two countries consider themselves open for business.

However, F1 has a contingency plan.

Imola in Italy is preparing to host a race on the weekend of Abu Dhabi.

If the two Middle Eastern races cannot happen as a result of an escalation of the situation in the Gulf, Imola would step in and hold the season finale on 4-6 December.

But unless and until that happens, there is no confirmation of changes to make, as there are currently no changes.

Why wasn't a virtual safety car called when Valtteri Bottas crashed right at the end in Azerbaijan? This was obviously a dangerous situation as the car was buried in the barrier. And it almost cost George Russell a well-deserved victory - Steve

Valtteri Bottas crashed at Turn 15 on the penultimate lap of the race, meaning his Cadillac was in the barriers there when leaders George Russell and Max Verstappen came around their last lap less than a second apart.

Normally, a car in the barriers on a street circuit means at least a virtual safety car.

However, in this instance a spokesperson for governing body the FIA says that race control "determined that it was safe to let the leaders race to the line - they were able to cut the apex at T15, as it's a relatively slow corner".

In the event, the Bottas incident, the FIA says, was "successfully managed by localised double yellows".

Whether this was the correct course of action, and whether the decision was influenced by wanting to prevent the grand prix finishing under caution, will remain a subject for debate.

On the one hand, it allowed the race to continue and be exciting to the end.

On the other, slowing for the incident caused a technical issue for Russell's Mercedes.

"I lifted off the power and when I went back, I had no turbo, so then I had no power," Russell said. "Max almost got me at the line."

Russell was able to mitigate this loss of power from the internal combustion engine because, it being the final lap, he could use up all his battery on the run to the flag, rather than have to keep it balanced for the following lap.

So he managed to hang on - but by less than 0.2 seconds.

Had he not, the decision by race control would have come under a great deal more scrutiny than it did.

I love your explainers. Please can you analyse the data explaining the jump Williams have made with their upgrades. It seems more significant than Aston Martin's much written-about 'leap'? What are the percentages, averages etc. - John

First of all, thanks very much for the compliment.

This is a complex topic. There is no doubt that the lighter chassis and aerodynamic upgrades introduced by Williams in Baku marked a step forward.

It was their best qualifying performance of the year in terms of positions, even if in percentage terms they were actually slightly closer to the front in Miami back in May.

But it's too early to judge the Williams upgrades - and Aston Martin provides a clue as to why.

This year, there is quite a swing in competitiveness for certain teams depending on circuit type.

Regardless of the upgrades, Williams always expected Baku to be one of their stronger circuits - short-duration corners and long straights suit their car.

But they struggle in long-duration corners, so it will be interesting to see how they go this weekend in Malaysia, because Sepang is full of them.

Likewise, Aston Martin have specific weaknesses.

Their aerodynamic upgrade in Hungary improved their chassis performance by in the region of two seconds a lap.

Hence their significant improvement there and in Zandvoort, where Fernando Alonso drove superbly to take two points for ninth place.

But, despite its upgrade for Zandvoort, the Honda engine remains the worst on the grid, in terms of overall power, driveability and energy management.

So, it's no surprise that on two hugely engine-dependent circuits such as Monza and Baku, they would struggle.

On that basis, Aston Martin can be expected to be relatively more competitive again in Singapore, with its low power-sensitivity, and where Alonso is usually outstanding.

title: How Manzambi became one of Europe's best young talents
description: Aston Villa's summer signing Johan Manzambi has been nominated for the best young player at the Ballon d'Or ceremony. BBC Sport looks at his rise.
fullText:
In just two years Johan Manzambi has gone from being an unknown teenager to a European star.

The 20-year-old could be named young talent of the year at the Ballon d'Or ceremony next month having only made his senior debut for Freiburg in 2024.

A breakout season in Germany last term convinced Villa to pay more than £50m for a player with just 47 club starts.

Manzambi scored on his full Villa debut to help secure a first Premier League win of the season and now faces Scotland with Switzerland in the Nations League on Tuesday looking to continue his progression.

Life bright for Gilmour after baseball and World Cup heartache

Vega hails Yakin and Manzambi as Swiss head for Hampden

Manzambi is already in the discussion with fellow nominees Lamine Yamal of Barcelona, Real Madrid's Yan Diomande and new Manchester City midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi for the best young player in the world award.

He scored three goals in four games for Switzerland at the World Cup before a knee injury ended his tournament, only a year after making his full international debut.

It is a rapid rise for a player who used to return to Freiburg's academy to do his washing.

Bernhard Weis, who gave Manzambi his debut for Freiburg Under-19s, told BBC Sport: "He is playing for the professionals and he comes to us at the academy and brings some dirty clothes.

"He didn't have a washing machine so he comes here and washes some clothes.

"I would speak with him and then he would pick up some young guys from the under-13s, under-14s and take them to the train station.

"He would see the guys and say, 'come with me, I'll take you to the station', so they could get home. That's Johan Manzambi."

As for his profile, though, Weis did not expect a Ballon d'Or nomination coming so quickly.

He added: "I didn't see that. I saw something for the first team, for us, but this way, no chance.

"The first half year at Freiburg it was not so easy for him, he's not so strong and he's not so stable. He put on five kilos and then he thought, 'now I go, it's the right moment, I will be faster and stronger'.

Massimo Lombardo, Servette's academy director agreed. He first worked with Manzambi when he was 15 and oversaw his early development before he moved to Freiburg as a 17-year-old in 2023.

"It is a real surprise for many people, that he can do something special so quickly," he told BBC Sport.

"For me, the difference he can make is because of his mentality, personality, enthusiasm and courage. He has the technical skills and tactical skills and the physical possibility now to perform in England.

Why Newcastle target Manzambi is in demand

"Mentally he was always a player who, when he came into the training session and games, always wanted to do something important. You can see that as a player who starts with Freiburg, he took his chance.

"I can remember his second game with Switzerland, against the USA and he scored. It was always important for him to come into the game and to do something."

Last season Manzambi was named the Europa League's Young Player of the Season, as Freiburg lost the final to Villa in May.

He scored 12 goals in 61 appearances and Weis, now Freiburg II boss, has watched him develop, with Manzambi also learning German in three months.

It helped him swiftly move from the academy to the first team, making his debut against Heidenheim a year after joining.

Weis described him a "difference maker" and, among players in the Bundesliga in his position last season, Manzambi ranked first for 10-plus metre progressive carries (116), shot-ending carries (13) and fouls won (78).

Villa knew he would move this summer so it was a case of now or never for Emery. Had he gone to Newcastle instead they believed his next move would put him out of their financial reach.

The Magpies were always wary of being hijacked, having previously lost Victor Munoz to Liverpool and, while they agreed a deal with Freiburg, they never got a yes from Manzambi.

Villa then turned the versatile forward into the most expensive Swiss player in history - surpassing Granit Xhaka's £38.25m move from Borussia Mönchengladbach to Arsenal 10 years ago.

Yet, despite signing a five-year deal, Weis backed him to make the next step quickly.

"I think Aston Villa is the right club for him. He will play every time when he is fit and that's the right way. Then I think he plays two seasons at Villa and then he goes to the next step," he added.

"After the World Cup I said he must go to the Premier League. Bayern Munich were mentioned, he didn't go to [Borussia] Dortmund, [Bayer] Leverkusen. It's the right way."

Freiburg have made light of Manzambi's absence and went into the international break unbeaten and sitting third, having topped the Bundesliga after three straight opening wins.

Without him they have won six of their seven games in all competitions, scoring 24 goals, and boss Julian Schuster said earlier this month he had hoped to keep the player.

It was the same for Lombardo at Servette, who fought to keep their young talent, but the former Switzerland international admitted Manzambi had made the right decisions.

"We wanted him to stay with us, we gave him a contract but he wouldn't sign and history would say it's a good way, he came to Freiburg and played with the under-19s and was always improving," said the ex-Perugia midfielder.

"Then Johan came into the first team and performed so well he started to play from the beginning and the coach couldn't move him from the starting XI.

"With us he was incredible, he wanted to stay on the pitch to improve, to stay in the games and he had a lot of personality at 15. You can see into a group of young players who has the personality to speak.

"He has a lot of personality. Other players were stronger and quicker but he trained with enthusiasm and I saw a young player who wanted to do something special."

title: Inside Liverpool's increasing global investment in youth
description: Liverpool are becoming increasingly proactive in their search for global young talent. BBC Sport takes a closer look.
fullText:
Liverpool may have made three signings worth more than £100m each over the past two summers in Florian Wirtz, Alexander Isak and Bradley Barcola, but internally there is a realisation that after a significant amount of young talent was sold last summer, the club need to replenish that talent pool.

Since 2020, Liverpool have made more than £230m from selling players who have represented them at youth level and that has been a major part of owner Fenway Sports Group's self-sustaining business model, with the funds reinvested into the club.

Since Brexit, there is a 'premium' on young English players and it is why Liverpool's global talent department, led by Matt Newberry since the winter of 2024, now have a major role to play.

Fifa rules state that international transfers of players are only permitted if the player is over 18 and, since Brexit, Premier League clubs are no longer permitted to sign players under 18 from European countries.

Newberry's team is responsible for deciding which young talents from overseas should be targeted for a move. Using their wealth of contacts across the world, including dedicated regional scouts, Liverpool are becoming increasingly aggressive in the space.

It helps that new sporting director Julian Ward is well known for his global network.

"Any player we sign, the first intention is that we want them to play in the first team and there's a belief that there's a chance for everyone that signs here," Alex Inglethorpe, Liverpool Academy director told BBC Sport.

"That really is no different since the impact of Brexit on the English market, which is quite significant. There's now a premium on young English players. Time will tell if that premium is worthwhile but it's definitely a change.

"So it's fairly natural for a club like Liverpool to look within Merseyside in the first instance then broaden that out - national recruitment happens at 14 and after that you look globally, which is what we've done."

Mor Talla Ndiaye's journey began in the Senegalese village of Sandiara where he played football in the streets.

He progressed through the ranks playing for Bousports Academy in the town of Thiadiaye before joining Amitie Football Club in the city of Thies.

Come January this year, Liverpool fended off interest from other European clubs and signed the 18-year-old for about £1m plus add-ons.

"You have access to certain talent based on points accrued from playing homegrown players. We had a couple of ESC (elite significant contribution) spots to explore the wider market and that's something which, even prior to Brexit, was a fairly normal thing," Inglethorpe adds.

Ndiaye is a left-footed centre-half who played for Liverpool in pre-season under Andoni Iraola and was an unused substitute in three games in the second half of last season under Arne Slot.

"He's an incredible story, isn't he? From where he's come from to where he is - and he's such a humble kid. He's an unbelievable lad to work with," Rob Page, Liverpool's U21 boss, told BBC Sport.

"There's exciting times ahead but he's got a lot of work to do. He's nowhere near the finished article but he's on the right path. His attitude is spot on and he's at the club that will definitely help him develop."

At Liverpool, there is an optimism regarding Ndiaye and a genuine belief that if he makes it to the top, it could be one of the great football stories.

Liverpool opened discussions with his academy and his agency, Sport Cover, after scouts spotted his performances at the U17 World Cup in Qatar last winter and several video calls were arranged before the club's representatives travelled to Senegal.

Once there, they visited where Ndiaye trained, as well as meeting the people that supported his development before presenting their vision to him directly.

A round-table meeting was organised with his family to help understand his environment, the story and the context in which he grew up.

Ultimately, Ndiaye chose Liverpool because they offered the clearest pathway and their approach in getting to know him stood out.

Ndiaye isn't the only player to have been identified and recruited by Liverpool's global talent team.

After the U17 World Cup, Liverpool also made a £2.6m move for another centre-half, Ifeanyi Ndukwe.

Ndukwe was impressive in pre-season and the 18-year-old Austrian has gone on loan to Levante in La Liga as he looks to obtain a UK work permit.

The list doesn't stop there. Samuel Martinez, the 17-year-old Colombian midfielder, will join next summer after having "30 offers from around the world, external", according to his father.

It doesn't always work. Arsenal beat Liverpool to the signing of Andria Bartishvili from Georgia last month and the 17-year-old will join the Gunners next summer when he is 18.

But the moves for Martinez and Ndiaye showcase Liverpool's willingness to spread beyond Europe and into areas they may not have explored before. Given the inevitability of other top clubs circling emerging talent, the idea of selling the pathway that Liverpool offers is imperative.

Since arriving, Ndiaye has settled in with a host family - which is normal when players aren't from the area - that are used to working with Liverpool.

"Players come from varying parts of the world and, when someone comes in and doesn't speak much English at the start, you have to help with that and help understand culturally the differences in food, the weather and even the pitches you play on," Inglethorpe said.

"There's a lot of understanding in terms of the level of support that's needed and the most important thing you can give a young player is the time.

"I'm delighted that Mor made such a strong impression and he's done as well as he has, but we hope that he's going to get better and better as he continues to adapt."

This summer, Liverpool also confirmed moves for Lucca Brughmans, the 18-year-old Belgian goalkeeper, and Djylian N'Guessan, the 18-year-old French forward, with both set to join the club permanently in 2027.

In the modern game, most talents are known and there aren't many hidden gems anymore, but Liverpool believe that by digging deeper and wider they can get ahead of the curve, using their global network and their reputation as a club that will help players develop.

title: 'I still feel as fast as anybody' - Alonso on why he's staying in F1
description: Fernando Alonso commits to staying in Formula 1 with Aston Martin for at least one more year. - and explains why to BBC Sport.
fullText:
Fernando Alonso has committed to staying in Formula 1 with Aston Martin for at least one more year - and says the biggest single reason for his decision is because he "still feels fast".

The 45-year-old Spaniard has been weighing up his future all year. And while, like Max Verstappen, he has been outspoken in his criticism of the new hybrid engines introduced in 2026, his love for the sport has won out.

"First, this is my life," Alonso told BBC Sport in his only English language interview about his decision, which was announced on Tuesday., external

"I have this in my blood and I keep racing and I keep enjoying and this is a way of life, in a way.

"Probably for me the biggest, or the clearest thing to keep racing is I still feel self-confidence that I have something extra.

"And when I think about stepping down or taking a different role in the team or not driving the car or whatever, in a way I feel it should not be like that because I still feel as fast as anybody. So let's have another go."

His own personal performance was only one factor at play in Alonso's decision, he explained in an extensive and open conversation.

Alonso also considered the new rules, and the competitiveness of his team, which has been close to rock bottom for most of this season.

Alonso is regarded as one of the all-time F1 greats, and has created an iconic status over a career that dates back to 2001.

And he continues to reject any suggestion that he has lost any of his ability.

"When I jump in the car, in free practice, I will see some people braking late in a corner, locking up the front tyres here or there, making mistakes there," Alonso says.

"I feel that I'm OK. Or, I'm faster than them.

"So when I get changed and I go back home, even if I'm P18, in a way I feel some satisfaction and pride inside, even if it should not be the case because we are not competitive.

"How will I be in the living room, watching TV, thinking that I can do better? That will be my feeling now. When that changes, if I see that I lost abilities, I lost speed, I lost reflexes, I lost something, then I will be happy to watch from my living room the race.

"At the moment, I feel it was not the time because I'm better than that guy. I'm better than that other guy. I will think like that. And I cannot stop racing if I still think like that."

Alonso has only had a couple of chances this year to prove his point that he's still as good as he ever was. One was at the Dutch Grand Prix, when he finished ninth, holding at bay the faster cars of Alpine's Pierre Gasly and Racing Bulls' Yuki Tsunoda in the final stint.

I suggest to him that it was a typical Alonso drive, proof to those who doubted that he still has it. But he says it will have had no impact on the audience.

"You only prove to people when you are in the podium or you are on TV," he says. "That's where eyes are open, and people remember suddenly that you're still on the grid.

"So now I'm at peace with this period of time that I'm anonymous, and no one knows that we're still there and we're still fast.

"We are preparing ourselves for the moment of truth and that will be a surprise for everybody again."

Along with Max Verstappen and Lando Norris, Alonso has been one of the drivers most critical of the 2026 rules.

Drivers feel the new hybrid engines, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power, have diminished F1's challenge.

The key problems are the fact the cars run out of half their energy long before some corners, a process known as "derating", and that some of the sport's most demanding corners have been neutered because they are used to charge the batteries.

Alonso, as is his way, has produced some particularly pithy turns of phrase this season to express his unhappiness.

He has called F1 the "battery world championship". He has described fast corners as "the charging station for the car" and said that "the chef could drive the car" in a particular corner in Bahrain that used to be a major challenge.

And he's been dismissive of the increased number of overtaking moves created by offsets in energy levels between cars, calling them "avoidance actions".

How did he square all that with deciding to keep racing these cars he dislikes so much?

"That's a good question," he says, "because that was the hardest thing for me."

He says he hopes the changes being made to change the power ratio to 60-40 in two steps by 2028 "will make things a little bit easier".

"This year, there have been some good races and some bad races," Alonso says. "Maybe some of the shorter circuits that you had the battery until the braking point are changing the way you perceive the driving.

"And some of the circuits like Silverstone, Spa, Suzuka, they were very bad, you know, because they derate and things like that.

"Maybe even for next year they can tweak a little bit the battery power to have a little bit maybe less battery for longer or something like that because F1 at the moment is not natural driving.

"Reaching the top speed in the middle of the straight, it goes against the driver instinct of braking late and going on power earlier. It seems that if you want to drive these cars fast, you ended up going slower and that's not the way it should be."

Alonso says that, as something of an elder statesman, he "feels some responsibility also in this regard to help the sport" make the right decisions for the future.

And the willingness of governing body the FIA and commercial rights holder F1 to accept there is a problem and make changes to address it has also been a reassurance.

"It does help that the sport keeps chasing ideas and talking to the drivers and the teams (about) how to make things better, even for the next set of regulations," he says.

"This gives me also some hope that I will enjoy more the driving next year than I did this year."

It has been a dismal year for Aston Martin, whose car has been uncompetitive, while Honda's engine has been the worst in the field on the Japanese manufacturer's official return to F1.

But a massive update to the car for the Hungarian Grand Prix cut something like two seconds off lap times, offering hope for next season.

A key influence in Alonso's decision was Adrian Newey, whose arrival as managing technical partner in March 2025 delayed the start of work on this year's car, the first of a cascading series of issues that led to this year's performance.

Alonso has been waiting his entire career to work with the man regarded as the greatest technical mind of his generation, perhaps ever. So giving up after just one, highly compromised, year together felt senseless.

"This team has all the ingredients to have success in the future," Alonso says, "and I didn't feel that this was the moment to leave. It was the moment to keep on going, giving a second chance to Honda as well to fix their problems as well and stay together with the team.

"Adrian was probably the biggest contributor to this. We didn't start it right this year but things are moving in the right direction and he's capable of changing things very quickly.

"Aston is my family. I know Lawrence (Stroll, the owner) and Lance (Stroll, Alonso's team-mate) for many, many years. We keep open conversations, many different topics, every week. And that will be the case also for next year."

Honda's engine upgrade, which debuted at the Dutch Grand Prix at the end of August, was not especially convincing.

Alonso has bad memories of Honda from his time with McLaren from 2015-17, and he admits living through a similar experience again "has been difficult".

But major steps have been taken to address the internal issues at the company and Alonso says: "They are moving in the right direction. There are no guarantees that next year the engine will be completely fixed but all the changes that are happening in Honda made sense, so I have faith.

"The trust that I have in the team, it didn't change even throughout this difficult year. In the future, I don't know how long it's going to take, but it will be a successful team, and I want to be part of it."

There was one final factor - family. Alonso became a father this year when his partner, the Spanish television presenter Melissa Jimenez, gave birth to their son, Leonard, in March.

Has that had any effect on his approach to life and his career?

"I would say not," Alonso says. "I was (initially) thinking yes, and I tried to think about, family first, what will be the best for my son next year if I have this tight calendar or not and things like that.

"But then quickly I realised that it was not really a key factor. This year it was difficult for him to travel; he's only six months old now. But I think next year he will come to 50% of the races or more.

"So I could even enjoy my life more, travelling around the world with my son. That's a huge privilege that I will hopefully enjoy next year.

"Racing next year, it was my natural, final decision. I will be racing in any car, even when I stop Formula 1, but F1 is still in my blood.

"One more year made all the sense in the world for now."

"I see that it would not be only one year, but I don't have any pressure to think about it."

title: Man City CEO defiant over Premier League charges
description: Manchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano issues a defiant message to the executives of other teams about the club being found guilty of a majority of Premier League charges, BBC Sport has been told.
fullText:
Manchester City chief executive Ferran Soriano has issued a defiant message to the executives of other teams about the club being found guilty of a majority of Premier League charges, BBC Sport has been told.

He was speaking at a board meeting of European Football Clubs (formerly the ECA) in Copenhagen before its general assembly on Tuesday.

Soriano was said to have vowed to fight the charges and the process had a long way to run, reiterating what the club's chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak said in a letter to fans.

The Press Association reported Soriano told the executives "it's taken eight years to get here and it's going to take a lot more time", referring to the start of the Premier League's investigation in 2018.

He then left the meeting without answering any questions from the media.

The report added Manchester United's chief of international football relations Jean-Claude Blanc and Everton owner Dan Friedkin - there in his capacity as owner of Roma - were among those to attend.

City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centering around claims they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent financial regulations.

On Friday, it emerged they had been found guilty of the vast majority of the 115 charges brought against them.

Premier League clubs are seeking legal advice about compensation relating to the charges, while BBC Sport has been told City will appeal.

Sanctions are yet to be announced, but repercussions could include a points deduction, expulsion from the top flight or a huge fine.

The Premier League has declined to comment, while City released a statement saying the "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality".

Chairman Al Mubarak told supporters on Saturday he was confident the club would prove their innocence.

"The Premier League process still has a long way to run, and our confidence and intent in proving the club's innocence is just as strong as when this began," he said.

"There are so many things that I would like to be able to share with you to help you understand why we feel so confident in our position.

"But the strict confidentiality of the legal process and our determination to respect it means I cannot do that at the moment. Even this letter underwent several legal checks to make sure it complies."

title: Is Premier League possession football on the way out?
description: Only 36% of teams with more than 60% possession have won this season in the Premier League. BBC Sport looks at why?
fullText:
In the early 2000s, Premier League defences tried to make the pitch as small as possible, giving their opposition less space to score in.

Coaches therefore encouraged their attackers to play quickly, taking advantage of open space that saw them face fewer defenders.

Logically, this made total sense.

It was Pep Guardiola's influence that, in part, flipped this logic on its head over the last decade.

His Manchester City sides looked to force teams back into a compact defence, a challenge that in theory should be harder to break down.

The counter logic was that they were forcing opponents to give them a familiar challenge they were prepared for.

City's defenders also had big spaces to cover, often standing at the halfway line.

But for Guardiola, those spaces were less worrying if the ball stayed near the opposition's goal for as long as possible.

After all, if you have the ball, the opposition cannot score.

So why now are teams that dominate the ball dropping points?

Across this season's opening 50 Premier League matches, teams recording at least 60% possession have won only 36.4% of those games, while in 2023-24, the figure was 53.5%.

Does this suggest possession football is on the way out? Well, the answer isn't that simple.

Are teams winning because of their low possession, or having less possession because they have taken the lead early?

There could be some truth in both answers.

Let's use Xabi Alonso's Chelsea as a case study.

They won their opening games against Fulham and Brighton - 3-2 and 4-3 respectively - with the minority of possession, then drew 2-2 with Hull and lost 3-0 to Brentford despite having considerably more of the ball.

Against Brighton, Chelsea's 25.6% possession and 146 successful passes were their lowest recorded figures in a Premier League match, with records beginning in 2003-04.

And yet, the Blues scored four goals.

For three of them, accelerating play from throw-ins and counter-attacks allowed their direct attackers to find space against fewer defenders.

This dynamic can partly be explained by Fabian Hurzeler's Brighton wanting to dominate the ball - with only Manchester City averaging more possession than the Seagulls this season - which played into Chelsea's hands.

Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer, Pedro Neto and Morgan Rogers boast skillsets suited to transition-heavy football, and the low possession against Brighton helped them play to their strengths.

Counter-attacking comes with a stigma.

It is more accepted underdogs like newly promoted Hull will play this way. For bigger teams, there is an expectation to eventually control the game with the ball.

This makes a low-possession approach harder to sell long term, even if the players might look better conceding possession.

And that disconnect between players' skillsets and tactics could help explain some dropped points.

Alongside Chelsea, Manchester United have also suffered in this way. Under Michael Carrick, they have averaged 1.5 points per game with more than 50% possession. With less, that rises to 2.6.

Clubs without the same expectation, like Brentford, Leeds and Hull, can concede possession and have built squads for that style.

With impressive box defenders, dangerous counter-attackers and set-piece specialists, their tactics can align with their players' strengths, helping them compete against more less aligned opponents, irrespective of their wealth gap.

In recent seasons, there has been a rise in man-to-man pressure that has made building out from the back challenging.

Teams, as a result, have looked to play long over the press or past its first line into space for players to drive with the ball - think the likes of City's Nico O'Reilly or Arsenal's Declan Rice.

Both of these have been great solutions to the initial problem, but it does mean that teams full of physical athletes, focused on bringing down long passes or driving with the ball over distance, could be less suited to the intricate play required to unlock stubborn defences - a situation commonly faced by teams who have more of the ball.

To dominate in 2026 likely requires a squad that has enough solutions in small spaces as well as big ones.

Opponents have used man-to-man defending closer to goal too, making it harder to find the unmarked player, a key attacking principle used in Guardiola's positional play.

With players marked, attacks can then depend on winning one-against-one situations, requiring individual quality often in the form of dribbling.

Given the way teams have been built over the last few years, certain sides may lack this type of problem solver.

It is important to note possession is an average across a match, which can hide how the scoreline changes a team's approach.

Chelsea scored within seven minutes in each of their opening four league games after which opponents pushed forward looking for a goal. The Blues dropped deeper, defending their lead and attacking the space left behind.

Across their opening five matches, Chelsea averaged 51.4% possession when level, 34.5% when ahead and 67.2% when behind - highlighting how much their possession has varied with the score.

Interestingly, protecting a lead created favourable opportunities for Chelsea's attackers to play intuitively, carry the ball and attack space. When chasing a goal, they had more possession but appeared to lack solutions against compact defences.

Arsenal show the value of being able to do both parts well when needed.

Bukayo Saka and Max Dowman's dribbling, combined with the passing of Martin Odegaard, Martin Zubimendi, Bruno Guimaraes and Christos Tzolis, provides repeatable solutions against packed defences.

Their set-piece threat can also give them the lead when clear chances are difficult to create despite dominating the ball.

Once ahead, Arsenal's possession falls from 60.4% to 56.6% - a small drop but a signal of intent.

Gabriel, Ezri Konsa, Jurrien Timber and Rice then offer the defensive quality to control the game with less of the ball.

Manchester City protect leads differently. Their possession remains at 64.9% when ahead. This approach works partly because it is familiar to the squad Enzo Maresca inherited from Guardiola in the summer.

Rather than repeatedly defending their penalty area, they protect their advantage by keeping the ball and keeping opponents away from their goal given their technical quality.

From all of the successful examples, the same objective is being achieved: a game that suits your players and one that makes the opposing players uncomfortable.

"If you are brave, they have to play a game that is not [the opponent's] preferred game," current Liverpool boss Andoni Iraola told The Independent in 2025.

At the time, he was managing Bournemouth - a team notorious for winning with less of the ball against some of the league's best.

It would be fair to argue fewer teams in the league now have the players or the solutions needed to break down teams given the evolution in defensive tactics, and advantages are more commonly found in attacking the big spaces.

Therefore bridging that gap, from thriving without the ball to dominating with it, will take time for those wanting to do so.

But at the top level, this is time not all coaches are afforded.
