title: Why are Arsenal struggling to score in WSL?
description: Arsenal are already playing catch-up in the WSL title race because they are struggling to score goals. BBC Sport examines why.
fullText:
Arsenal go into their Women's Super League game at Stamford Bridge knowing defeat by rivals Chelsea would be a damaging result just four weeks into the season.

It feels like an extreme assessment but the Gunners know all too well that if they fall behind early on, it is hard to catch up in the WSL title race.

Renee Slegers' side are already seven points behind leaders Manchester City, albeit with a game in hand, and it would be foolish to give them further breathing space.

Successive draws against Crystal Palace and Manchester United have dented Arsenal's start to the campaign.

Their slow starts have proven to be their undoing in previous campaigns as their search for another WSL title has gone on for seven years.

In that time, they have lifted the Women's Champions League and Women's Champions Cup, proving they have a squad capable of winning major trophies.

But it is the same story so far in 2026-27 as Arsenal's shooting boots have been missing and their lack of ruthlessness in front of goal has proven costly.

They face serial winners Chelsea on Sunday (16:30 BST) knowing they need to get over the line this time.

"If I look at the last two games, not turning that dominance into goals and wins, is something we have to look at," said Slegers.

"We believe in the quality of the squad and their ideas. We can create in a variety of ways. When that starts clicking, it will be really good.

"It really is about the details in the final third."

Fox makes 'easy decision' to sign three-year Arsenal deal

Unanswered questions for English teams as Women's Champions League returns

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

Arsenal were tipped by many to win the WSL this season having invested in their squad in the transfer window.

Germany duo Lisa Baum and Selina Cerci boosted their attacking ranks, though England winger Beth Mead left to join Manchester City.

Slegers still has a wealth of options to choose from up front with Chloe Kelly, Olivia Smith, Alessia Russo, Stina Blackstenius and Caitlin Foord all available, as well as the anticipated return of Michelle Agyemang later in the season.

But despite an array of talent, Arsenal have struggled to score goals.

Across their first three WSL games they have had 56 shots and scored just twice.

They needed a 95th-minute equaliser to draw 1-1 with Manchester United and only beat HB Koge with a 93rd-minute penalty in the Champions League on Tuesday.

They had 70 touches in Crystal Palace's box and 79% possession but were held to a 0-0 draw by the newly promoted side two weeks ago.

"It's a combination of things. There's some details in decision-making and some details in the technical execution," said Slegers after their draw with United.

"It's also the ruthlessness in front of goal. I know the players want it. They want to execute for Arsenal.

"What kind of situations are we setting up? What spaces do we occupy in the box? What are the runs like, but also other moments in the game?

"Counter-attacking moments and set-pieces - those are also moments for us to be dangerous from so it's not only breaking down a low block."

Arsenal are creating chances so that is not the problem - but is there anything Slegers can do to change things?

The obvious question is why England's number nine, Russo, is not playing in that position.

Only Manchester City striker Khadija Shaw scored more goals in the WSL than Russo's 13 last season and she was second in European competition, behind Barcelona's Ewa Pajor.

But Slegers, who has often rotated Russo's position, has preferred her in the number 10 role at some point in all their WSL games so far this season.

It has not paid off for Russo, who is yet to get off the mark, despite attempting 11 shots, including 10 from inside the box.

In total, she has netted just three times in 507 minutes as an attacking midfielder, compared with the 21 she has scored in 2,913 minutes as a striker under Slegers.

Russo has created 1.42 chances per 90 minutes in the number 10 role, more than as a striker (1.27) but she has fewer shots and passes finishing in the final third, and fewer shots from inside the box.

Another striking statistic is that Russo and team-mate Blackstenius have never directly combined for a goal while the England forward has started in midfield.

Against Manchester United, as Arsenal trailed 1-0 and were pushing for an equaliser - which eventually came from full-back Smilla Holmberg - Russo continued to play in midfield.

When asked what Slegers' plan was, she said: "Basically, we were expecting to be spending a lot of time in their half.

"It was looking at how we could pose as much threat as possible in the box, hence why both Stina Blackstenius and Alessia Russo started.

"There was double threat in that position. We wanted to keep Alessia as high as possible on the pitch. We know she can do both roles really well for us.

"She's a fantastic number nine. Stina played her role. Selina Cerci also made her official debut. She has other threats, like her aerial play and instincts in the box.

"We have three [players who can play there] but the plan was to have two number nines in the box as much as possible for crosses."

title: Man City? I feel cheated - when do Stoke City get our FA Cup?
description: BBC Sport columnist Tony Pulis explains what he and all Stoke fans are thinking after Manchester City are found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges they faced.
fullText:
That is what all Stoke City fans have been asking me since the news broke on Friday that Manchester City had been found guilty of breaking the majority of the 115 financial rules they have been accused of breaching.

While the process is far from over because Manchester City are expected to appeal, I have to say this verdict and the whole situation has left a very sour taste in my mouth.

Taking my Stoke side to the 2011 FA Cup final was one of the highlights - if not THE highlight - of my 50 years in football as a player and manager.

That day in May will also live long in the memory of all Stoke fans who followed their team to Wembley dreaming that they would win the greatest club cup competition in world football for the first time in their long history.

The club we were playing, Manchester City, were on their way to dominating English football.

At that time they had not won a major trophy for 35 years but they were a team that, in transfer fees and wages, cost well above anything Stoke City could ever aspire to.

Think back now, and I can still picture walking out before kick-off to see our end of the ground decked in red and white and hear the amazing rendition of Delilah from our supporters.

Many of those fans had come from all corners of the world, and had spent or borrowed fortunes to make it, just to say: "I was there."

For me, experiencing that game and occasion with Stoke City's owners, the Coates family, was really touching too.

Continuously, over many decades, they have helped to finance their own community's local professional team.

For Peter, Denise, John and all the family and friends who in good times and bad found the money and spirit to back the club, it was their one day in the sun.

It was the same for all of us connected with Stoke. This was our day, that day that many smaller clubs and their fans pray for.

Although we lost 1-0, our players were fantastic and gave, as always, a fully committed performance against the odds.

Yaya Toure, who scored the winning goal, was reportedly earning 10 times what we were paying any of our players and, on his own, had cost more than our entire starting 11 when they had signed him from Barcelona in 2010.

After the game, my disappointment was buried in the fact we had played a team full of superstars, and faced an elite coach in Roberto Mancini, and had just fallen short.

Today, I feel very differently, as I am sure people connected with the other clubs affected by City's successes in the same period, between 2009 and 2018, do too.

We lost, but to a team that have been found guilty of breaking the financial rules set out by the Premier League.

In doing so, they did not just beat Stoke in an FA Cup final, they collected a stack of titles and went on to completely dominate English football for more than a decade.

So, with those rules having been broken, what will the punishment be?

Well, I know all Stoke supporters will be demanding that City pass the trophy over and every club that has been affected by their actions will be considering their legal options.

I don't expect Manchester City to phone me or the club up and offer back the 2011 FA Cup and the winners' medals their players received.

I don't seriously believe any other trophies and titles will be handed back over either. A points deduction and a massive fine feels far more likely.

But I still feel cheated. Whatever happens next, we won't ever get that day back and the chance to celebrate around Stoke-on-Trent with the cup and medals we so honestly fought for. After breaking the rules, Manchester City got to do that instead.

Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

The computer hacker who tried to take down Man City

Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? What next for Man City

Man City legal fight could spiral out of control - Purslow

title: From turgid to thrusting - mixed start for new Scotland
description: BBC Sport Scotland's Tom English reviews a mixed start to life as Scotland head coach for Sebastien Pocognoli as his side open their Nations League campaign with a goalless draw in Slovenia.
fullText:
For 45 turgid minutes in Slovenia, some in the Tartan Army might have reimagined the Steve Clarke years as a time of plenty, the halcyon era of ambitious football when Scotland were an all-electric thrill-fest.

The opening half of the Sebastien Pocognoli regime was, as expected, disjointed.

It was also, rather unexpectedly, devoid of anything remotely related to what Pocognoli laid out as his non-negotiables - front-foot pressing, high intensity, speed of thought and mind, goal threat.

They had no shot on target and lost so many aerial duels that you stopped counting beyond the half-hour mark. They took 38 minutes to touch the ball in Slovenia's penalty area.

It wasn't like they were under major pressure - the hosts are a pretty toothless side - but neither were they accurate or energetic. Everybody who preached patience in the new era gulped hard. This was not good. We didn't expect champagne, but this was stale beer.

And then it changed, not so completely that Scotland roared and won the game, but they certainly cleared their throats as an attacking force.

Gilmour catalyst, impressive Welsh, but same issue for Scotland?

Scotland begin Pocognoli era with encouraging Slovenia draw

From being impotent, they became thrusting. That second half was as big a 0-0 rout as you're likely to see. Frustrating, but encouraging at the same time.

It will be agonising for Oli McBurnie that he's still without an international goal - he said he wouldn't sleep after failing to convert a one-on-one with Jan Oblak - but his second-half performance was full of good things; efforts on goal, link-up play, presence and danger.

Robbie Ure hit a post, Kieron Bowie had a terrific chance, but missed. The three strikers drew a blank, but as far as 0-0s go, it offered hope that more productive days may lay ahead with these guys.

There are two ways of looking at the draw. All 10 starting outfield players had a shot on goal, the first time that's happened since June 2022, against Armenia.

Scotland had 17 shots, their most attempts in a competitive game in more than 14 years. The flipside is that they have now failed to score in three tournament games in a row for the first time in almost 22 years.

After the break, Pocognoli dropped McBurnie a little deeper, in a pocket just behind Robbie Ure and then Bowie when he came on. He got Billy Gilmour to sit lower in midfield, where he had time to dictate, which he absolutely did. Gilmour tied it all together in the second half.

Pocognoli called it "two games in one game" and he was right. The subtle shift in McBurnie's and Gilmour's positioning brought Scotland alive.

It was an impressive watch; ambition, relentlessness, belief. No cherry on top but enough there to leave most folk happy about day one and motivated ahead of day two, against Switzerland on Tuesday night at Hampden.

McBurnie, not so much the prodigal son but now the forgiven one, had that big chance six minutes into the new half - the one he would have dreamed about. He created it for himself, winning possession and getting into a wonderful position right in front of an isolated Oblak.

He could have dinked it as the goalkeeper committed himself, he could have slid it home to Oblak's left or through his legs. Instead, he went for the flourish, trying to take it round the Slovenian and marking his return to the side after 2,005 days in the wilderness with a first goal on his 17th appearance.

Oblak won the duel. Painful, for sure, but a prelude to a stirring second half from the striker and his new-old team-mates. McBurnie played a slick one-two with the increasingly dominant Gilmour, who had his shot saved. Oblak was by a million miles Slovenia's best player.

McBurnie had a header fly over, Aaron Hickey had a header just wide, Bowie came on and had an immediate impact. He had three chances in eight minutes - a tame shot, a clipped attempt and then the big one - played in by Gilmour but pulled wide. In that moment, he joined McBurnie and Ure (after hitting a post late in the first half) in the torture chamber.

In the midst of all of that, McBurnie powered a header on goal, but Oblak was equal to it. That was Scotland's ninth consecutive crack without reply. They were utterly dominant but achingly goalless. So much encouraging stuff and yet just one point to show for it when it really should have been three.

Pocognoli said he was heartened by that second half. Scotland fans should be buoyed by the new head coach recognising the problems in his team and then fixing them.

With such a small track record to feed off, the subject of his tactical acumen was always going to be an interesting one - the ownership of the second 45 minutes showed that he's no slouch in identifying and changing the things that need to be changed.

Going with McBurnie and Ure up front was something of a surprise, but it sent a signal out that Scotland are here to go on the offensive rather than just defend their way to decent outcomes.

That didn't materialise in the first half, but it clicked in the second. It's a touch surreal that, at the end of another game when Scotland failed to score, there is a lot to be hopeful about in the men who are there to supply the goals.

McBurnie, Ure and Bowie are an exciting trio. When others are fit, there's Che Adams, Lawrence Shankland, Tommy Conway and Ross Stewart. Young James Wilson will have his moment at some point. New blood has joined the old guard and things should be better when everything settles down.

For Pocognoli, the next test is the biggest one. Switzerland, ranked 14th in the world, are missing some serious operators, but they are brilliantly coached by Murat Yakin and they're settled and formidable.

Their whole is greater than the sum of their parts. This will be a fascinating examination of Pocognoli's prowess. Win on Tuesday night and it's lift-off time.

title: Who made an uncharacteristic error? England player ratings v Spain
description: England were beaten 3-2 in an entertaining game by world champions Spain in the Nations League - here's how BBC Sport rated the Three Lions' players.
fullText:
England were beaten 3-2 in an entertaining game by world champions Spain in the Nations League - the Three Lions' first match since this summer's World Cup.

Lamine Yamal gave Spain the lead before goals from Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane put England ahead.

Kane then missed a penalty before Alex Baena curled in to level the score, with Mikel Oyarzabal scoring the winner.

Here's how we rated England's players - and you can have your say in the comments at the bottom.

James Trafford: Showed early on his ability to play with the ball at his feet but conceded after just two minutes when Guehi gifted the ball to Lamine Yamal. An important save stopped Torres making it 2-0 in the first half. 6

Jarell Quansah: Continued at right-back after showing what he could do in the position at the World Cup. A physically dominant performance and had a chance to score but headed over. 6

Ezri Konsa: Some shaky moments for Konsa and England's back four but the centre-back regrouped and got better as the game went on. 6

Marc Guehi: An uncharacteristic error gifted the ball - and the opening goal - to Lamine Yamal. 5

Nico O'Reilly: Put in the cross for Kane's goal as England took the lead in the first half. Did a good job of trying to deal with Lamine Yamal. However he gave the ball away for Spain's second goal. 6

Elliot Anderson: Nearly punished for giving the ball away in a dangerous position in the first half but Ferran Torres rolled his shot wide. Anderson and midfield partner Lewis-Skelly took some time to settle in what was a tough night in the middle of the pitch against a Spain side who moved the ball so well. 6

Myles Lewis-Skelly: A first England start in centre midfield for Lewis-Skelly after shining for Arsenal. Given the tough task of trying to shut off the supply to Spain's conductor, Rodri. A solid performance. Replaced after 70 minutes. 6

Jude Bellingham: The Real Madrid midfielder produced another dominant display and was unlucky to be on the losing side. He provided an assist for England's equaliser and won a penalty which Kane hit against the bar after slipping. Stung Simon's palms with a drive in stoppage time. 8

Bukayo Saka: Won a couple of free-kicks around the box and shot over from the edge of the area in the first half. Curled just wide with the score level but a quiet night for the winger. 6

Anthony Gordon: The Barcelona winger scored an excellent goal on the counter-attack. He kept calm when played through on goal by Bellingham when his pace put him clear. A dangerous cross in the first half after England went behind and a threat in behind all night. 8

Harry Kane: Started dropping deep in the first half in search of the ball after England went behind. Scored the second with a deflected header to put England in the lead but missed a penalty when they had the chance to add a third in the second half. 7

James Garner (on 70, Lewis-Skelly): Took on Lewis-Skelly's role of trying to keep Rodri quiet. 6

Morgan Rogers (on 70, Gordon): Did not get much of the ball in his 20 minutes on the pitch. 6

Morgan Gibbs-White (on 83, Saka): Came on and played on the left wing. 6

Calvert-Lewin (on 83, Kane): Not much time to impact the play. 6

Jarrad Branthwaite, (on 89, Guehi): A late change for Guehi in the England backline. No time to make an impression. 6

Subs not used: Pickford, Steele, Alexander-Arnold, Scott, Chalobah, Hall, Eze.

England embrace the chaos - but control also needed to win big prizes

Spain beat England in thriller after Kane penalty miss

Tuchel rues 'big mistakes' - did Man City charges have impact?

title: Russell faultless and Hadjar excellent on return - driver ratings
description: BBC Radio 5 Live F1 commentator Harry Benjamin rates how the drivers performed during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
fullText:
George Russell led from start to finish as he dominated the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

The victory reduced the championship lead of his Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli to 66 points - from 81 - after the Italian finished fifth, although he had recovered from starting 16th on the grid.

Max Verstappen pushed Russell for the win as he took second place, less than two tenths of a second behind. Fellow Red Bull driver Isack Hadjar completed the podium by finishing third on his return to racing following a wrist injury.

Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in Baku.

Pretty difficult to find fault with this one. Fastest on Thursday, produced a stunning qualifying lap to take pole by more than eight tenths and controlled the race before holding off Max Verstappen under huge pressure at the end.

His eighth place in qualifying looked poor on paper but came with genuine power and energy deployment problems. Charged through the field on Saturday, passed Oscar Piastri for second and pushed Russell all the way to the line. An excellent recovery.

What a way to return after three races on the sidelines. Out-qualified Verstappen with fourth on the grid, showed excellent pace early in the race and finished on the podium while also playing the team game when Verstappen came through.

Second on the grid was an excellent qualifying result, although a tow certainly helped him get there. Ferrari simply didn't have the race pace to stay with Russell and the Red Bulls and fourth felt about the maximum available by the end.

A weekend of two very different halves. Crashing out in Q1 was a costly and unnecessary mistake, but he responded with a patient recovery from 16th to fifth despite picking up floor damage during the race.

His qualifying result was hurt by Ferrari's run plan leaving him without the tow he needed, but sixth in both qualifying and the race still made for a fairly quiet weekend. Solid enough, although Leclerc had the upper hand when it mattered.

Recovered again impressively after crashing in practice and starting 15th. Took advantage of the chaos when it came and then stole seventh from Esteban Ocon by the tiniest of margins at the finish. Goes a long way to limiting the grief he might get from punting into his Racing Bulls team-mate at Turn One.

A really strong race from the Haas driver after starting outside the top 10. Made some decisive moves as others fell into trouble and briefly looked set for seventh before Lindblad pinched it on the line.

Good enough to narrowly miss Q3 and stayed in the points despite losing out to Ocon during the race. Contact with Antonelli at the first restart was a slightly messy moment in an otherwise useful result for Haas.

The pace was encouraging and ninth in qualifying would have been Williams' best grid position of the season but failing to slow sufficiently for yellow flags earned him a five-place grid penalty. Recovered from as low as 19th in the race to grab the final point.

Russell wins despite late Verstappen challenge

Norris says Colapinto should be banned after accident

Audi's big upgrade didn't translate into qualifying. However, Hulk recovered reasonably well to 11th thanks to the carnage ahead but lost the final point to Sainz late on.

Back at Racing Bulls after three races with Red Bull and showed reasonable pace to qualify 12th before penalties moved him up the grid. His race was badly affected when team-mate Lindblad made contact with him in the chaotic second restart, leaving 12th a difficult result to judge too harshly.

For most of the weekend this was heading towards a very high score for the McLaren driver. Third in qualifying and running in the podium positions for much of the race. But his big lock-up at Turn One dropped him all the way down the order and threw away a potentially excellent result.

Looked rapid compared with Cadillac team-mate Valtteri Bottas in the early part of the weekend. But a suspected Q2 challenge didn't quite materialise.

Another difficult weekend for Audi despite all the new parts on the car. Out in Q1 alongside Hulkenberg and although he made progress on race day, it was not the return he would have hoped for.

His final qualifying lap was deleted for being set under double-waved yellow flags, leaving him at the back of the order. Almost made it to the finish but found the barriers late on.

The weekend had actually been going well after reaching Q3 and starting ninth. But his enormous lock-up at the second restart wiped out team-mate Pierre Gasly and Lando Norris as well as his own race, turning a potential double points finish for Alpine into nothing.

A really good weekend that deserved so much better. Qualified seventh and was still running there at the final restart before being taken out by his team-mate through no fault of his own.

Not the cleanest weekend for McLaren's world champion. A mistake on his final qualifying lap left him fifth and another lock-up during the race had already cost him places before he became an innocent victim of Colapinto's restart crash.

Was behind Sainz in qualifying before his team-mate's penalty shuffled the grid. His race ended with an error into the barriers at Turn Four which brought out the first safety car, so a difficult weekend despite signs of improvement from the car.

Another weekend where there wasn't much opportunity to show anything. Qualified 19th, took a back-of-grid power-unit penalty and then retired with a mechanical problem in a miserable race for Aston Martin.

Qualified behind Alonso before also taking his own penalty. Another mechanical retirement meant Aston Martin left Baku without either car reaching the finish.

title: Gilmour catalyst, impressive Welsh, but same issue for Scotland?
description: BBC Sport Scotland picks out what we learned from Sebastien Pocognoli's first game in charge as Scotland drew with Slovenia.
fullText:
New head coach Sebastien Pocognoli said his Scotland bow against Slovenia was "two games in the same game" as his side claimed a Nations League point after a much-improved second half showing.

The Scots struggled in a disjointed first half, but took control of the game in the second period and created enough chances to win, but had to settle for a 0-0 draw.

"First half, was not what we expected in terms of structure, " Pocognoli told BBC Scotland.

"We were in between for the press, actually we were a little bit surprised about the formation of Slovenia, but at half-time we fixed this and you can see that the second half was much better.

"We produced what we wanted to show every minute, but first half we learned to stick together, to defend the box, to be resilient and to be patient to change the game."

There were two debuts in Ljubljana, a return for Oli McBurnie, and a change of shape after seven years of Steve Clarke ended after the World Cup in the summer.

It is only the first of four games in this international window, but here are the key takeaways from Pocognoli's debut.

Scotland begin Pocognoli era with encouraging Slovenia draw

'Eternally grateful' McBurnie ready to show what Scotland have missed

Napoli midfielder Billy Gilmour missed the World Cup campaign after a heartbreaking injury against Curacao in Scotland's final home warm-up game.

He returned to the heart of midfield alongside Lewis Ferguson and, according to former Scotland midfielder John Collins was "the catalyst for everything" in the second half.

"Straight from the start of the second half he was getting the ball, playing forward passes and following his pass to the strikers," Collins said.

Gilmour played further up the pitch than Ferguson, "close to a creative 10" according to former Scotland winger Pat Nevin, and played 32 passes into the final third, more than any player on the pitch.

The former Chelsea man combined well with McBurnie on the edge of the box to set up a shot for himself; he slipped in Robbie Ure who opted to cross rather than shoot; and picked out Kieron Bowie with a wonderful through ball which should have resulted in a goal.

Those were just a handful of his key moments. Pocognoli spoke afterwards about the half-time tweak to bring Gilmour deeper to make it harder for Slovenia to play through them and have greater control of the ball.

"We fixed the position of Billy to be a little bit lower and to have Oli McBurnie a little bit 

"Also, that creates some imbalance in the defence from Slovenia, where we can go through the lines with a good chance of Billy or through the depth with the chance of Kieron Bowie or with some crosses.

"He's a fantastic player, I really like him. He's a creative player who always looks forward, always ready to find a solution with a clear game plan, also a good presence around the box and also very good defensively."

Swansea City defender Stephen Welsh was one of two debutants in Slovenia, playing on the left of a back three despite being right footed.

Scotland struggled defensively at times in the first half, with Slovenia playing over the top of them, but Welsh's positioning after the break also helped change the game.

In the first half, his average position was short of the halfway line, but by the end of the game it was in Slovenian territory.

His most common pass went from being to his fellow centre-back Scott McKenna, to Andy Robertson at wing-back.

"It was the starting position of the back three for which changed it - they were in a really good starting position," former Scotland defender Callum Davidson told BBC Scotland.

"In the first half they were quite deep and worried about the ball over the top. But we managed to nullify that and then keep the ball."

The former Motherwell and Celtic defender created a clear goalscoring chance with a wonderful through ball to Bowie, and he finished the game with 16 passes into the final third and the highest accuracy rating.

More aggressive play from Welsh helped set the tone after the break, as he looked assured on his international debut.

With a new manager, injuries to Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland, and on the back of his strong form with Hull City, Oli McBurnie made his first Scotland appearance since 2021 in attack.

Ure, fresh from his move from Sirius in Sweden to Sevilla, made his debut while Sassuolo's Kieron Bowie came off the bench in the second half.

Those three have one club goal between them this season - Bowie's against Juventus - and none for Scotland in their limited caps.

All three were presented chances to score in the second half, though. McBurnie nicked possession and when through, but failed to round Jan Oblak in the Slovenia goal.

His header from a corner was also beaten away by the Atletico Madrid's goalkeeper. Ure drove a low shot off the post in the first half from outside the box, a difficult chance, but then later opted to go for a cut back when slipped in by Gilmour.

Bowie ended with the highest expected goals rating in the Scotland team (0.94) despite playing only 25 minutes - after twice staring at the whites of Oblak's eyes and failing to find the net.

It is only one game, and Scotland will not face a goalkeeper of Oblak's quality in every match, but there is a lingering concern about the national side's goalscoring ability - they have managed one in their last four competitive games.

For all the positives the attackers brought in the second half in general play, do Scotland have someone with a killer instinct?

"International level is all about taking your chances, you don't get too many," Davidson said.

"It's about being really clinical, so for these strikers it's important when you get games like this to take your chances. That's the disappointment from today."

title: The computer hacker who tried to take down Man City
description: BBC Sport travelled to Portugal to find out more about Rui Pinto - the computer hacker who sparked the Manchester City investigation.
fullText:
Mention Rui Pinto's name to Manchester City fans outside Etihad Stadium, and you mostly get blank faces.

But while they might not know his name, they are more than familiar with his work.

Pinto is the Portuguese computer hacker who tried to bring down City.

Through his website Football Leaks, he published a cache of confidential club documents, including internal emails about sponsorship deals and payments.

That ultimately led to the Premier League charges for breaching of financial rules and Friday's news that the club had been found guilty of the majority of the 115 counts.

For some, 37-year-old Pinto is no more than a criminal who stole information with sinister intentions.

To others, though, he is a bastion of truth who has shone a light on the darker side of the beautiful game.

BBC Sport has been on a journey across Europe to find out more about the mysterious figure who was the catalyst for so much controversy.

We spoke to one of Pinto's former teachers, a Portuguese politician fighting for him to be protected as a whistleblower, journalists who published the leaks, and a former financial adviser at Manchester City.

And we sat just a few feet from Pinto in the latest of his court cases.

With his cherubic face and spiky hair, Pinto is instantly recognisable. And it seems he hasn't changed.

It is how Mario Falcao, his former geography teacher, remembers him.

In a small courtyard garden in Portugal, we got a glimpse of what Pinto was like as a boy.

"Rui was a perfectly normal pupil. He was nice, with his spiky hair, he was quite sociable but not extrovert," Falcao said.

"He had a good relationship with the teachers, although he did miss these classes quite often. His father was always on top of things, so in the end he passed quite easily."

Did he spot a strong interest in computers in a young Pinto?

"Certainly he was very good in computers. All the work that he did for various courses were very good, when he put his mind to it," his former teacher explained.

The now-retired Falcao speaks fondly of Pinto, who he says behaved just like his friends and would "go to the gym, go to McDonald's".

Pinto had a modest upbringing. He grew up in an area called Vila Nova de Gaia, just across the Douro River from Porto, Portugal's second-largest city. We visited the road where he used to live, which featured tile-fronted houses with terracotta roofs.

His school, Escola Secundaria Almeida Garrett, was well-regarded and was known by locals as 'the university'.

His father, Francisco, worked in a shoe factory and later as an antiques dealer. His mother had died when he was 11.

Falcao said he never predicted what was to come of his former pupil.

"We were very surprised," he said of the moment Pinto was named as the founder of Football Leaks in 2019.

"We weren't imagining anything like this could happen, that he could have problems with justice.

"I certainly wouldn't wish him and his family to be in this situation. Perhaps it was a question of the excesses of youth, his ability with computers, and maybe an excess of club-ism."

"So, you know, the fact that he supported FC Porto prompted him to commit some acts, but maybe he also felt the need for justice that young people very often do feel."

Clubs seek legal advice over Man City charges compensation

Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? What next for Man City

Pinto set up Football Leaks in 2015, to - in his words - expose "the hidden side of football".

Antonio Varela remembers the website's launch like it was yesterday. The Portuguese journalist was the first person contacted by Pinto, whose real identity would not be known for years to come, and was initially known by the pseudonym "John".

"It was a common day of September 2015. I was at the news room at [Portuguese sports newspaper] Record and I got an email from Football Leaks. It was strange. Then I immediately go to the site, and I can't believe there is lots of information that you never heard or read. We made the conclusion this is very, very important."

Re-publishing what had been leaked by Pinto brought legal and ethical conundrums.

"We realised that [Football Leaks] got the information illegally. But since the moment they publish the information on the site, that's public information," said Varela.

"You can't ignore that. Ethically, it's complicated, but the public interest is more relevant than the ethical issue. That was the conclusion."

It wasn't just eight-time Premier League champions Manchester City that Pinto targeted.

The early revelations on Football Leaks focused on matters closer to home, with leaks around Benfica and even the side he supported, FC Porto.

Later, there were leaked documents and communications relating to some of the world's most famous players, clubs and agents, including Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Neymar.

Pinto agreed to meet a journalist, Rafael Buschmann from the German magazine Der Spiegel. Once he knew he could trust him, he shared tens of millions of documents with him.

It was then up to a team of journalists in the Der Spiegel headquarters in Hamburg to meticulously go through it all, producing some of the most explosive articles the football world has ever seen.

Christoph Winterbach, a data journalist, was part of that team.

"In the beginning it was very much a fascinating feeling of like a child in a candy store," he said.

"If you're a football fan, if you're a sports journalist, it was amazing to see the actual documents, to see those emails where things are negotiated and to get a real look behind the curtain, how things work.

"It's very important when you have this type of documents, this type of data, that you make a lot of cross checks, that you use some software which we did that can put it all into context and you can see if there's any reliability issues.

"We always need to make sure that it's authentic material and whenever we publish something about it, it needs to be in the public interest to start writing."

Winterbach finally met Pinto in person in 2019, when he was being held in prison in Lisbon awaiting his trial. He conducted another interview with Pinto in witness protection, in a secret location with high security, describing the arrangements for getting there as being "like a Hollywood movie".

He said: "Rui Pinto is not very tall. He has very distinctive hair, like spiky hair. He usually has red cheeks and he's a youthful, cheeky, funny character. He's friendly and warm when you meet him.

"He's a very impressive character, he's very focused, he's very concentrated. He's very, very intelligent. He's very idealistic about the topics that he uncovered.

"He's one of the most important whistleblowers that we have in Europe or maybe the world."

In all, Pinto provided more than three terabytes - equivalent to about 3,000 copies of the Encyclopedia Britannica - of information to Der Spiegel and other outlets in the European Investigative Collaborations consortium.

We encountered stark contrasts in perceptions of Pinto wherever we went.

Former Portuguese politician and diplomat Ana Gomes has also met Pinto in prison and testified on his behalf at one of his trials. She is firmly of the view that he deserves to be protected, not prosecuted.

"What he has exposed is very important. In Portugal, definitely he is by far the most important whistleblower," the former Member of the European Parliament told us in Lisbon.

"He should be made an ally of our judicial and criminal investigative authorities. He has helped the authorities of other European countries in going after the corrupt and the criminals, instead of being the subject of this judicial prosecution by the choice of our public prosecutors."

When asked what she would say to Manchester City, who had their emails hacked by him, her answer is blunt.

"I couldn't care less. If they have nothing to hide, what's their problem?"

Jose Carlos Freitas, a retired journalist, said Gomes's sympathetic view is not a widely held one.

"For the majority of the people, they look at him as a thief," he said. "For some people, he is a kind of hero, a Robin Hood, you can say because he was exposing the dark side of the business of so many clubs, but unfortunately for the majority of the people, he is not a good person."

Varela is on the fence. "Nowadays, I think I put him in the middle [between whistleblower and criminal hacker] because he got the information illegally. But he gave us, all of us, a view, a dark view of European football, so he did a job to the society illegally."

Wherever you sit in the debate, he has faced serious consequences for what he did. As Winterbach puts it, Pinto "has powerful enemies through the work that he has done".

For the past six years, Pinto's life has been far from normal.

Having been arrested in Hungary in 2019, he was extradited to Portugal and has at various points been in solitary confinement, under house arrest and in witness protection.

Following his first trial in Portugal, in 2023 he received a four-year suspended sentence having been found guilty of attempted extortion, illegal access to data and breach of correspondence.

A separate trial in France resulted in a six-month suspended prison sentence a few months later.

And in January last year, Pinto's latest trial began in Lisbon. The opening day at the Central Criminal Court encapsulated the realities of his life and the difference in opinions of him.

Pinto arrived with members of his witness protection team, two of whom stayed in the courtroom throughout the hearing, along with an armed police presence.

He was dressed casually in a blue, long-sleeved top, jeans and brown boots, and had his distinctive spiky hair and some facial hair. He was fairly expressionless throughout, aside from the occasional shrug of the shoulders or glance at his team.

We sat just a few feet from him, as he conversed with his legal team in hushed tones and spoke to the judge purely to confirm details like his name and age. When asked for his address, he said he could not give this for security reasons.

Local journalist Miguel Dantas explained the security arrangements were scaled back compared with the first trial, when he wore a bulletproof jacket and there were snipers on the roof.

Rui Patricio, the lawyer representing Benfica, told the court Pinto was "no more, no less than a burglar", that he had obtained the information by "illegal and condemnable methods" and that the ends did not justify the means.

Outside court, Patricio added: "Our argument is very, very simple. He's a hacker, period, just like that. What he did is not allowed - it's a crime and there are no excuses. It's very, very simple. Very, very straightforward."

In his statement in court, Francisco Texeira da Mota, representing Pinto, accepted that his client was "not a hero and not a saint" but said he had brought "advantages for society".

The impact of Football Leaks is still being felt a decade on.

The Premier League's case against Manchester City has been one of unprecedented scale and significance.

From speaking to his legal team after the court hearing, it became clear Pinto has been closely monitoring that case from witness protection since the Premier League brought the charges in February 2023.

Asked if the outcome mattered, Texeira da Mota said: "I think it's important for him because it's very difficult to be like he is, living a very difficult life, more or less hiding, because he made some revelations, he whistle-blowed lots of important things, namely about Manchester City.

"So it would be important for him to feel vindicated that it was useful, that something happened, because what of what he said."

Speaking before the announcement of the decision in the City case, Stefan Borson, a former financial adviser to Manchester City, said: "I think for City, really, the whole of the Sheikh Mansour era is at stake if the core allegations are proven against the club.

"I think the consequences could be very far reaching for the club, and it would be a very difficult thing for them to deal with.

"Over time, clearly there would have to be some kind of reset. I think in many ways the Premier League is a loser either way."

Borson's view was that Pinto should not be seen as "some kind of warrior for freedom".

He said: "We know that what he carried out was a criminal act and he's been prosecuted for it.

"We also know that hackers of that nature do try and reframe themselves as part of the defence process as purveyors of freedom of speech. But, once those documents are in the public domain, then I think it's for the authorities to act."

For some, Rui Pinto is a criminal hacker who stole information with sinister intentions. To others he is a heroic whistleblower who shone a light on the darker side of the beautiful game.

What is undeniable is that one Portuguese man on his computer in Budapest has had a seismic impact on global football.

title: Do England have a problem against top-10 teams?
description: As England prepare to take on Spain in their opening Nations League match, BBC Sport takes a look at whether they have a problem when faced with teams in the world top 10.
fullText:
When England take on Spain in their opening Nations League match on Saturday, it will be tinged with a feeling of 'what could have been' for Three Lions fans.

The Wembley match comes three months after England agonisingly missed out on the chance to face La Roja in the World Cup final, having lost to Argentina in the last four.

That would have been a repeat of the 2024 Euros final, which England also lost.

In fact, their record against top-10 sides leaves much to be desired.

In their past 15 matches against sides ranked in the top 10 in the world - according to Fifa's rankings - England have won six matches.

Three of those wins were at major tournaments - the Euros semi-finals in 2021 and 2024 against Denmark and the Netherlands, and the bronze-medal match against France at this summer's World Cup.

The victory over Les Bleus to take third place was Thomas Tuchel's first win as England boss over a top-10 opponent.

And his first win over opposition ranked inside the top 20 came in their opening group game at the tournament against Croatia.

So do England have a problem against top-10 opposition?

Six wins in their past 15 games against top-10 opponents are not the kind of numbers an England team with the ambition of winning major tournaments can be happy with.

Two of those wins meant the Three Lions advanced to the Euro finals of 2020 and 2024. One was in the World Cup match no one wants to play in, two were Euro qualifying matches against an Italy side already on a sharp decline and one came against Belgium in a Nations League match six years ago.

To put it simply, when faced with really elite opposition, England continue to stumble. Particularly at the World Cup.

England have been eliminated every time they have faced a top-10 ranked nation in the knockout stages of the World Cup since 1998 - seven times out of seven.

In their past 10 World Cup games against sides ranked in the top 10, their sole win came in the 2002 group stage against Argentina.

When faced with the defending world champions at the World Cup, they have lost on all four occasions.

England have fared better at the Euros, overcoming top-10 opponents in Denmark and the Netherlands to reach the final at the past two tournaments but ultimately falling at the final hurdle on both occasions against Spain (2024) and Italy (2020).

Meanwhile, their lowest possession in their last 15 games against top-10 opponents came in the semi-final against Argentina (35.8%) at this summer's World Cup and in those Euros finals against Spain (34.9%) and Italy (42.1%).

England's all-time top scorer Kane, with 85 goals, was asked which missing ingredient was needed to get them over the line.

"I think it's just in those biggest moments, still being ourselves," he told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"The Argentina game was so hard to take, because we had a mindset of going to win the tournament, win in our way and our style, and if we lose trying to do that then we will take that.

"The Argentina game was maybe the first game we tried 'not to lose' in the last 30 minutes and then we ended up losing anyway."

Kane has scored 152 goals in 154 games for Bayern, winning two Bundesliga titles.

"I have experienced it at Bayern Munich for example, you don't fear anyone," the 33-year-old said.

"You go and be yourself, if a team beats you, shake their hand after and say well done.

"You have an identity that you keep throughout.

"I think with England now that is where we need to look.

"We are very close, we have been very close but ultimately, we don't need to fear anyone.

"We just need to be ourselves in the biggest moments and hopefully get over the line."

England have been getting closer to major tournament glory over a number of years but the same question remains - can they dominate the ball and beat elite opposition?

At Euro 2020, the last-16 win over Germany was huge - beating one of the historic footballing powers. But that was a German side in transition who were, at the time, ranked outside the world's top 10.

England were then beaten by Italy in the final after taking the lead, dropping deep and giving up possession before losing on penalties.

At the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, the Three Lions started the tournament with a free-flowing 6-2 win over Iran. Although this was not top opposition, the change in mentality from previous tournaments was notable.

But yet again the same issues resurfaced. Despite largely being the better team against France, a Harry Kane missed penalty and Les Bleus' know-how put England out at the quarter-final stage.

Euro 2024 proved to be one tournament too far for Gareth Southgate and that team did not play anywhere near their best, relying on individual quality to get them through.

A last-gasp Ollie Watkins strike was needed to beat the Netherlands in the semis while Kane was not at full fitness and without him at his best, the team never troubled a formidable Spain side.

After a flawless 2026 World Cup qualifying campaign and a new elite coach in Tuchel, many thought this was England's time for glory.

But, despite showing a huge amount of togetherness and grit in the last-16 win over Mexico, the same old problems once again sunk England.

The Three Lions cannot seem to translate world class talent into ball possession and control of the game, with Tuchel saying he may have to embrace the chaos, and Anthony Gordon adding that England should lean on their traditional direct style.

Perhaps that is what is needed to finally end their long wait for a trophy.

title: From shaky start to statement wins - 100 days of McInnes at Rangers
description: BBC Scotland charts the first tumultuous 100 days of Derek McInnes' tenure as Rangers manager.
fullText:
Derek McInnes has been in charge for 100 days at Rangers - the club he grew up supporting, played for and previously turned down the opportunity to manage.

In his brief but busy tenure, there has been a huge squad overhaul, while a sluggish start led to Ibrox jeers and the failure to qualify for European football for the first time in a decade.

Then came September. A golden start to autumn quietened talk of crisis as a winning streak extended to six games, including two Old Firm derby victories.

BBC Sport Scotland charts the key moments of McInnes' reign.

Penrice focuses on Rangers as Scotland remains a target

How derby masterclasses provide stark Rangers contrast

I wasn't good enough for Rangers - Ure

One month and one day after his Heart of Midlothian side were pipped to the title by Celtic on the final day of last season, McInnes is announced as Rangers manager, replacing the departed Danny Rohl.

It is 26 years since his days as a Rangers player ended with a move to West Bromwich Albion and eight-and-a-half years since he turned down the chance to become boss under the chairmanship of Dave King.

"It is no secret that I grew up a Rangers supporter and I am convinced this is the right time to take on this prestigious role," McInnes says. "There is a lot of hard work ahead."

The new era begins at Tannadice with a whimper rather than a bang as Thelo Aasgaard scores a second-half equaliser in a 1-1 draw with Dundee United.

"We worked hard to get back into it, but I don't think we were good enough to win the game," McInnes says. "I thought the point was the right scoreline and we're disappointed with that first half.

"We wasted a lot, we didn't create too much and it was a bit too frantic."

Curtain up on Rangers European campaign - and it does not start well.

A trip to eastern Poland in the first leg of their Europa League third qualifying round tie ends in a 2-1 defeat by Jagellonia Bialystok.

McInnes notes: "I just felt we beat ourselves, to be honest. We got off to a good start, being patient with what we were trying to do. We made two mistakes for the two goals."

Rangers' first home match of the season ends also ends in a 2-1 defeat, this time by Hibernian.

A late Callum Wright goal seals victory for the Edinburgh side and, to make matters worse, striker Youseff Chermitti suffers an ACL injury that scuppers any potential big-money sale amid reports of interest from Galatasaray.

"There are little things going against us at the minute, but we have to stay strong - we're not as bad as people think," McInnes insists. "At the minute, we are trying to work boys back to the same level of fitness and trying to manage that situation.

"I understand the fan frustration. They want and expect to see their team win. I share the frustration."

Another below-par performance has supporters up in arms.

Shankland scores from the penalty spot, but a second-half goal from Nik Prelec earns Jagellonia a draw on the night and progress on aggregate.

McInnes confesses: "It is not great to watch. My team go from some good highs in the first half to being as poor as we were in the second half and you have to say we didn't do enough. We should be winning this game."

Five games into the new season and Rangers record their first win under McInnes - an emphatic 5-1 thumping of holders St Mirren in the Premier Sports Cup.

"We gave up a couple of chances, which we weren't too pleased about, but there was a good attacking threat from the team," McInnes concludes.

"The players deserved that moment today against a St Mirren team who have been doing well."

A penalty shoot-out defeat by the unfancied Czechs eliminates Rangers from Europe altogether.

Missed spot kicks by Findlay Curtis and James Penrice hand victory to Jablonec after a 1-0 defeat. A bitter blow for the balance sheet too as the Ibrox club face up to life without European football proper for the first time in 10 years.

"I'm embarrassed with the performance," McInnes says. "I think the only people who represented the club well tonight were my support staff and the supporters who, to a man, were outstanding, getting behind the team despite watching what we all watched."

McInnes registers his first Scottish Premiership win as Rangers manager at his old stamping ground of Pittodrie.

A Shankland penalty gets the job done, much to McInnes' relief as he praises Kim Min-Su as evidence that the summer recruitment is beginning to bear fruit.

"It was a tough few days for us all," he says. "I thought we were far more like the Rangers team I want us to be."

After a 2-1 success at Falkirk, a third successive Premiership win, but it comes at a cost as Shankland tears a hamstring against Motherwell at Ibrox and will be sidelined for months. Ryan Nederi replaces the captain and scores the only goal.

"We'd have taken any sort of win because we're up against a good team, but I really enjoyed how many chances we created," McInnes says.

It looks like Rangers' winning run is coming to an end until Bojan Miovski comes off the bench to score a stoppage-time winner at home to St Mirren to spark wild celebrations.

Rangers move into second place in the Premiership, five points behind leaders Celtic.

With four wins on the bounce, McInnes is sounding more optimistic.

"There are obviously loads we have to improve on, but we have to keep winning while we are looking for those improvements," he says.

McInnes demanded a big performance from his players in his Old Firm managerial debut - and he got it.

He pulled a few tactical surprises and they paid off as Rangers power into the Premier Sports Cup semi-finals.

Two goals from the inspired Dan Neill and a first for Kelsy set up a meeting with Aberdeen at Hampden.

"It was the performance and result we were all looking for," McInnes says. "It's a good reference point for my players. They're a young squad and they saw how much that result means to the supporters."

Glasgow's big two meet again, this time at Celtic Park in the Premiership.

A Naderi goal stuns the 60,000 home supporters and moves Rangers two points behind their Glasgow rivals.

Afterwards, McInnes reflects: "It's just three points and it gets us three points closer to Celtic. We understood if we lost the game, that distance just starts to feel uncomfortable for us.

"I like putting my name to this team at the minute and I think we've got a good thing going."

Former Rangers interim boss and Captain Barry Ferguson

"I've been really impressed since exiting in Europe.

"I think the reaction, not just the manager and the coaching staff, the players, I've been very impressed. Even before the two Celtic games, they played well in parts of it, other parts they didn't, but they found a way to win, and that's so important.

"It's always going to take a bit of time because there was a big turnaround of players and some players hit the ground running.

"It takes some players a wee bit of time to get going. But now I think you're starting to see a team that's got a real togetherness. That's the biggest thing for me."

title: The FA Cup final assistant ref whose life was turned upside down by tumour discovery
description: Dan Robathan tells BBC Newsbeat how his career as a Premier League assistant referee was brought to an end by the discovery of spinal tumours.
fullText:
It was May 2025 and life was good for Premier League and Fifa assistant referee Dan Robathan.

Years of climbing the football ladder had paid off and he was running the line at the FA Cup final between Crystal Palace and Manchester City.

But just months after this career highlight, symptoms Dan thought were sciatic nerve pain and wear and tear were revealed to be benign tumours in his spine, which needed to be operated on immediately.

"I saw a neurosurgeon who told me I had two tumours, initially I thought it was one, but it was two," Dan tells BBC Newsbeat.

"It was compressing nerves, there was a chance it could affect a motor nerve which means it could affect function in my leg.

"I needed to go home, lay down and not move. I did that for 15 days, my life turned upside down overnight."

BBC Newsbeat met Dan at a football pitch in Norwich, close to where he lives, where he revealed the struggles he has had in trying to regain his fitness and mobility.

Dan picked up his first flag at 10 years old, working his way up from grassroots football to the lines at more than 200 Premier League clashes and World Cup qualifiers.

Speaking at the time of the FA Cup final, Dan said it was "a privilege to stand there on behalf of over 37,000 referees across the country".

The chances of becoming an elite level referee are low.

The FA describes Fifa match officials, external as the "pinnacle of the officiating ladder".

And in his social media posts, Dan gives a glimpse of everything you would expect from an official at elite level - from the roar of fans to sprinting to be in the right place during split second decisions.

To the outside world, all looked well.

"I started having quite bad problems with sexual dysfunction or bladder issues where I'd have to sit down to urinate and I couldn't stand up," he explains.

"It got to a point in September [2025] where something's not right at all."

A neurosurgeon confirmed to Dan he had two tumours in his spine – and his life ground to a halt.

"It was fear, anxiety, not knowing how long it will take me to get back.

"What would my life look like? Will I be a normal man? Will I walk again?"

Surgeons removed one tumour and left one alone, which was deemed safe.

The tumours were non-cancerous, but have caused significant damage to Dan, who describes his post-operation recovery as "brutal".

Yet there was "no doubt" in his mind that he would return.

But by Christmas 2025, Dan was still feeling fatigued and struggling to lift his heel, walk, or feel his calf.

"The surgeon said I had under a 10% chance of ever getting back on the field but even then I was like I don't care I will prove everyone wrong," Dan recalls.

Yet despite fighting "like mad", he was unable to regain his fitness levels.

This week, Dan was forced to medically retire, saying in effect "the decision was made for me".

The 38-year-old says he still has days where he struggles to walk, or where his back feels "on fire".

"My body just can't do what I want it to do," he says.

Dan underwent testing to confirm his tumours weren't linked to genetics, which was reassuring, but still leaves him facing the unknown.

"It's a loss of identity. I've been 'Dan the ref' since I was 10 years old.

"It's 28 years of being who I am, it's my personality.

"When you have the recognition that that sort of life is over, psychologically it is really tough."

Dan is now working with a psychologist to decide the path forward.

"I feel like a 16-year-old who's just left school and trying to work out what I want to do with my life," he jokes.

"I have a few options, staying in football.

"[But] I don't know if I will be able to with the mental health problems I've had.

"Can I stay involved in a sport that I loved but can't do myself?"

One thing he is certain of, is going into the future with his family.

"I want to put my son, fiancée, my stepchildren first. I want to try and advocate for men's mental health, for men speaking about health issues.

"If I can help one or two men in the process, I've done my job."

And Dan accepts that if he gets back into football it would need to be for the right reasons.

"I need to get that fire my belly."

title: Why schoolboys have become a huge part of football's transfer market
description: BBC Sport explores why clubs at the top of English football are increasingly trading academy players and what the impact is on the youngsters themselves.
fullText:
A 15-year-old growing up in the UK faces many tough personal decisions about their future - which school subjects to study, which social circle suits them, and where their priorities lie in life.

But in the past few weeks the choices teenage Manchester United striker JJ Gabriel has been making about his future in football have drawn huge public attention in sports media and online.

Gabriel has informed United he wants to leave the club and join another. BBC Sport has reported that he has stayed away from training and begun talking to other clubs because he and his representatives are unhappy with United's handling of the 15-year-old's progress.

That a transfer saga involving a footballer so young could generate so much interest highlights a truth that to many is uncomfortable - money is changing how the football transfer market works, and children are increasingly deemed to be among its most valuable commodities.

So what is behind the rise in transfers involving boys who in some cases are not even old enough to have taken their GCSEs, what kind of influence can the money on offer have on agents and parents, and what exactly are the country's top football clubs getting out of it?

"It's crazy when you think about it," says Ryan Cardwell, former youth scout at Liverpool and Southampton.

"In what other kind of world would 15 and 16-year-olds be spoken about in the media like this?"

This summer alone, all six of the Premier League's wealthiest clubs either signed a highly-rated academy player from another, or lost a youngster to a direct rival.

"It is such a competitive market," Cardwell explains. "There are now tens of transfers between the elite academies every summer, when it used to be the case that if you were already at one of those, you would likely stay the course.

"The race for talent is huge – you look at what teams are spending on transfers for senior players and it's enormous, so if you can spot a player earlier and offset some of that financial risk, you're going to do so."

Some inside football claim that the transfer of Rio Ngumoha - the now 18-year-old winger who was called up to this month's senior England squad - from Chelsea to Liverpool at the age of 15 in 2024 ushered in a new era of competition for academy players among the nation's elite.

One of the major factors is Brexit. Before 2021 English clubs were allowed to sign academy players over the age of 16 who held European Union passports.

Since the UK left the EU, foreign players cannot join English clubs until they reach 18.

"Heathrow and Gatwick [airports] on a Friday night were inundated with scouts going to other countries to look for young players", says Caldwell.

"Belgium and the Netherlands were full of scouts for Premier League clubs.

"Now it's the competition between English clubs that has increased, looking at each other's players, including the old-school 'top six' but also the likes of Southampton, Aston Villa, and Fulham."

Young players have further added financial value - youth signings don't count towards the Premier League's squad cost ratio rules, and any future sale counts as 'pure profit' in club accounts.

Advances in video technology and data analysis mean more young players are being identified, tracked and approached by rival clubs than ever before.

Players can de-register from their academy at the end of their under-12, under-14 and under-16 seasons if they wish to explore options elsewhere.

They can be offered paid scholarship contracts from the season in which they turn 14, and can sign professional deals from the season in which they turn 16.

Some pundits and fans have criticised Gabriel's family over the controversy in recent weeks.

Gabriel can potentially join clubs in Europe because he has an Irish passport.

"It's a really tough world - players and families want the best for their kids and you can't give them stick without knowing what their motivations are," says Phil Jagielka, whose son Zac left Liverpool in 2024 and signed a scholarship deal at Hull City at 16.

"The harsh reality is that if a young player fails to progress, or gets a bad injury, teams will stop being interested in them. So there is an element of strike while the iron's hot."

When a club signs a player from a rival academy, they pay a set compensation fee based on how long they had been trained there.

Depending on the player's age, the fee can reach millions of pounds.

The increasing allure of signing young academy players from rivals means some parents are now compiling data packs on their sons to give to potential clubs, and more and more children are represented by football agents.

"There are good agents and bad agents," Cardwell says.

"You certainly speak to some and think 'that's completely the wrong idea', or, ' this player is going to be misguided'. Sometimes they push for a move when a player isn't ready.

"The contracts can be enormous and [money] can be a huge motivation to move. It could set a young player's family up for life.

"I would quite like to see some form of financial cap. My fear for some of the young players is they're on the biggest salaries they'll ever have, because if they don't make it at the top level, they can go from being on tens of thousands (of pounds) a week to one or two thousand lower down the pyramid."

In decades gone by, development of academy players would be combined with menial tasks around the training ground.

The idea was to keep young footballers grounded and make them feel a part of the wider club.

But the Gabriel case demonstrates the significant changes football has undergone.

"We would clean boots, sweep floors, tidy the changing rooms," says Jagielka, who came through Sheffield United's academy in the late 1990s.

"I fully back that system. It taught us responsibility and discipline. It was a way of getting to know the first-team players, and you would get a proper telling off if you didn't do your jobs properly.

"There was nowhere near as much outside influence on young players back then. Now there is an entourage, people wanting to play the long game with, 9, 10, 11-year-olds because of the millions of pounds of commission if they turn out to be a superstar.

"There are far more people out there now who are prepared to rock the boat between the different clubs."

The public scrutiny on young players has increased significantly, and the elite clubs' desire to succeed in the market means that high-profile youth transfers involving big money seem to be here to stay.

"Young players now have such a big platform on social media that intrigue is part of day-to-day life for them," says Cardwell.

"When you're in elite sport you have to grow up really, really fast. Teenagers are expected to cope with the pressure and naturally some people fall into the trap of thinking 'well, he's a young man already' and forget about everything else.

"The race for talent is never, ever going to change."

title: The compromises and power struggles that shaped Fury-Joshua
description: BBC Sport takes a look at the compromises, power struggles and competing interests behind Tyson Fury v Anthony Joshua.
fullText:
After a decade of stalled negotiations, public squabbling and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will finally meet in the ring on 11 December at Cardiff's Principality Stadium.

BBC Sport understands the WBA 'Super' heavyweight title is expected to be on the line, although confirmation from the governing body is still awaited.

It would give both former world champions the chance to regain a version of the heavyweight crown, although Fury-Joshua has always been about more than belts.

The fight arrives later than anybody wanted, with both in the twilight of their careers, but for years British boxing's biggest heavyweight rivalry seemed destined to remain a story of what might have been.

Yet Thursday's announcement of an 80,000-capacity showdown, broadcast globally by Netflix, did more than finally provide a date and venue.

It also offered a glimpse of the competing interests, egos and power struggles involved in getting one of boxing's most elusive fights over the line.

Speaking to BBC Sport after the fight was announced, Fury's promoter Frank Warren repeatedly returned to one word: compromise.

"Everybody's got to make a compromise," the Queensberry boss said. "Tyson really compromised. He didn't dig his heels in.

"He said, 'Fine, wherever they want it, I'll do it. If they want me to go to New York, I'll go. They want it in the UK, I just want to get the fight on."

The fighters had already agreed to the contest but the venue was a sticking point.

Warren says Netflix wanted New York, while Joshua, 36, was determined to fight in Britain. Predictably, their camps disagree over who finally got it done.

Joshua's promoter Eddie Hearn described the push to keep the fight in Britain as a "two-man crusade".

"AJ has turned down money to keep it in the UK," Hearn told the Matchroom YouTube channel. "I wouldn't be able to look people in the eye if I was part of the movement to take this to the US."

Hearn says Joshua had specifically requested protection for a UK fight in his contract and refused to relent.

"We were under so much pressure to fold," he added. "It was only really the support of the British public that made Joshua stand 10 toes down and say no."

He says Fury, 38, could have insisted on his own contractual position but instead accepted Britain to ensure the fight did not collapse.

Perhaps the biggest sideshow has been the struggle for influence around the promotion itself.

Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh announced the fight, having previously insisted any confirmation would come from him.

"For 15 years no-one has been able to make this fight," he wrote. "Back in April, I said that any announcement would come from me. I can now confirm that Fury v Joshua will be coming to the UK, as I promised British boxing fans. The time for talking is over."

Dana White's involvement is particularly intriguing.

The UFC chief is partnered with Alalshikh through Zuffa Boxing and featured prominently in the announcement, with Netflix describing the event as a collaboration involving White and Alalshikh's The Ring. Hearn and Warren were absent.

Hearn had previously said White would not be involved in promoting the fight, while Warren says both fighters' contracts stipulated the same.

Yet Warren says White ultimately helped secure the Netflix deal but believes fans care little about the promotional politics.

"I don't know whether he will be front and centre or not," Warren said.

Wednesday's news conference in London may tell us more - not least how prominent White is and how he and Hearn share the stage after months of back-and-forth.

Even Cardiff comes with competing claims of credit.

Hearn had publicly pushed for the Principality Stadium in recent weeks, while Warren told BBC Sport Queensberry and Saudi events company Sela spent several months working "quietly" with the venue and local authorities.

The stadium's retractable roof makes it well suited to a December event and there is precedent for late night boxing.

Joe Calzaghe's victory over Mikkel Kessler there in 2007 took place under a closed roof, with the fight starting after 01:00 GMT to accommodate American television. Fury-Joshua is expected to follow a similar pattern.

The exact ringwalk time remains in the hands of Netflix, with Hearn saying his current understanding is around 01:00 or 01:30 GMT. Warren has ruled out anything as late as 04:00.

"If it went on in America you'd be watching it five o'clock in the morning," Warren said. "It's a compromise and it's an event."

There is no contractual rematch clause, according to Hearn. "We're coming in for the kind of victory that no-one will need to see the fight again," he said.

Warren believes the winner can continue towards further world-title opportunities. For the loser, he thinks the road may end in Cardiff.

Whatever the outcome, Fury-Joshua has long been defined by the reasons it did not happen.

But in just over eleven weeks there will be no more negotiations, competing claims or hypothetical outcomes - just Fury and Joshua, in the same ring at last.
