title: What are Welsh sides' chances for new URC season?
description: BBC Sport Wales looks at the prospects for Cardiff, Dragons, Ospreys and Scarlets in the 2026-27 United Rugby Championship season.
fullText:
Perhaps it is down to the hope and excitement of pre-season but all four Welsh clubs go into the 2026-27 United Rugby Championship (URC) with dreams of making the play-offs.

Last season Cardiff were the only side from Wales to make the top eight while Scarlets and Ospreys were the sole Welsh representatives in 2025 and 2024 respectively.

Those three, and Dragons, have shown they can mix it with the best in the league on their day and all will feel the top eight is not out of reach if they have some luck with injury.

They will attempt to set the tone for the season in the first block of the URC, with Saturday's meeting between Scarlets and Cardiff in Llanelli the first of five derbies before the break for the November internationals.

BBC Sport Wales assesses the chances of all four Welsh teams for the coming season.

Wales beat the Boks and the rest of the URC preview

Behind the scenes on URC Media Day

Welsh rugby's ins, outs and re-signings for 2026-27

Key man: Teddy Williams - Cardiff will hope the Wales lock, their player of the year in 2024-25, can stay fit having been limited to three appearances in the past season after a dislocated right foot last October.

Prospects: The Blue and Blacks aim to celebrate their 150th anniversary by building on a strong 2025-26 when they made the play-offs for the first time.

After a blow on the eve of the season when boss Matt Sherratt left for Wales, Corniel van Zyl guided Cardiff to sixth in the table and Champions Cup qualification.

The South African is now charged with continuing an upward trend, helped by clarity about his future after being officially appointed permanent head coach in April.

"It does feel way better to know what is coming," said the former lock, who held talks with Benetton about their top job before they appointed ex-Wales boss Wayne Pivac.

"It helps to manage and plan well, whereas if you are thrown in at the deep end then you can make decisions quickly and it's not necessarily the right thing to do."

Cardiff's success was built on their formidable Arms Park record, with Scarlets the only team to beat them in the Welsh capital.

Expectations are high and they must mix top-tier European rugby with another tilt at the top eight, with a tricky five-day turnaround from Northampton in the Champions Cup to a home URC fixture with Sharks in October.

"Look at the last three years and Cardiff has grown. That's the main focus for us, to be a better team, and better individually and collectively as a club," said Van Zyl.

"We are not the cream of the crop yet, so the mission is to get better and have consistency in our performance.

"Last year we were very good at the Arms Park and we would love to replicate that, and also get better away from home. That's the challenge."

Derbies in the first block against Scarlets in Llanelli and Ospreys at St Helen's are key to that desire.

Cardiff will want to be Wales' top team once more.

Sio hopes Cardiff move leads to World Cup hat-trick

Wales back row Faletau signs new Cardiff deal

Co-captains: Sam Parry and Owen Watkin

Key man: Lalaki Foketi - The nine-times Wallabies centre arrives from Super Rugby side Chiefs and has the ability to prove a real game-breaker.

Wing Marika Koroibete is the more household name but Foketi can provide something that Ospreys or very few Welsh sides possess.

Prospects: It will be a fascinating season for Ospreys on and off the field.

To improve on last season's 11th place finish, Mark Jones' side must repeat the home form and their success in derbies that saw them lift the Welsh shield.

Put simply, Ospreys have to start winning more away games if they want to launch a play-off push, and they start their season in South Africa against Sharks and Lions.

"We had seven wins and two draws last season and 10 wins would normally get you in the play-offs," said Ospreys head coach Jones.

"We know we are not a million miles away and we have been in and around the play-offs and we want to be in there competing this season."

Ospreylia: How Welsh club turned to a land down under

Resilient Ospreys players need certainty - Jones

Ospreys have launched a recruitment drive in Australia with three Wallabies arriving in back-row forward Liam Wright, centre Foketi and wing Koroibete.

Australian fly-half Lawson Creighton has also come in to go alongside lock Ryan Smith, who was a resounding success last season.

It is policy that has excited supporters after the loss of Wales captains Jac Morgan and Dewi Lake, but one that is happening amid uncertainty over the club's future with the Welsh Rugby Union (WRU) getting rid of a west Wales region in 2028.

The Ospreys, aided by Swansea Council, hope to secure the long-term future and to do this by moving into their new seaside St Helen's home, while Wales legend Alun Wyn Jones has joined the board.

The opening home game is against the Dragons on 24 October and the Ospreys' faithful have one final major chance to demonstrate they will back their team. A successful start to the season will help that quest.

"Having your own home is massive," said Mark Jones. "The Swansea.com Stadium and Bridgend were great, but this gives us the opportunity to bring the city and the rest of the region in."

Director of rugby: Nigel Davies

Key man: Fletcher Anderson - The number eight from New Zealand was the Welsh signing of the season last year with his powerful bursts. Once he recovers from a groin injury, Anderson will aim to avoid suffering the dreaded second season syndrome against teams that now know what he can do.

Prospects: Scarlets players and fans will expect a noticeable improvement from last season. No Champions Cup victories and 14th place in the URC was not acceptable for a side that is the most recent Welsh team to win the league in 2017.

Nigel Davies has become the permanent director of rugby with Dwayne Peel continuing as head coach.

"We were absolutely not happy with 14th," said Davies.

"I'm not going to sit here and give any predictions of where we're going to finish, but what we're going to see is a Scarlets team with intent, wanting to play quickly, wanting to excite our crowd and be hugely competitive and abrasive."

Scarlets have lost international forwards Marnus van der Merwe, Alec Hepburn and Jake Ball.

The main new signing is one-cap All Blacks flanker Cullen Grace who does not arrive until October. Scarlets will hope he has the same impact as his fellow New Zealander Anderson.

"We've had an honest review of where we were," said Davies.

"There's been a lot of work behind the scenes, a lot of detail, and we've put a lot of new processes in place.

"We've brought in new coaches and some new players. I know they're not all available at the moment, but that will come."

With doubts over the region's long-term future as the WRU prepares to cut a men's professional side by 2028, all eyes will be on the team's performances this season.

Scarlets ready to come out fighting for future

Scarlets vow to remain at heart of west Wales

Co-captains: Ben Carter and Angus O'Brien

Key man: Ryan Woodman - The loss of number eight Aaron Wainwright to Leicester is huge but the blind-side flanker can help soften the blow. After facing Barbarians with Wales last summer, the uncapped forward can put himself in the mix for the World Cup.

Prospects: Dragons' much-improved 2025-26 has led to them setting a lofty target of being in the mix for the play-offs.

Filo Tiatia's side made the semi-finals of the Challenge Cup and had the biggest points swing in the URC, claiming 28 after the previous year's embarrassing tally of nine.

After four draws, Dragons feel that they can push into the race for the top eight.

They will at least want to avoid being Wales' lowest-ranked side - something they have been in 18 of 23 seasons - and end their 21-game losing streak against closest rivals Cardiff that goes back to 2015.

Dragons have made just three signings and only one of them, Tonga wing Anzelo Tu'itavuki, will feature in the first block of the season.

After plenty of summers of upheaval, influential centre Aneurin Owen sees the lack of change as a positive.

"It has meant we have been able to build on last season, we've not started from scratch," he said.

"Changes can be good but they can also be disruptive. We have banked all of the stuff from last season and been able to develop our game a lot more."

Dragons travel to Benetton but then play five fixtures in Wales before the break for the Nations Championship.

They have home URC derbies against Scarlets and Ospreys, a Challenge Cup opener against Perpignan, an away fixture against Ospreys at the revamped St Helen's and then a Newport fixture versus Zebre.

"Last year it felt we didn't get our season going until December when we got a win and confidence grew," said Owen.

"We need to kick on. There were some promising signs last season, especially in the cup, but we still finished 15th.

"The challenge we have set as a group is to get after it in the league and Europe, and it all starts with this first block. We can get some momentum and belief."

Tiatia in talks over new Dragons deal

Your guide to Welsh rugby's pre-season fixtures

Now for the elephant in the room.

There are four Welsh clubs to look at before the 2026-27 season, but it promises to be a crucial year as to whether that remains the case from 2028 onwards.

The WRU is pressing ahead with controversial plans to cut a professional men's side.

Cardiff and Dragons are poised to be given licences, leaving Ospreys and Scarlets fighting it out to be the team in the west.

The WRU has said the process to decide the framework for the final decision will begin in December and finish before the end of this season.

Welsh players will once again be tasked with putting uncertainty over the future to the back of their minds, a situation that could well lead to others joining the growing contingent playing in England after the loss of Wales co-captains Morgan and Lake to Gloucester.

WRU condemns abuse and doubles down on three-team plan

Davies calls for WRU board to step down

title: Charles taking record-breaking price tag in his stride
description: Fulham midfielder Shea Charles tells BBC Sport NI he does "not really think about" the price tag which saw him become Northern Ireland's most expensive footballer when he joined Premier League Fulham from Southampton.
fullText:
If Shea Charles is feeling a weight of expectation from being the most expensive Northern Ireland footballer ever his demeanour does not betray it.

Interviewed by BBC Sport NI before the forthcoming four-game Nations League bonanza, the Fulham midfielder cuts a laid-back but determined figure who is keen to play a key part in helping a young Northern Ireland side continue to build on recent progress.

Charles' record-breaking £30m move from Championship side Southampton to the Cottagers in the summer gave him the opportunity to move up a division and ply his trade in the Premier League.

He describes becoming NI's most expensive footballer as "quite crazy".

"I think I was like second or third before that. But to be number one, it's really cool. Just to be in the Premier League and just being able to play my football is amazing," he told BBC Sport NI's Stephen Watson.

"For me, I don't really think about it [the price tag] too much, and you see what a lot of people are going for these days, it's kind of crazy.

"I've just got really good people around me, living with my younger brother and my older brother, mum and dad. I've got a really good friendship group that keep me grounded."

International football, rather than the club game, will occupy the 22-year-old's attention over the coming weeks as Michael O'Neill's side face Georgia home and away, Hungary and Ukraine over the coming weeks.

Already capped 35 times since making his debut in June 2022, Charles emphasises the influence international football has had on advancing his career prospects and improving his game.

"International football has always been massive for me ever since I made my debut – the types of players you play against, the teams you are playing, you rarely got to play against them when you're playing in the Championship.

"Being able to show your level against those kind of players was always going to help.

"I feel like he [O'Neill] has really trusted me from the moment that I came in, starting me in any game that he could really, and I'm obviously very thankful for that.

"I feel like Michael has given me a bit of responsibility, especially taking the armband a couple of times, so I just try to set an example, whether that's on the pitch or off the pitch, and just be someone the young lads can look up to."

Charles has played a part in all five of Fulham's Premier League matches this season, starting in three of those, including draws against Liverpool and Manchester United in recent weeks.

Alvaro Arbeloa's side sit 19th in the table, with two draws and three defeats to date.

"Whether it was with Southampton or by getting a move the aim was always to get back to the Premier League.

"It's really exciting and I've settled in really well. It's a really good club and when I spoke to the manager we saw football in the same way.

"Against Man United it was a really good game and I thought we were unlucky not to win the game. To play in a game like that so early after my move was really good."

His brother, goalkeeper Pierce, currently on loan at Queen's Park Rangers from Manchester City after a summer switch, is also an integral part of the Northern Ireland squad.

"It's kind of the stuff of dreams to play with your brother on the international stage. When you're playing teams like France and Italy and he's playing alongside you it's really cool.

"We're really close, we played football together when we were younger, we've always been best mates."

English-born Charles qualifies to play for Northern Ireland through his mother, who follows the careers of her sons avidly.

"She is dead proud, you can see on her face when you see her in the crowd at Windsor Park in particular.

"I can tell how proud she is of us and for us both to be playing together is just incredible.

"I can't remember the last one she has missed at Windsor Park. She is there all the time. She was in Italy and she tries to get to as many away games as possible.

"I told her that when I was younger [that I would play for Northern Ireland], me and Pierce, and I've definitely followed through with that promise."

Charles feels the "potential is definitely there" for the squad "to prove how good we are".

"It's a really tight-knit group, everyone gets along. Whenever any new boys come in I always feel like they fit in so well.

"When you get the likes of Ceadach [O'Neill] and Braiden [Graham] coming in you begin to feel that little bit older. It's a really good group."

title: Will Saints reign again or new winners rise? - Prem Rugby club guide
description: BBC Sport commentators and reporters analyse how the 10 Prem Rugby clubs will fare ahead of the start of the 2026-27 season.
fullText:
Blink and it seems like a Prem Rugby season has only just finished but it has already been 97 days since 2025-26 wrapped up at Allianz Stadium, Twickenham.

A new campaign of the English top flight stretches before us, with 18 rounds of games between now and early next June, all against the backdrop of a World Cup that is just over 12 months away.

BBC Sport commentators and pundits from across England analyse what we can expect from each club when the games get under way.

Commentary of every Prem Rugby game is available on BBC local radio, via BBC Sounds or the BBC Sport website.

Key signing: Dan du Preez, number eight

Dan Albutt, BBC Radio Bristol commentator

Bath's recruitment has been low-key with only two prime additions in South African number eight Dan du Preez and Scotland prop Jamie Bhatti, so the concern for them will be the loss of big ball carriers, especially prop Thomas du Toit and back-rower Alfie Barbeary.

Replacing their impact will be tough, but Bath still have a loaded squad that will once again have Scotland fly-half Finn Russell pulling the strings.

Last season's home semi-final defeat by Exeter will still sting, but head of rugby Johann van Graan has proven to be a master of learning from bad experiences and turning them into positives.

If they can, then they should challenge for honours again, but Du Toit and Barbeary are big losses and it may make that task a lot harder.

Scotland forward Josh Bayliss may be the most underrated player in the Prem; his power and pace will be a big asset to Bath in a stacked back row.

Listen to The Scrum every Tuesday at 18:00 on BBC Radio Bristol and BBC Sounds.

Key signing: Ethan Staddon, back-row forward

Damian Derrick, BBC Points West sports reporter

Bristol Bears enter Pat Lam's 10th season with the clearly stated ambition of getting back into the top four play-off places.

Strangely for Bears, it was their attack and lack of tries that cost them last season. A second full season back in rugby union for Wales and British and Irish Lions winger Louis Rees-Zammit, along with a stated preference for the wing over full-back, should help enormously.

The continued development and influence of Bristolian prop George Kloska, now an England international, will be key. So is keeping Argentina international lock Pedro Rubiolo fit.

The depth of their squad is still a concern - particularly in the front five and at fly-half - so they'll need better luck with injuries.

Bristol's form after the mid-season Six Nations break must also improve as it's let them down over the past two seasons.

Get that right and Lam, who appears to be under little pressure, could be in a tussle for a trip to Twickenham.

Listen to The Scrum every Tuesday at 18:00 on BBC Radio Bristol and BBC Sounds.

Rees-Zammit to return to wing for new season

Bristol sign ex-Tigers lock Wells on three-month deal

Key signing: Dallas McLeod, centre

Brent Pilnick, BBC Sport, South West of England

Exeter surprised many by going from their worst-ever top flight season to beaten Prem finalists in June.

Rob Baxter's new-look coaching team has had more chance to bed in their ideas, and aside from Australia centre Len Ikitau have lost relatively few frontline players - once-capped All Black Dallas McLeod has come in to replace the Wallabies star while Exeter look strong elsewhere.

In England winger Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, the Prem's leading points scorer Henry Slade and barnstorming number eight Greg Fisilau, Exeter possess the attacking weapons to cause any defence problems, while in Wales forward Dafydd Jenkins, Australia flanker Tom Hooper and the highly-rated Kane James they have a pack that can dominate matches.

Off the field, Exeter were taken over by Premier League football side AFC Bournemouth's owners Black Knight earlier this year – that, along with the positivity around the squad from last season, has Exeter fans dreaming of a return to the success that started just over a decade ago where they became perennial title contenders.

Injured Exeter winger Ridl to miss most of season

Exeter and Cherries share expertise after takeover

Key signing: Jac Morgan, flanker

Andrew Pugh, BBC Radio Gloucestershire commentator

Gloucester have undergone considerable transition on and off the pitch and now look better placed to shake off the frequent 'serial underachievers' tag.

With Chris Boyd on board as technical director, Rob Burgess as general manager and George Skivington reverting to his preferred head coach role, the management structure looks more able to cope with the Prem's demands.

Further coaching changes have come with the arrival of Brett Deacon (forwards) and Joel Tomkins (defence).

There have been a significant number of player departures from Kingsholm, offset by the signing of the outstanding Wales international duo of Jac Morgan and Dewi Lake; with more experience added by the return of scrum-half Dan Robson and the acquisition of physical locks Joe Joyce and Jean Kleyn.

The Cherry and Whites scraped into this season's European Champions Cup, but Shedheads will probably view a top four Prem finish as the true benchmark of progress.

Key signing: George Furbank, full-back

Andrew Rowley, BBC Radio London commentator

Last season was possibly the most turbulent at Harlequins for almost 20 years, as a series of heavy defeats led to the club issuing a statement acknowledging that things had to change.

Chief executive Laurie Dalrymple and chairman David Morgan stated that "performances and results in the men's team are not at the level we expect at Harlequins and are not considered acceptable by anyone within the club".

A wholesale review followed and there have been big changes in the coaching staff, with former Crusaders and Australia coach Robbie Deans joining as performance director to work with head coach Jason Gilmore.

Rob Hunter, Brad Cooper, Sean Long and Jordan Turner-Hall are also involved alongside Adam Jones.

Supporters will be desperate to see that some of the promised cultural changes are reflected on the field before too long, as last season felt like a line in the sand.

Injured Dombrandt set for long spell on sidelines

Long and Turner-Hall take full-time roles at Quins

Key signing: Aaron Wainwright, number eight

Adam Whitty, BBC Radio Leicester sports editor

Having covered Leicester Tigers for nearly a decade, I find myself in the bizarre scenario of the club having the same head coach as the previous season. That's only happened once since 2018.

Geoff Parling has finally brought some stability to English rugby's most successful club, but more than that he has set the foundations for a bright future ahead.

Leicester play in a more attacking style, led by the recently re-signed Billy Searle, and have developed a new leadership group including England trio Ollie Chessum, Freddie Steward and Jack van Poortvliet.

There hasn't been much player churn, although England lock George Martin and South African flanker Hanro Liebenberg will be big misses in the pack.

Lock Cam Henderson and the very exciting Wales flanker Aaron Wainwright will have big roles to play – and seeing Mako Vunipola in a Tigers shirt will seem strange.

After semi-final heartbreak to Northampton last year, Tigers looked like a team with a huge ceiling that needed to learn how to handle the big moments.

I expect them to be around the play-off race again, perhaps with those experiences behind them.

Listen to the Leicester Tigers Rugby Show every Wednesday at 18:00 on BBC Radio Leicester and BBC Sounds

Vunipola planned to retire before Leicester called

Key signing: Raffi Quirke, scrum-half

Dean Gray, BBC Radio Newcastle commentator

Newcastle have finished bottom of the Prem Rugby table over the past four seasons, with the Red Bull takeover last August too late to avoid that disappointment once again.

However, 23 new players have been brought into the squad this term (with around the same number exiting). The squad includes a mix of internationals including Argentina's Franco Molina, Hoskins Sotutu of New Zealand and Scotland duo Elliot Millar Mills and George Turner, seasoned campaigners like Rusi Tuima and Sam Graham, and returnees to the fold such as Josh Hodge and Chris Harris.

A revamped coaching team is in place under head coach Dan McFarland, with former Wales fly-half Stephen Jones in charge of attack and Calum MacRae returning as defence coach.

Their challenge will be to assimilate these new players into a competitive and cohesive team environment quickly.

The club's strapline is 'A New Dawn'. Ambitions and hopes are high but tempered with a realism that evolution doesn't come overnight.

Quirke excited by 'new project' at Newcastle

Key signing: Retaining most of squad on new contracts

Graham McKechnie, BBC Radio Northampton commentator:

For the second time in three seasons, Saints start the new campaign as defending Prem champions and they'll want to make a better defence this time around.

In 2024-25 they started as reigning champions but finished a lowly eighth in the Prem table – reaching the Champions Cup final came as some consolation, but the focus this season is all about trying to win back-to-back domestic titles.

Although they lost captain George Furbank this summer, there should be more than enough experience and leadership to make up for that, with centre Fraser Dingwall rightly taking over Furbank's role.

Henry Pollock might be grabbing all the headlines but the key players for Saints last season were the likes of Tommy Freeman, Fin Smith, Alex Mitchell and Alex Coles. This is still a young squad, but they're reaching their prime.

As always, having their key players fit at the crucial stage of the season will make all the difference, but there's real belief around Franklin's Gardens that they can win the Prem again.

Listen to The Saints Show every Wednesday at 18:00 on BBC Radio Northampton and BBC Sounds.

Saints better prepared for Prem title defence - Dowson

Pollock signs new Northampton deal in excess of £400K

Key signing: Joe Marchant, centre

Adam Lanigan, BBC Sport England

Last season was a rude awakening for Sale Sharks as their run of three straight top-four finishes was emphatically ended.

The fact that they were out of play-off contention by the January break for the Six Nations was even more damning, eventually finishing 27 points behind fourth spot, leading to the question of whether the Sharks and their physical style of play had been rumbled.

To back up some of their local talent, director of rugby Alex Sanderson has recruited a wealth of experience led by ex-Northampton and England second-rower Courtney Lawes, while there are a trio of Wales recruits in the forwards with Tomas Francis, Nicky Smith and Christ Tshuinza on board.

But the most interesting signing is that of Joe Marchant. The centre returns to the Prem after three years at Stade Francais and he has his heart set on making the England squad for next year's World Cup.

To do that, he has to play well at club level where he will fill the gap left by the influential Rob du Preez.

This feels like a pivotal season for Sanderson, who maintains the support of the club's hierarchy, to show that last season was just a blip.

The north west club will expect to compete near the top again, but the first task will be to restore order at CorpAcq Stadium after a losing record there last season.

You can hear coverage of Sale Sharks in Total Sport on BBC Radio Manchester

Key signing: Tomos Williams, scrum-half

Andrew Rowley, BBC Radio London commentator

Saracens are celebrating their 150th season and will set out to try to make it a campaign to remember as they aim for more consistency and a ruthless edge.

It will certainly be memorable for long-serving hooker Jamie George, who announced that it will be his last season - he has been a cornerstone of the successful era under Mark McCall that saw the club win six Premiership titles and three European Champions Cups.

The supporters will be keen to give him a send off and will also be eagerly anticipating Brendan Venter's return as director of rugby.

The South African set the platform for so much success in the past 15 years and his determination is likely to make Saracens a formidable opponent for the rest.

Number eight Tom Willis is a notable departure but the arrivals of England lock George Martin, back-rower Alfie Barbeary and Wales scrum-half Tomos Williams should add plenty, while the talented young players such as Charlie Bracken, Tobias Elliott, Angus Hall, Toby Knight and Noah Caluori should continue their progression.

Compiled by BBC Sport England's Sophie Hurcom

title: How serious is the risk of heat death in sport?
description: BBC Sport explores the health impact of extreme heat on athletes, following the death of a Fijian rugby player in Japan in August.
fullText:
On Monday, 3 August, Fijian rugby player Saimoni Vunilagi set off from home to train with his team-mates.

After the session, he was taken to hospital. A few days later, the 26-year-old was dead.

In a statement announcing his death, Japanese second division club Kyuden Voltex said Vunilagi "displayed symptoms consistent with severe heatstroke" during the training session, adding "despite the best efforts of the medical team, he sadly passed away".

Japan, like the UK, Europe and many other parts of the world, suffered severe heatwaves this summer.

In the weeks before, the daily high was between 32 and 37C. It had been a month since the daily high was below 30C.

No formal cause of death has been publicly released, but the link suggested by the club between training in heat and Vunilagi's death has caused alarm, given the increase in global temperatures and the rising frequency of extremely hot days.

So, how serious a threat is extreme heat to athletes, what measures could help and do perceptions within sport need to change?

There have been a variety of heat-related medical incidents during sports events in 2026.

Tennis players Jakub Mensik and Ekaterina Alexandrova collapsed during matches played at more than 30C, and eight runners had to be taken to hospital during a marathon in South Korea in April at which temperatures reached 29C.

Tour de France winner Tadej Pogacar called this year's heat "dangerous" during the event, while Matthew Brennan asked "what are we doing?" after the temperature topped 40C at the Vuelta a Espana, in which he won five stages.

This summer's World Cup also featured controversial hydration breaks at every match, which Fifa insisted were introduced to aid player welfare.

Many sports - including tennis, athletics and cycling - monitor potentially dangerous levels of extreme heat using the Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT), which produces a measure for heat stress levels by assessing air temperature, humidity, wind speed, sun angle and solar radiation.

But some experts believe athletes need greater protection, or the risk of further fatalities will increase.

"We have seen an increase in the number of heat illness events in rugby and many other sports around the world in recent years," says Dr Madeleine Orr - assistant professor of sport ecology at the University of Toronto.

"People assume we've seen such extreme heat before and think, 'it was fine, we pushed through, we can do it again'.

"That's not necessarily true - the heatwaves we're experiencing today are hotter than the ones in your childhood, because heatwaves are relative to the local normal, and 'normal' levels have risen."

Though the requirements of each sport mean the impact of high temperatures can differ, there are growing calls for blanket rules to be implemented across sports which offer more cast-iron protection when things become really extreme.

"Different leagues have different policies - there needs to be more of a standardised approach so that everyone just knows what to do," says Orr.

"It's similar to lightning - most people are familiar with the idea that when there's lightning near a sports event, we take a break for 30 minutes and start once it has gone away.

"We need a similar policy on heat and we need it to apply everywhere - it's easier for people to get behind if it's universal that once we get to a certain threshold, we know what happens."

One of the big challenges with heat-related illnesses in sport is convincing athletes and their coaches to do what is best for their health.

"I've got no doubt that a lot of coaches think that heat regulation is a hindrance," says Christian Day - general secretary of the Rugby Players' Association.

"And it's a tough one for the player, isn't it? Because you don't want to be the player who puts their hand up and says they're not feeling well, or that it's too hot to train on a certain day. Players need protecting from themselves sometimes.

"It's important for team staff to have a regulatory number that they know if it hits it, there's no discussion, you just stop playing.

"It's also about educating players as to what signs to look for to identify one of their team-mates who is struggling in training."

World Rugby updated its heat and air-quality guidelines in 2025, including use of a heat stress index - a measure from 0 to 250 used to determine how dangerous hot conditions are for players, with provisions for water breaks and extended half-time periods at low levels of danger, and potentially suspending or postponing matches at the higher end of the scale.

But players spend far more time training than they do playing matches.

"If this level of heat is going to become the norm, then we need central regulation and governance as to how we help clubs manage their players and how they should react to these kind of temperatures," says Day.

"Maybe there are cases where perhaps training needs to be limited in time, or doesn't take place at all that day outdoors.

"It's not a matter of trying to call people out or produce problems. It's trying to ensure the safest possible training environment."

Pre-season can be an especially dangerous time for athletes across sports.

On 5 June 2026, the Japan Rugby Football Union (JRFU) warned clubs heatstroke was an increasing concern during the summer, and told teams safety should be the overriding priority when planning summer training camps.

Heatstroke is a sudden, dangerous health condition which occurs when the body overheats and can no longer cool itself.

This can damage the organs, cause the intestines to release toxins and potentially be fatal within little more than an hour.

Symptoms include dizziness, nausea, headache, confusion and slurring.

"Heatstroke is 100% preventable, so every single death is one too many," says Orr.

"It's not the case that athletes can handle heat better because of their fitness.

"And the bigger the body the faster it heats up, so bigger bodies are more vulnerable as well. Moving that mass around takes a lot of energy.

"So while yes, professional athletes are extraordinarily fit, that doesn't save them when the issue of concern is cooling off the body."

Amateur athletes playing for the love of the game can be at risk too.

"Whatever the elite level does, we'll see it trickle down into grassroots," says Day.

"And that's why it's crucial that the elite level of every sport sets the right example because the kids, the players of tomorrow, will absolutely copy whatever they see their heroes doing."

title: How Man City overhauled their squad from a 650,000-strong database
description: BBC Sport goes inside Manchester City's data team, who have been a key part of their rebuild over the past 18 months.
fullText:
Inside the confines of Manchester City's sophisticated data operation is a fundamental phrase its experts work towards: "What does it take to win?"

In practice, the motto is broken down into three sections: identifying players, evaluating them and assessing how the club could improve them, all with a view to enhancing the statistical probability of City winning the Premier League.

Last season, the club's data department projected they would be there or thereabouts when it came to the title race, but their metrics indicated Arsenal were favourites to be champions. They were accurate.

This time around, City prefer to keep their projections under wraps - but five wins from five Premier League games have prompted predictions from supporters and pundits they will again be the Gunners' closest challengers.

City's devotion to data is at the heart of their efforts to close the gap on Arsenal and BBC Sport has been given unprecedent access to the inner workings of the club's metrics machine as we uncover some of the secrets guiding their work - particularly regarding player recruitment and sales.

Their work is a sign of the times in the Premier League, with clubs across the top flight and beyond increasingly using data for transfers and monitoring their teams' performance.

At City, one of the fundamental aims is to reduce risk of any market transaction, be it a purchase or a sale.

The system they play in at their current club and how the manager is asking him and the team to play.

Once those four aspects are observed, City's aim is to understand not just how good the player is but how good he could become at the Etihad.

Since winning the Treble in 2023, City's squad has undergone a vast overhaul using this approach. Only four players from that historic campaign remain.

It is crucial to stress, however, that while data has made an indefinite impact on how City operate in the transfer market, the work of traditional scouts continues to be the primary gauge of whether they decide to move for a player.

"Data plays a role in our decision-making, but it is just one part of the overall picture," City sporting director Hugo Viana told BBC Sport.

"We know data cannot tell us everything about a player. It cannot fully show a person's character, mentality or behaviour.

"That is why we study data insights but focus on the expertise of our scouts and other specialists."

The prominence of data, however, has grown significantly behind the scenes at the Etihad.

Here BBC Sport can take you to the core of some of City's key transfer calls from their extensive three-year squad revamp - including the £116m signing of Elliot Anderson.

The starting point for any new signing is City's database of 650,000 footballers from around the world.

The next step is the brief: what sort of player is the club wanting to recruit.

This usually starts with a position, though that process isn't as simple as it sounds.

City, for example, categorise their full-backs into three types: those who are defensive, those who come inside, and those who play high and wide.

Once the club's data departments have the brief, filters that grade a player's overall ability are applied to whittle down the 650,000-man database to 20-50 names.

Juventus full-back Andrea Cambiaso is one player who has been on City's radar after the data highlighted him, particularly his ability to coming inside to build play in midfield.

That he is comfortable with both feet rated highly on the data, too.

In accordance with the data and the scouting reports it was decided the club would not proceed with their interest in Cambiaso in the previous window, but City's approach is likely to mean he will continue to be monitored.

The longlist of 20-50 names is cross-referenced with the scouting longlist. Generally there is a significant overlap between the players identified by data and the ones already on scouts' radar.

From there, further, more refined metrics are applied to rank and prioritise the longlist.

Scouts will then complete further diligence on the players to reduce the list to a maximum of about six players.

At this point, the club will complete deeper dives into the remaining players, including diligence on their injury record, athletic performance and behavioural habits.

The information is then collated into individual reports called acquisition packs which contain all the key metrics used to inform the decision on a player.

This includes a 'radar chart', which rates a range of specific on-field metrics.

For example, when Jeremy Doku was signed in 2023, then manager Pep Guardiola decided he wanted a winger who was direct, akin to Leroy Sane, because at the time they had Jack Grealish and Riyad Mahrez, who preferred to keep the ball and cut inside.

Among the criteria applied in City's brief were the following: making (running into) the box, pressure regains, take-on percentage and opposition-half pressure.

Doku's overall numbers ticked the boxes Guardiola was looking for, although the Belgian's 'making the box' score was among his lowest readings.

Since his arrival, Doku has improved this rating - an example City say shows how their data systems are helping to improve existing players.

There is also a 'utilisation chart' that records how often the player has been used over a three-year period, as well as a scouting grade that indicates how highly the traditional scouts rate the individual.

Each player is also awarded an overall "current impact score" - which predicts what impression he would be expected to make immediately on signing - and a "potential impact score" that projects the contribution the player could make in the future.

Perhaps the most intriguing reading on the acquisition packs is a player's "action value score". This positions them in a league table that includes City players and ones from rival clubs who play in a similar role.

Once the acquisition reports are evaluated, the list is further reduced to 2-3 players once City's valuation of the player has been factored in.

Data contributes heavily to the price range City believe a player falls in, and the valuation is never a single number.

A decision is then made on which player is the priority, though all players on the shortlist are worked on simultaneously in the event of changing circumstances, for example if a player becomes unavailable.

Indeed, being able to move according to the market is something the data team feel they have become adept at.

The sudden emergence of Yan Diomande last season led to City completing checks on him before he joined Real Madrid from RB Leipzig.

The club also paid close attention to Eduardo Camavinga's metrics in case Real decided to sell a midfielder.

Anderson was an obvious signing for a top Premier League club.

The 23-year-old had developed into a key player for Nottingham Forest. An added appeal was the fact he is English, and had cemented his position in the national team.

City fought off other top clubs, including Manchester United, to sign him.

It would seem, on the face of it, a straightforward decision.

But the way City analysed it underlines their incredibly forensic approach even when, outwardly, it might be considered they did not need to be so comprehensive given Anderson's obvious talents.

The fact they still used their algorithm and went through all their normal steps says a lot about elite football in the modern day - and also the limitations of data alone.

That is because - perhaps surprisingly - Anderson's metrics didn't necessarily catch the eye.

At the start of last season, despite emerging uncertainty over Guardiola's future, the club knew they would be in the market for at least one central midfielder come the summer.

They knew Bernardo Silva was leaving while there were doubts over the futures of Rodri and Nico Gonzalez.

There was an acknowledgement that replacing Silva and Rodri like-for-like would be virtually impossible, so they looked for a player who was equally adept at building play from either deep or high central midfield.

As last season developed, doubt also emerged over the future of Tijjani Reijnders - but Enzo Fernandez was viewed as the favoured replacement for the Dutchman.

Anderson made the initial cut from the 650,000-man database to the longlist - but was not high in that group. However, his metric readings didn't immediately scream out the "no-brainer" he ultimately became.

As City took a closer look, there was an acknowledgement Anderson's case does highlight some of the limitations of data.

Anderson did not score lots of goals for Forest, or consistently provide assists. Because, generally speaking, Forest aren't a possession team like City, his general metrics in their algorithm did not grab the attention.

With that in mind, City's data analysts had to consider that, because Anderson was generally playing closer to his own goal than he would at City, he wasn't getting the opportunities to impress in the final third of the pitch.

So they paid close attention to what he was doing at Forest and modelled his potential role in a City team that generally plays closer to the opposition's goal, dominates possession and has more elite players.

Among the criteria graded on Anderson's 'radar chart' were defensive regains, duel success, line-breaking passes, aerial-duel success and defensive errors.

With his reading for defensive errors, it was acknowledged that, because Forest were a transitional side, some were a result of the area of the pitch in which he was asked to operate.

He may, for example, have regained possession deep inside his own half but lost the ball because he had to play a longer and a riskier pass after being asked to play forward quickly.

In the same scenario at City, it is anticipated Anderson would have options to play a shorter pass with a greater success rate.

"Just because a player doesn't have the opportunity to perform a particular action on a regular basis because of the team he is playing doesn't mean he can't do it," said a source.

Anderson's data readings improved significantly as the season developed, which compelled the club's scouts to watch him on a regular basis.

He stood up very favourably against City's existing midfielders - and a list of rival players the club had identified as possible signings in that area.

The results of the diligence completed by City's data team, scouts and other experts meant that even though Anderson's price increased beyond what City believed was his true valuation, they felt the risk was low.

"Elliot Anderson is a great example of how the process works," Viana said.

"The data was positive for Elliot and gave us real confidence in his profile, but it was the insight from our scouts and wider performance team that helped us understand the player and his attributes and this proved our belief that he was the right fit for the club."

BBC Sport was also provided with fascinating insight into how data was used to sign Julian Alvarez from River Plate for £14m in 2022.

The initial recommendation came from scouts, and given Alvarez was not a player originally identified by his metrics, the data team had to take a closer look.

Because the Argentine league isn't recognised as one of the strongest globally, City's general data settings mean players will reach a natural ceiling with their readings in comparison to those playing in one of Europe's top five divisions.

So, City dug deeper into Alvarez's stats, and his impact on both the ball and River's scorelines.

The stats showed he was by far the best player in the Argentine top flight, and City believed they had enough evidence to say he would develop into a starter for a top-half club in one of Europe's top five leagues within two-and-half years.

The data model valued Alvarez between £26m and £40m. City signed him for £14m so believed they were signing an undervalued player.

Alvarez's projected value was £70m after three years. They eventually sold him to Atletico Madrid in 2024 for £81m.

The signing of Abdukodir Khusanov from Lens also provides intriguing insight into City's reliance on data.

The 22-year-old didn't initially make City's 50-man longlist, but on closer inspection they found while his output on the ball needed to improve, his physical data - for example his covering runs behind - was through the roof.

Khusanov's on-the-ball metrics, City say, have improved significantly since he signed in January 2025.

The departure of Guardiola and the arrival of Enzo Maresca is not expected to alter the club's approach significantly.

The key metrics Maresca looks for in a player are understood to be very similar to Guardiola's, with the notable difference that the Italian prefers his full-backs to be more direct.

Rooted in City's coach recruitment process is a certain team philosophy and way of playing, with any new manager expected to produce a side that is possession dominant, can press high, regain possession high up the pitch, produce quality chances and entertain.

That philosophy was designed before Guardiola's appointment, and the Spaniard produced the purest form of City's footballing ideology.

With that in mind, the change in manager has not drastically altered the way City's data department approach their work.

Maresca will continue to work closely with them as he looks to build his own dynasty - but much of the hard work in building a squad to last is complete.

Before City's Treble-winning season, the internal data indicators were such that the club knew they would soon need to overhaul a squad that had reached its peak.

Selling players such as Kevin de Bruyne, Kyle Walker, Riyad Mahrez and Ilkay Gundogan wasn't easy given their illustrious service and the fact they were still performing at a very high level.

Data, though, allows the club to spot declining trends well in advance - often two or three years - before a player is offloaded.

Those particular metrics help City identify when the right time is to sell a player is - perhaps even before the buying club have spotted a drop in performance.

And when those trends are identified, the club can plan well in advance.

From there the club decide whether to start embedding a player from the academy or enter the market to replace.

Ayyoub Bouaddi's arrival from Lille this summer is a prime example. At 18, City realise he isn't necessarily going to have a profound impact this season - but the club believe the Moroccan will be able to make a bigger contribution within two years.

After the Treble season, the recruitment remit at City was to lower the average age of the squad and build a set of players that could deliver sustained success.

But doing that at City comes with a catch. Because at City, the team are always expected to compete for trophies.

Lowering the age of a squad is one thing; doing so while continuing to win is far more complicated.

In previous years, for example, City's data systems identified former Brighton trio Moises Caicedo, Marc Cucurella and Carlos Baleba, who have been lauded as data successes.

But there was a sense at City that the development of such signings would take too long for them to make an impact on a team that has the remit of winning titles or assets that could be developed and sold for a profit.

City have successfully lowered the average age of the squad to the extent they now have the third youngest set of players in the Premier League behind Newcastle and Chelsea.

But with the signings of goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, defender Marc Guehi, and Fernandez and Anderson they have added players who can not only grow with that new generation but also already have vast experience of top-level football.

City's data indicates their current squad will not peak for another two to three years - but also projects they are likely be among the title challengers this season.

Time will tell if they are right.

title: Debbie Beard and Amanda Thorpe lost their husbands - this is their story
description: Debbie Beard and Amanda Thorpe speak to the BBC's Simon Jack at the launch of a new suicide prevention toolkit.
fullText:
Warning: This story contains discussion of suicide and information some readers may find distressing

Two women, united in grief, are meeting for the first time.

Debbie Beard lost her husband just over a year ago. Matt Beard, the former Liverpool Women manager, died in hospital on 20 September 2025. He is believed to have taken his own life, though an inquest is yet to conclude.

Amanda Thorpe's husband Graham, the former England and Surrey cricketer, took his own life in 2024. He had "spiralled into depression" after losing his job as a batting coach in 2022.

The two women, who had never met before, came together at an event launched by the Prince of Wales and the Royal Foundation to urge sport at every level to make suicide prevention part of its culture through a new nationwide toolkit.

There they spoke to the BBC's business editor Simon Jack, who was 17 when his father took his own life.

On Your Side, external is a set of resources available online that aims "to make suicide prevention as much a part of sport as warm-up, training and performance".

Amanda Thorpe has said previously she believes her husband would still be alive had he received more support from the England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) after leaving his coaching role. Following the inquest into his death, the ECB said it was "a profound tragedy" and added Thorpe's passing was a "stark reminder" of the challenges many face with mental health.

Matt Beard died a month after leaving his role as manager of Burnley Women. He had been in the post for only two months. When the inquest into his death was postponed indefinitely, Burnley said they were "aware of an ongoing legal process" and would "not be making any comment at this time".

Amanda: "Graham had been struggling for the previous year to 18 months during Covid. Graham didn't really like following rules and there were quite a few in Covid - like playing under bubble conditions. So he had been having some medication and therapy in his job. But then Graham lost his job and he didn't see it coming.

"He did pride himself with having been in the game his whole life. He just couldn't believe that he was blindsided by it.

"I think at least two other people were sacked at the same time, which does happen at the end of disastrous Ashes series.

"Also he was probably drinking too much and found the whole of the last trip in Covid very stressful. He then took a playful video at the end of the tour, when they had a few drinks with the opposition. One of the players sent it to two friends and someone unfortunately leaked it, so it was in the Sydney Morning Herald."

Simon: "Going for a few drinks with the opposition - you would think that that happens in sport all the time, but they lost?"

Amanda: "Yes. It's OK if you win but you're not allowed to have a drink if you lose. He was probably in shock. He couldn't believe it. And he was embarrassed and ashamed about this stupid video, which to me he blew way out of proportion. But he was in this tunnel where he thought he'd messed it all up. So he went into a quick and steep decline."

Simon: "During that period, what could have been done? You said that he was seeking some help. What might have made a difference, do you think?"

Amanda: "He was having therapy sessions. He had 10 sessions. There's obviously the confidentiality but I found out after he made a very serious attempt on his life, when he really hurt himself very badly, that he'd mentioned suicide. I didn't know about that at the time. Of course, I feel that if I'd known, things could have been different. And I did feel that he wasn't really getting better. It was difficult. I felt like maybe he did need more help - maybe residential but we didn't really know where to find that."

Simon: "Debbie, Matt also lost his job..."

Simon: "Were there any signs that he was struggling with mental health, and then was there a steep decline afterwards?"

Debbie: "I think there were changes in behaviour, looking back. Performance-wise the team weren't doing well so there was a lot of abuse on social media. He could never really speak his truth during media interviews of what was going on behind the scenes and he used to sound off to me at home.

"I've found out since that he had spoken to his brother quite a lot about his mental health. But whenever I would say to Matt 'how are things?', he'd be, 'I'm all right, I'm all right', because he always wanted the best for other people.

"He didn't want to concern me and the family that he was having these thoughts and that he was going through these different struggles.

"The sacking came out of the blue and there was a lot of speculation around that. He was starting to drink more than he would have done normally. In terms of his behaviour, I would say he was taking a lot of risks as well. So maybe that was the start of this with him."

Amanda: "Graham was known as a tough competitor. He was a very happy person and loved life, but it can happen to anyone. He wasn't thinking straight really because everything kind of became a vortex. And he just sort of lost the ability to be able to be grounded and think straight. Also you think you're thinking straight when you're not."

Simon: "One of the things about sport that's been discussed is that its reach is enormous. Coaches have a very intimate and closely proximate relationship with people. They can see what's going on with them - even at grassroots level. What would you encourage people to do if they see other people struggling, either in their family or in their community?"

Debbie: "It's a very difficult conversation. It's very hard. But if you're with these people day in, day out, you notice the changes in them. Matt was very intuitive with his players - he could sense things if they weren't playing right. He might have had a conversation with them just one-to-one, away from everyone else, and then make suggestions. There's an awful lot of emphasis on the physical side of someone's wellbeing, but not the mental side. That needs to be explored with people."

Simon: "It's a tough conversation to have, isn't it? Even with your nearest and dearest, let alone with someone on the team. I wonder whether Matt found it difficult when he had to sack players or drop them from the team.

Debbie: "He did. He used to come home and say: 'I've had a hard conversation today with such and such, I've had to let them go and there were tears.' And he'd say: 'I feel guilty.' He was the one who had to deliver the news. He felt tremendous guilt about letting people go."

Simon: "What did Graham's friends in the game come and say to you afterwards? You must have known them - you would have been part of that community."

Amanda: "They were really sad and really gutted. When he was really ill he was ashamed and he shut a lot of people out. So it was hard to get through to him. He would say: 'I've lost all my friends.' And I'm like: 'You haven't.' You know that's his brain. 'You haven't lost your friends at all,' I'd say. But that's how he felt. He felt very isolated."

Simon: "Did Graham have high highs and low lows? I mean, when he scored 100 against Australia or whatever? I just wonder whether he was a person of heightened emotions?"

Amanda: "He always used to say: 'Don't get too down about it... it might not be your day.' And I think if you're going to be like that, then when there are the highs you don't go overboard. He'd say it's his job but it is difficult with people scrutinising what you're doing and everything."

Simon: "What is it that you hope comes out of talking to us and what the Royal Foundation is doing?"

Debbie: "I think with the Royal Foundation, it is exposing the issue and people are going to be talking about it. But there needs to be the right support for when people need it - when they ask for that help.

"It's just making sure that toolkit is followed through and there are people that you can connect with and talk to.

"A connection with a therapist is a difficult one because it's someone you're going to be opening a box to. You want to let everything out but you need to trust that therapist. So it's making sure that there's a good connection there as well - that you feel comfortable talking about your innermost feelings."

Simon: "This is pretty raw for you. Why do you think it's important to talk to the world about this?"

Debbie: "For me and my children, we don't want another family to go through this. It is pretty raw and it's not just the grief, it's the practical side. You've lost a second income. I've still got to pay the same amount of rent, bills, etc. It is the practicality of it and you're juggling all the time - making sure the children are OK... still doing the school runs."

Simon: "You're obviously sad. Are you're angry? Determined?"

Amanda: "I'm angry at myself as well - the guilt you have. 'Why didn't I say that?' And you've got all these 'what ifs'. So all of that nonsense. And, yes - angry as well. 'Couldn't we just have done something?' But, you know, we fall. You know I'm his wife and I still didn't expect that to happen and I ask why he had to go through such a horrible thing. You wouldn't wish it on your worst enemy - and then there's the family as well - my daughters.

"My youngest went off to uni and then Emma went too. So it was just me and the geriatric dog. So it was quite hard."

Debbie: "It's going to be a long road."

Simon: "But it's a road you're both on and I think it's a road you've helped a lot of people with by talking to us."

Debbie: "We've got each other. We've met today and we are going to meet again."

Amanda: "Yes, be a force to be reckoned with! Isn't that what they say?"

Debbie: "Yeah, so I'll come down to you, you come up to me. We're part of this club that we never wanted to be in but we are going to make people listen to what we've got to say. We just want to make a change and help people and just highlight it - we never want anyone else to be in this position. We're going to go great guns aren't we?"

If you are suffering distress or despair, details of help and support are available at BBC Action Line.

title: Antonelli on 'stepping up' after 2024 crash 'stayed in my head for a very long time'
description: Championship leader Kimi Antonelli tells BBC Sport how he is "still finding my way" in F1 after a 2024 crash "stayed in my head for a very long time".
fullText:
Kimi Antonelli says he knew from the first moment he drove this year's Mercedes that he would be transformed as a Formula 1 driver in 2026.

The 20-year-old Italian, who is running away with the world championship in only his second season in F1, is reflecting on his breakthrough year in the sport in an exclusive interview with BBC Sport.

A difficult debut season last year had left external expectations of Antonelli low at the start of 2026. But on a typically damp and cold January day at Silverstone, he already sensed that something special might be on the cards.

"It was just a few laps in the wet," Antonelli says, "but I just felt better in the car, much better than I felt last year. Also the car felt well, but I just felt better mentally in the car. Less tense, more relaxed and more mature."

Last year, he says, was "not great". "I was driving very tense most of the time, I wasn't able to extract the potential out of me," he says.

"This year, it's a lot different. The mindset has been the biggest change."

Fast forward eight months and the effects of that new headspace are plain to see.

After 14 grands prix, and with either eight or nine remaining depending on the war in the Middle East, Antonelli is a massive 81 points clear of team-mate George Russell.

Not only that, but he looks so in control. Always fast, always composed, a factor in every grand prix. Everyone knows the championship is basically over, barring some kind of dramatic misfortune.

Even then, Antonelli says he is "still finding my way" in F1.

The journey Antonelli has been on in the past two years is remarkable, and he says even he is "surprised" by the extent of his progress this year.

He was comprehensively outperformed by Russell in 2025. So when it was obvious that Mercedes would start the new regulatory era with an advantage, it was the Briton who started the season as championship favourite.

Russell duly won the opening race in Australia, but Antonelli was less than three seconds behind him at the flag. This, he says, was the second moment of realisation of what might be possible.

"I had a big, big crash in FP3," Antonelli recalls. "But then thanks to the mechanics - who all throughout the season have done an incredible job, but on that specific occasion, it is a miracle - I was able to go back in the car and push again in the high speed and getting close to the limit.

"The crash, definitely it compromised a little bit qualifying and the race because we couldn't set up properly the car. I mean, the car was still very quick. But it was not easy.

"Still being able to stay close despite that, I was like, 'OK, you know, it's not going to be a walk in the park. It's going to be very tough', but I knew already that it was a different story compared to last year.

"If it would have happened last year, I wouldn't have been able to overcome that."

Antonelli's first season in F1 was haunted by an incident that happened the first time he drove on a grand prix weekend.

At the 2024 Italian Grand Prix, the day before they formally announced Antonelli was the replacement for Ferrari-bound Lewis Hamilton, Mercedes gave him an outing in first practice at Monza.

He was blindingly fast on his first flying lap - but then crashed heavily on his second.

Team principal Toto Wolff played it down at the time, saying he was well aware there would be mistakes from Antonelli as he found his feet in F1. But behind the scenes the incident had had a big impact on the young man.

"Monza stayed in my head for a very long time," Antonelli says. "I think all throughout last season, at least. Definitely that was a big thing that was kind of slowing me down.

"This memory of being afraid to do a mistake, also because going through the difficult period (in the middle of 2025), this memory was even stronger in my head, if you know what I mean.

"Because it was already a difficult period and I was like, 'If I even do a mistake or I crash, it's even worse.'

"So yeah, it's been a thing that has been bothering me a lot last year. This year I was able to just put it behind."

Doing so has involved a lot of work behind the scenes, analysing what happened in 2025, understanding what had gone well, what had not, and why, and what he could do to improve.

"The mindset going into this season, it was mainly trying to be able to extract more out of my potential," Antonelli says. "Trying to, first of all, do a better job than previous year. But as well trying to put things more together.

"The preparation that I did in pre-season was very, very intense. But it helped me a lot to arrive ready for this season.

"Plus, I did a lot of work with my mental coach. Trying to get my head right, my thoughts right on understanding the goal, and understanding that the most important thing is to be ready and to stay present in the moment.

"Not trying to think about final results or what would happen if I wouldn't achieve that. But just trying to be present and trying to do the best with what you can do in the moment."

Still, though, he admits to be "definitely surprised" at how much progress he has made.

"I knew that I was going to be better than my first year," he says. "Obviously, because I think last year, towards the end of the season, I started to put things more together, starting to extract more performance. But still, it was still not great.

"Whereas this year, it's a lot different. Also as well, with the first win, the first pole, it took a lot of weight off my shoulder."

Antonelli has blossomed. Everything seems to be coming so easily to him. If he drops back in a race, he recovers seamlessly and quickly. Overtaking moves are done quickly and decisively. There's not been a circuit on which he has lacked pace.

Russell, by contrast, has admitted to struggling and - while not trying to take anything away from Antonelli, who he is always quick to praise - has expressed his opinion that his his driving style does not suit this year's new cars.

All of which raises a key question - how much of what is happening this year is Antonelli stepping it up, and how much Russell falling back?

"That's a very difficult question," Antonelli says. "I've definitely stepped up.

"This year definitely everything is new. So it requires also a little bit of a different approach. And trying to adapt to a different car, which hasn't been easy."

His consistency this year, he says, has come from the fact he has found "a nice rhythm in the season".

"I always try to follow my routines," Antonelli says, "the way I approach the weekend. I try to approach it all the time the same.

"I'm still finding my way, but I've found a way that helps me to be consistent and also helps me to be consistently ready when I go in the car."

There are still moments when he misjudges things, though. He cites the Barcelona-Catalunya Grand Prix, just days after his outstanding win in Monaco, one of the most dominant at that storied track for years.

"Monaco was a very high moment for me in the season, and then I went to Barcelona and I was probably a bit too excited, especially over a single lap," he says.

"So I was overdriving, I was chasing the lap time and the result didn't come in qualifying. I was actually a bit far back and didn't do a good lap.

"But that's because I was trying to do a bit too much after a very high moment in my career. And then I understood that that is not the way."

The lesson was applied after his spellbinding win from 19th on the grid at Monza, his home race, a result that Wolff said "closed a cycle" from his 2024 crash.

Antonelli says: "After Monza, I reminded myself, 'Don't make the same mistake as you did after Monaco.'"

He won the Spanish Grand Prix seven days later, an eighth victory from 14 races so far this season.

Success has inevitably led to fame, and with it attention.

"Life has changed a lot," Antonelli says. "I'm not going to lie. It's been a big change, but it's nice to see so much support. Definitely, one side is very nice, but on the other side, you have to be careful. You've got to protect yourself a bit more because obviously you're more exposed."

All year, Antonelli has talked about focusing on process, about doing the best he can on every single day, not thinking about the big picture.

Now, though, for the first time, he acknowledges the title - an achievement that would make him the youngest world champion in F1 history - is on his mind.

"Yes, I thought about it," he says. "But again, thinking about it, I came always to the same conclusion that the earlier I finish all this, the better it is.

"So I've got to just keep pushing. I keep doing the best I can every race. Because, yeah, that's the way. Just not finish. And until it's done, it's not over."
